topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 1000 More or Less
topic.description: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
evidence: Given 4,562, state that 1000 more is 5,562 and 1000 less is 3,562
Explain using place value that only the thousands digit changes
Apply this skill to numbers beyond 10,000
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '1,000 more than 3,456' or '1,000 less than 7,200' in their head — knowing only the thousands digit changes?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Find 1000 more or less than a number by recognising that only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 / 3,562), extending the 10-more/100-more pattern to the next place — unless a boundary forces a roll-over (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): count in multiples and find 1000 more or less than a given number (place-value fluency).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): generalises 2.NBT.8 (±10/±100) into the thousands place; 4.NBT.1 place-value relationships.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so +1000 steps the thousands digit while others hold; connect to counting in 1000s on a number line. Contrast +10, +100, +1000 side by side so the child tracks which column responds. Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly. Demand the 'which digit changes' reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): finds 1000 more/less with no boundary, using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): does it mentally, naming the thousands digit as the one that changes. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles roll-overs (9,500+1000) and generalises to numbers beyond 10,000.
bestPractices: Extend the established pattern: +1000 steps the thousands digit, others unchanged — keep asking 'which digit?'.
Contrast +10 / +100 / +1000 side by side so the child locates the responding column.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so one digit visibly changes per operation.
Teach roll-over boundaries (9,500 + 1000) as the interesting case.
Insist on place-value reasoning, not counting on, and generalise beyond 10,000.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (thousands row)
Th|H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 1000)
0-10,000 number line with ±1000 hops
Side-by-side ±10/±100/±1000 comparison
Base-ten thousand-cubes for the concrete move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (stepping hundreds instead of thousands).
Boundary errors at 9,000s / crossing 10,000.
Counting on in smaller steps instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 1000 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, mishandling roll-over.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: find 1000 more or less than a four-digit number by recognising that normally only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 or 3,562), extending the earlier +10/+100 pattern into the next place. The key exceptions are boundary crossings: adding 1000 when the thousands digit is 9 regroups into the ten-thousands place (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500), and subtracting 1000 can remove or reduce a higher digit (1,562 − 1000 = 562; 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500). Learners should justify which digit changes, not count on in smaller steps, and generalise beyond 10,000, where crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 change the ten-thousands digit too.

activities.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
feedback: If the learner expects the hundreds or ones to change, show only the thousands digit ticking and ask them to re-state which column a thousand lives in.
If they confuse 1000 more with 100 more (e.g. answer 4,662), run +100 and +1000 side by side so the differing columns are visible.
Reinforce correct predictions by having the learner say the thousands digit aloud before and after the press.
activities.rationale: Acting on the number and watching a single column respond makes 'which digit changes' concrete and self-correcting; side-by-side comparison with +10/+100 locates the responding column. An interactive stepper is one effective medium, but a place-value chart with counters or a labelled number line can carry the same comparison.
sourceClaims: Mentally adding/subtracting a power of ten changing a single place generalises the Grade 2 ±10/±100 standard.
learnerActions: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

activities.title: The roll-over: when a place fills up
feedback: If the answer is 0,300 or stays 9,300, point out that the thousand must be carried; walk through 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
If the answer is 19,300, check that they added exactly one thousand, not ten thousand.
Treat the boundary as a short targeted rehearsal of the single roll, not a re-teach of the whole idea.
activities.rationale: Boundary cases are where place-value reasoning is genuinely tested, so making the carry explicit addresses the common 9,000s/10,000-crossing error directly.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case for more/less across places.
learnerActions: Start from a boundary number such as 9,500 or 9,300.
Press +1000 and watch the thousands digit pass 9: it rolls 9→0 while a carry moves left, opening a new ten-thousands column (9,500 → 10,500; 9,300 → 10,300).
State in words why the number gains a digit: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands.
Rehearse just the single roll in reasoning: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands, so 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — not 0,300, not 9,300, not 19,300.
Try numbers beyond 10,000 to confirm the same place-value rule continues, including crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 and 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500.
activities.intendedInsight: When the thousands digit passes 9, the 'only one digit changes' pattern has a principled exception: the place fills up and regroups into the ten-thousands place (opening a new place for 9,500 → 10,500, or raising an existing ten-thousands digit for 19,500 → 20,500); the reverse crossing happens when subtracting (10,500 − 1000 = 9,500).

activities.title: Scored fluency and boundary checks
feedback: For a plain-case slip, ask which single digit should have moved.
For a boundary slip, redirect to the single-roll rehearsal (9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands).
Note: scored practice confirms fluency but does not by itself build the conceptual 'which digit' reasoning — pair it with the stepper/chart activities.
activities.rationale: Mixed plain and boundary items discriminate between a learner who only handles the easy case and one who regroups correctly across the thousands boundary.
learnerActions: Answer fill-in items such as '1000 more than 4,562 = __' and '1000 less than 4,562 = __'.
Answer which-digit-changes questions for ordinary cases.
Tackle boundary items deliberately, e.g. 9,500 + 1000 and 9,300 + 1000, writing the full regrouped answer.
Use a slider on a 0–10,000 line to land exactly 1000 away from a given point.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, quick retrieval of 1000 more/less, including the regrouping boundary, confirms the place-value reasoning is fluent.

constraints: Demand place-value reasoning ('which digit changes, and why') rather than counting on in 1000s.
A static annotated chart is a useful reference but does not let the learner perform the transformation; pair any static image with an action (counters, stepper, or spoken prediction).

Recognition-only items (multiple choice 'which digit changes?') confirm identification but do not elicit independent construction of the answer; include fill-in and boundary items that require producing the regrouped number.
Scored quizzes assess and rehearse fluency; they do not substitute for the comparison work that builds the underlying concept.
Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly as the key case, and generalise to numbers beyond 10,000.
Timed/fluency modes are optional for securing speed, not a prerequisite for understanding.

Arithmetic check: 4,562 + 1000 = 5,562; 4,562 − 1000 = 3,562; 9,500 + 1000 = 10,500; 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — all confirmed correct as stated in the source.

The DfE claim establishes the curriculum skill/topic and underpins the overall objective, but it was removed from activity[0].sourceClaims because that activity's rationale is about the action/comparison pedagogy, not the topic itself; only the CCSS ±10/±100 generalisation claim was retained there.

probeDeeper: Which digit changes when you find 1000 more? Does any other digit move?
9,300 + 1000 — does it become a five-digit number? Why?
1000 less than 4,562 — did the hundreds/tens/ones change at all?
assess.correctAnswer: 5,562; 3,562; 10,300 — changing only the thousands digit, and rolling into a new place when it passes 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — changes the hundreds (or another digit) instead of the thousands
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the thousands column; add one thousand-block and watch only that column change (unless it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 1000 more than 4,562 comes out as 4,662 or 4,563.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to roll into a new place: 9,300 + 1000 → 0,300 or stays 9,300 or gives 19,300
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole idea — rehearse the single roll: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary case is malformed or not carried to ten-thousands.

responseLevels.gap: Adjusts the wrong place or cannot cross the thousands boundary.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1000 more/less for any number, changing only the thousands digit and regrouping into a new place when needed.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the plain case but stumbles when the thousands digit rolls past 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch the method: '1000 more than 4,562? ... 1000 less than 4,562? ... 1000 more than 9,300?' The last one crosses into the ten-thousands — watch what happens.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4,562 checks the plain case (only the thousands digit moves); 9,300 + 1000 forces a roll from 9 thousands into ten-thousands, exposing whether the child regroups or malforms the number. Watching the working shows which digit they touch.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing Large Numbers
topic.description: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
evidence: Compare two four-digit numbers using >, <, and = by examining digits from the highest place value
Order a set of numbers up to 10,000 from smallest to largest
Justify the ordering using place-value reasoning
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} put a set of four-digit numbers like 4,321, 1,876, and 9,045 in order from smallest to largest — comparing them digit by digit?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Order and compare numbers beyond 1000 with >, <, = by scanning from the highest place value down (thousands first, then hundreds, tens, ones). Directly generalises the three-digit most-significant-digit-first procedure to four digits and beyond.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'order and compare numbers beyond 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 'compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols'.
• Operational details — Reinforce the general rule 'compare the highest place first; drop to the next place only on a tie' with aligned numerals/place-value charts and number-line placement. Stress-test with same-leading-digit pairs (4,562 vs 4,526), mixed-length comparisons (987 vs 1,024) and multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005). Progress from pairs to ordering sets, using real contexts (populations, distances).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): compares four-digit numbers with different thousands. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): orders a set beyond 1000 and states the scan rule. Tier C (age 9, extending): resolves same-leading-digit, mixed-length and multi-zero cases with place-value justification.
bestPractices: Generalise the scan: compare the highest place first, descend only on a tie — identical logic, more columns.
Align numerals/charts so digits stack by place and the deciding column is visible.
Use same-leading-digit (4,562/4,526), mixed-length (987/1,024) and multi-zero (4,050/4,005) traps.
Anchor to the number line for magnitude and connect to real large-number contexts.
Progress pair → ordered set, justifying each comparison by place value.
keyRepresentations: Aligned numerals / place-value charts stacked by place
0-10,000+ number line for magnitude
>, =, < symbols (open to larger)
Ordered card rails (smallest→largest)
Real-context data (populations, distances) as numbers to order
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by number of digits incorrectly, or by the largest single digit.
Not descending to the next place on a tie (declaring equal too early).
Mishandling multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005).
Aligning numbers to the left instead of by place value (mixed lengths).
Reversing the symbol or binding it to reading order.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: order and compare numbers beyond 1000 using >, <, = by scanning from the highest place value down (thousands, then hundreds, tens, ones), descending to the next place only when a place ties. This generalises the three-digit most-significant-digit-first procedure to four digits and beyond, in line with the Year 4 objective to 'order and compare numbers beyond 1000'. Core moves: right-align numbers by place, compare the highest place first, and justify each decision by place value. Stress-test with same-leading-digit pairs (4,562 vs 4,526), mixed-length pairs (987 vs 1,024), and multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005). Progress from single comparisons to ordering whole sets using real contexts such as populations and distances.

activities.title: Place-aligned comparison bench
feedback: For 4,562 vs 4,526: thousands tie, hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 6 beats 2, so 4,562 > 4,526. The decision is made at the first differing place.

For 987 vs 1,024: once aligned by place, 1,024 reaches the thousands place and 987 does not, so 1,024 is larger. For whole numbers, more digits does mean larger because the number reaches a higher place; the error comes from left-aligning and comparing 9 with 1.
For 4,050 vs 4,005: thousands tie, hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 5 beats 0, so 4,050 > 4,005. Zeros still hold a place and must be compared in their column.
If the symbol was placed by scanning from the right or by picking the number with the biggest single digit, re-align the columns and restart from the leftmost place.
activities.rationale: Comparison beyond 1000 is a left-to-right place-value decision. Acting on aligned numbers and resolving the deciding place—with explicit attention to ties, zeros, and mixed lengths—targets the common errors of left-alignment, judging by the biggest single digit, and declaring equality too early. An optional interactive version can auto-align the two numbers into a stacked chart, animate the highest-place-first scan (pulsing 'tie — keep going' until the deciding column lights), swing the symbol toward the larger number, and offer a live 'order the set' rail plus number-line placement for magnitude; these examples make the mechanism concrete but are not required.
sourceClaims: Compare two multi-digit numbers based on the meanings of the digits in each place using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
Aligning by place value and scanning most-significant-digit-first, with mixed-length and multi-zero cases, addresses the core comparison errors.
learnerActions: Take two numbers (including different lengths like 987 and 1,024) and write or place them so the digits stack by place value, right-justified into a place-value chart.
Starting at the highest place, compare column by column; mark each tied place and move down one place only when the current place is equal.
Place a > or < symbol between the numbers based on the first place that differs, and say which place decided it; use = only if every place ties.
Work the trap pairs: 4,562 vs 4,526 (same thousands and hundreds), 4,050 vs 4,005 (multi-zero), and 987 vs 1,024 (mixed length).
Then order a set of 5 numbers from smallest to largest using real data such as city populations, justifying each neighbouring comparison by place value.
activities.intendedInsight: Once two numbers are lined up by place, the larger number is decided at the first (highest) place where they differ, not by which number has a big digit somewhere. On a tie you keep going down to the next place; if every place ties, the numbers are equal. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place.

activities.title: Number-line placement for magnitude
feedback: If 999 is placed to the right of 1,001, note that 1,001 crosses into the thousands and sits further right, so 1,001 is larger even though 999 shows big 9s.
When line positions are close (e.g. 8,901 vs 8,910), fall back to the column scan: thousands and hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 1 beats 0, so 8,910 > 8,901.
activities.rationale: Anchoring comparison to magnitude on a number line connects the symbolic rule to quantity and guards against treating comparison as a symbol game detached from size. This magnitude-anchoring link is a research-informed proposal rather than a claim backed by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Place given numbers (e.g. 8,091; 8,901; 8,910) at their approximate positions on a 0–10,000 number line.
Use the positions to read off the order from smallest to largest.
Check the line ordering against the place-value scan and resolve any disagreement by column comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering reflects magnitude on the number line, and the place-value scan should agree with where numbers sit on the line.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut the big-digit claim
feedback: A strong rebuttal: 'Line them up by place — 1,024 has a digit in the thousands and 987 does not, so 1,024 is larger. Big digits in a lower place can't beat a filled higher place.'
If the rebuttal only restates the answer, push for the reason: which place decided, and why do we start there?
activities.rationale: The skill is procedural, but a brief justification/rebuttal task reinforces place-value reasoning and is useful alongside, not instead of, hands-on comparison practice. Its efficacy over other formats is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Aligning by place value and scanning most-significant-digit-first, with mixed-length and multi-zero cases, addresses the core comparison errors.
learnerActions: Read a character's claim such as '987 > 1,024 because it has more big digits'.
Write or say a rebuttal that aligns the numbers by place and names the deciding place.
Give a second example (e.g. 999 vs 1,001) that shows why a big single digit does not make a number larger.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a comparison out loud forces the most-significant-place reasoning to the surface and exposes big-digit and left-alignment shortcuts as faulty.

activities.title: Annotated worked scan (reference)
feedback: Each 'tie' means keep going; the first place that differs fixes the answer — for example thousands equal, then hundreds decide.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-through worked example gives a clear reference for the scan. It supports understanding of the procedure but does not by itself provide varied practice, so pair it with the comparison bench and ordering tasks.
learnerActions: Step through a worked comparison where thousands are equal, then hundreds decide, noting at each step whether the place ties or decides.
Use this as a reference model before attempting fresh pairs independently.
activities.intendedInsight: The procedure is: compare highest place first, descend only on a tie, stop at the first differing place.

constraints: Right-align by place value, not to the left; left-alignment causes mixed-length errors such as judging 987 larger than 1,024.
On a tie at any place, descend to the next lower place rather than declaring the numbers equal; only if every place, including the ones, ties are the numbers equal.
Treat zeros as place-holders that must be compared in their column (4,050 vs 4,005 is decided in the tens).

Recognition-only formats (choosing a symbol from options) consolidate and assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the aligned comparison or state the deciding place; include tasks where the learner lines up numbers and justifies the order.
A worked/annotated scan is a reference scaffold, not varied practice; learners still need to compare and order fresh numbers themselves.

Interactive auto-alignment, animated scans, and live 'order the set' checking are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same learning is achievable with aligned numerals on paper and a drawn number line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS 4.NBT.2 claim and the NCETM claim are marked unverified. Treat the NCETM statement about which practices 'address the core comparison errors' as a legacy claim, not independently confirmed effectiveness evidence.

The DfE claim ('order and compare numbers beyond 1000') is a curriculum objective/topic and is reflected in the summary; it is not attached as sourceClaims support for any activity's specific teaching principle (which concerns the place-value scanning method), consistent with the number-line activity carrying [].

The legacy source asserted that a static image 'can't provide varied practice' and that magnitude ordering is 'planar' (rejecting 3D); these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to narrowly scoped scaffold limits.

Worked example arithmetic was re-checked: 4,562 vs 4,526 decided in the tens (6>2); 4,050 vs 4,005 decided in the tens (5>0); 8,091 < 8,901 < 8,910; 8,910 vs 8,901 decided in the tens (1>0). No arithmetic errors found.
The number-line magnitude-anchoring principle and the rebuttal-task efficacy are agent proposals not directly backed by any cited source claim.

probeDeeper: Which place did you compare first? Why start there?
3,472 and 3,427 have the same digits — which is bigger and how do you know?
Order 999 and 1,001 — what makes 1,001 bigger even though 9 is a big digit?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,472 > 3,427; order 8,091 < 8,901 < 8,910; comparing from the highest place value down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares digit-by-digit from the right, or by which number has a bigger digit somewhere, instead of from the highest place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Right-align the numbers in place-value columns and compare from the leftmost place, stopping at the first place that differs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3,472 vs 3,427 is judged by the ones/tens rather than the hundreds; ordering is scrambled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses digit-count carelessly, misaligning numbers of different lengths (999 vs 1,001)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line numbers up by columns; a number reaching a higher place (thousands) beats one that doesn't. Contrast 999 and 1,001.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A shorter number is called larger, or numbers aren't lined up by place before comparing.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by digit-count or a stray big digit; ordering ignores place value.
responseLevels.full: Compares from the highest differing place, orders numbers to 10,000 reliably, and justifies with place-value reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Orders clearly different numbers but errs on same-digit or different-length cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order beyond 1000. 'Put a symbol between 3,472 and 3,427. Now order these: 8,910; 8,091; 8,901. Tell me which place you looked at and why.' The 3,472/3,427 pair (same digits) forces highest-place-first reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Same-digit and near-identical numbers cannot be ordered by digit-count or first-glance size — only by scanning from the most significant differing place. Watching where the child starts (highest place) versus scanning from the right exposes the method.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Numbers to 10,000
topic.description: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
evidence: Represent a four-digit number on a place-value chart or with base-ten materials
Estimate where a number falls on a 0–10,000 number line
Match different representations of the same number (e.g. expanded form, place-value counters, numeral)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark a number like 6,400 roughly in the right place on a number line that goes from 0 to 10,000 — and explain how they decided where to put it?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (REPRESENTATIONAL). Identify, represent and estimate numbers to 10,000 across MULTIPLE representations — place-value counters, base-ten, expanded form, numeral, and crucially position on a 0-10,000 number line — and move between them. Estimation on the line makes four-digit magnitude concrete.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 read/write/compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms; number-line reasoning about magnitude.
• Operational details — Teach representations as interchangeable views of one number, with the number line as the magnitude spine: locate/estimate a four-digit number on 0-10,000 using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5000, quarters, thousands). Move both ways: given a numeral, place it; given a point, name it. Connect estimation to rounding and to reasoning about 'about how big'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): places a four-digit number roughly on a landmarked 0-10,000 line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): translates among numeral/expanded/counters and estimates position using benchmarks. Tier C (age 9, extending): estimates on a sparsely-marked line and justifies using nearest landmarks.
bestPractices: Use the 0-10,000 number line as the magnitude spine, with benchmark landmarks (5000 halfway, thousands, 2500/7500) to anchor estimation.
Treat numeral / expanded form / counters / number-line point as interchangeable views and translate in all directions.
Practise both directions on the line: place a given number, and name a marked point.
Progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.
keyRepresentations: 0-10,000 number line with benchmark landmarks (the magnitude spine)
Place-value counters and Th|H|T|O chart
Expanded form and numeral (with comma)
Base-ten thousand/hundred/ten/one pieces
Bar/strip model for proportional estimation on the line
commonMisconceptions: Placing numbers by leading digit only (putting 4,900 and 4,100 at the same spot).
Treating the number line as evenly-spaced counting rather than proportional magnitude.
Ignoring landmarks and guessing position.
Confusing representations (reading expanded form as separate numbers).
Mis-scaling: putting 5,000 not at the halfway point of 0-10,000.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, teach four-digit numbers (to 10,000) as one quantity seen through interchangeable views — numeral, expanded form, place-value counters/base-ten, and a point on a 0-10,000 number line — and have learners translate in every direction. The number line acts as the magnitude spine: estimate and place numbers using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5,000, quarters at 2,500/7,500, thousands), so four-digit magnitude becomes a felt distance rather than a string of digits. A bar/strip model can support proportional reasoning about position. Link estimation to rounding and sense-checking.

activities.title: Linked-representations estimator on a 0-10,000 line
feedback: If the marker is placed by leading digit only (6,300 near a '6' tick on a miscounted scale), reveal the true position lit against the 5,000 halfway and 7,500 three-quarter landmarks so the learner sees 6,300 sits a little past 6,000, past halfway but not yet three-quarters, about midway between 5,000 and 7,500.

When a learner bunches numbers at one end or spaces them evenly regardless of value, build the landmarks together — locate 5,000 first, then 2,500 — and let them self-adjust rather than marking it wrong; proportional sense is still forming at this age.
When one view disagrees with another, translate back and forth explicitly: point to a digit and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form, and where that moves the marker.
activities.rationale: Estimation and multi-representation can be made concrete by acting — moving a marker and seeing proportional feedback, or changing one view and watching the others recompute. Linked, recompute-on-action panels (numeral, expanded, counters, line marker), a bar/strip model, and a fading-ticks estimation game are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the essential element is the learner acting on the line and reasoning from benchmarks, which is achievable on paper too.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
The number line as a proportional magnitude model, with benchmark landmarks, is central to estimation and to number sense.
learnerActions: Work with four synced views of one number: numeral, expanded form, place-value counters (Th|H|T|O), and a draggable marker on a 0-10,000 number line.
Change any one view (e.g. add/remove counters) and watch the others, including the marker's position on the line, update to match.
Play an estimation round: a target such as 6,300 appears; drag the marker to where you think it sits, then compare with the revealed true position and your error.

Use landmark hints — find 5,000 (halfway) first, then 2,500 and 7,500 — and decide where the number falls: ask yourself 'is 6,300 past halfway? is it yet past three-quarters?' and justify your answer before checking.
Optionally use a bar/strip model alongside the line to reason about proportion (e.g. shade roughly 6,300 out of a 10,000 strip) and relate the shaded length to where the marker should sit.
As you improve, work on lines where tick marks are removed so placement must come from proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Say aloud what you found first on the line and why the number lands where it does (e.g. '6,300 is past the middle but not yet at three-quarters, about halfway between 5,000 and 7,500').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be expressed as a numeral, expanded form, and counters, and these all correspond to one proportional position on the number line; magnitude is a distance anchored by landmarks, not the leading digit alone.

activities.title: Three-view translation with a placeholder zero
feedback: If a learner drops the empty hundreds column or misplaces digits (342, 3,42, or 30,042), return to the columns and show that removing the zero slides the 3 down into the hundreds place (342), while an extra zero pushes it up into the ten-thousands place (30,042); either way its value changes. The zero holds the hundreds place open.

If the expanded form or line placement contradicts the numeral just written (e.g. writing 3,000 + 400 + 2 for 3,042), translate explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).

Probe with: 'Why is there no "+ something hundred" in the expanded form?', 'If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?', and 'How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?'
activities.rationale: A number with an internal zero forces learners to reveal whether they treat position as value. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) from one source exposes whether the views are genuinely linked or memorised separately.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Read place-value counters such as 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones and write the numeral (3,042).
Write the same number in expanded form (3,000 + 40 + 2) and explain why there is no hundreds term.
Show roughly where 3,042 sits on a 0-10,000 line — a little above the 3,000 mark, just under a third of the way along.
Translate in the reverse directions too: given a marked point, name the number; given expanded form, build the counters.
Explore what changes if a column changes: e.g. 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones gives 3,402 — and discuss how moving the counts between columns shifts the number's value and its line position.
activities.intendedInsight: Position determines value: the zero in the hundreds column is a placeholder that must be kept, and the numeral, expanded form, and line position must all agree because they describe one number.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference poster (scaffold)
feedback: Use the highlighted links to confirm or correct your own translation; for estimation, you still need to place the marker yourself to build proportional judgement.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal reference clarifies the links between the different representations of one number and is a useful reference. As an observable affordance, it shows correspondences rather than requiring the learner to estimate or construct, so independent line placement still needs separate learner action.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
learnerActions: Study one number shown simultaneously as numeral, expanded form, counters, and a point on the line.
Tap a representation to highlight the matching parts in the others and the matching line position.
Use it as a reference check after attempting a translation yourself, not as a substitute for acting on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the correspondences across representations highlighted together reinforces that they are views of one quantity.

activities.title: Quick-check items for placement and matching
feedback: For 'which point is 4,900?', if 4,900 and 4,100 are placed at the same spot (leading-digit error), re-anchor on the nearest thousand and halfway landmarks to separate them.
Use mismatches between a chosen match and the line position to prompt a re-check in both directions.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and slider items efficiently sample matching and placement across many numbers. As an observable limit, selection-based items confirm fluency but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and reasoning that the translation and estimator activities require.
sourceClaims: Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Place a given number (e.g. 6,300) on a 0-10,000 line using a slider.
Match a numeral to its expanded form and to a counter/base-ten depiction.
Choose which marked point on the line is 4,900 (distinguished from 4,100).
Supply a missing representation given one of the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent movement between representations and benchmark-based placement can be demonstrated across short, varied prompts.

constraints: Treat numeral, expanded form, counters/base-ten, and the number-line point as interchangeable views of one number and practise translating in all directions, not just one way.

Use the 0-10,000 line as the magnitude spine with benchmark landmarks (5,000 halfway, 2,500/7,500 quarters, thousands); progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning rather than counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.

The tap-to-reveal poster and selection/slider quick-checks are scaffolds and samples: they show or test correspondences but do not require the learner to construct or estimate independently; include construction and line-placement tasks for that.

Address common errors directly: placing by leading digit only, treating the line as even counting rather than proportional magnitude, ignoring landmarks, reading expanded form as separate numbers, and mis-scaling (5,000 not at the halfway point).

For the developmental error of bunching/even spacing, do not mark it wrong or drill in isolation — co-build landmarks and let the learner self-adjust, as proportional sense is still forming at ages 8-9.

Linked live-recompute panels, draggable markers, fading tick marks, landmark hints, and a bar/strip model for proportional estimation are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; the learning goal is learner action and benchmark reasoning on the line, achievable on paper too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source list marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified; the CCSS-M 4.NBT.2 and NCETM number-line claims are listed as not verified in the original row — treat their support as unconfirmed.

sourceClaims on the scaffold (poster) and quick-check activities support the representational/number-line CONTENT being shown or sampled; they do not evidence the affordance LIMITATIONS stated in those rationales, which are objective/pedagogical observations (recognition/selection does not itself elicit independent construction), not sourced findings.

The original rated open dialogue and 3D as 'poor' with rationales like 'open dialogue can't capture line placement' and 'magnitude on a line is planar'. These are reframed as narrow affordance notes (selection/discussion does not by itself elicit independent line placement) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach; no catalog ranking is asserted as a pedagogical law.

Arithmetic/representation self-audit: 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones = 3,042 = 3,000 + 40 + 2, placed just above the 3,000 mark (3,042/10,000 ≈ 0.304, a little under a third) — consistent. The variant 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 3,402. 6,300/10,000 = 0.63 — past halfway, not yet three-quarters.
The bar/strip model (an original keyRepresentation omitted from the prior candidate) has been restored as an optional proportional-estimation representation.
Error-pattern examples (342, 3,42, 30,042, and 3,000 + 400 + 2) are retained as diagnostic signs of dropping/concatenating the placeholder or detaching representations, not as correct answers.

probeDeeper: Why is there no '+ something hundred' in the expanded form?
If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?
How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?
What if the counters were 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones — how does the number change?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,042 — placed just under a third of the way along the line (a little above the 3,000 mark) — expanded as 3,000 + 40 + 2.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the empty hundreds column or concatenates the counts — writes 342, or writes 3,42 / 30042, because the zero 'has nothing so it doesn't count'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the columns: show that removing the zero slides the 3 out of the thousands place and changes its value; the zero holds the hundreds place open.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Numeral has the wrong number of digits or a missing placeholder; child cannot say why a zero is needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bunches numbers at one end of the number line or spaces them evenly regardless of value — places 3,042 near the middle or crams small-thousands together.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark it wrong or drill placement in isolation; build the line's landmarks together (find 5,000 first, then 2,500) and let the child self-adjust — the sense of proportional position is still forming.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Number-line placement ignores relative magnitude (e.g. 3,042 put at the halfway mark).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the three representations as unrelated tasks — can write the numeral but the expanded form or line does not match it (e.g. writes 3,000+400+2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Translate back and forth explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expanded form or line contradicts the numeral the child just wrote; no cross-checking.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a correct numeral from the counters; loses the placeholder or the digit order.
responseLevels.full: Produces all three consistently, uses the zero as a placeholder deliberately, places on the line by proportional reasoning, and can translate from any one representation to the others.
responseLevels.partial: Writes 3,042 correctly but one representation is detached — expanded form or line placement does not agree with the numeral, or cannot translate back.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are place-value counters: 3 in the thousands column, none in the hundreds, 4 in the tens, 2 in the ones. Write this as a number. Then show me roughly where it sits on a 0-to-10,000 number line, and write it in expanded form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The empty hundreds column forces the child to reveal whether they treat position as value: a child who understands place value writes 3,042 and holds the zero as a placeholder, while a child who reads columns as a running total writes 342 or 3,42 or 30,042. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) exposes whether they are linked or memorised separately.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Place value of each digit
topic.description: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
evidence: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number (e.g. in 7,345 the 7 represents 7 thousands)
Partition a four-digit number into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones
Compose a four-digit number from given place-value parts (e.g. 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 5,347, can they tell you the value of each digit — that the 5 means 5,000, the 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, and the 7 means 7?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones): in 7,345 the 7 is 7 thousands (7000). Partition and recompose four-digit numbers (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452). The ×10 column structure extends one more place, and the thousands separator/comma enters.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.1/4.NBT.2 generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
• Operational details — Extend the H|T|O bench to Th|H|T|O with base-ten (thousand-cube), place-value counters and arrow cards; keep build + numeral + expanded form synced. Introduce the thousands-cube as the next unitising rung (ten hundreds = one thousand) and the comma/space grouping. Attend to multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) as the key difficulty.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): states each digit's value in a four-digit number using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): partitions/recomposes any four-digit number incl. one internal zero. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles multi-zero numbers (3,006) and explains the thousands place as ten hundreds.
bestPractices: Extend the column bench to Th|H|T|O so the thousands place is 'the same ×10 idea, one more column'.
Introduce the thousand-cube as the next unitising step (ten hundred-flats = one thousand-cube), reinforcing the repeating pattern.
Keep build, numeral (with comma/space grouping) and expanded form (3000+400+50+2) synchronised.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050) — the biggest source of four-digit errors.
Use place-value counters for larger numbers where physical thousand-cubes become unwieldy, keeping the column meaning.
keyRepresentations: Th|H|T|O place-value chart with base-ten (thousand-cube/flat/rod/cube) or counters
Arrow / place-value cards (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 → 3,452)
Expanded form and numeral with thousands separator
Gattegno chart extended to the thousands row
0-10,000 number line for magnitude
commonMisconceptions: Mishandling multi-zero numbers (writing 'three thousand and six' as 3006 wrong-length, or 3,600).
Losing a placeholder in 4,050 or 7,000.
Assigning the wrong value (the 7 in 7,345 read as 7 hundreds).
Concatenation of expanded parts (3000+400+50+2 written as 3000400502).
Misplacing or ignoring the thousands comma so magnitude is misread.

learn.summary: Four-digit place value for ages 8-9: recognise the value of each digit in a four-digit number (in 7,345 the 7 is 7 thousands = 7000), partition and recompose (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452), understand that thousands extend the same ×10 column pattern one place further, and handle multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) with correct placeholders and comma/space grouping. Building and recomposing numbers in a Th|H|T|O structure is the central activity for this objective; checking-style and reference activities support but are not a substitute for construction.

activities.title: Build and recompose in the Th|H|T|O bench
feedback: When ten hundred-flats fuse into a thousand-cube, confirm: 'Ten hundreds became one thousand — the same trade as ten tens for a hundred, just one column further left (and the same as ten ones for a ten, two columns further left).'

If a learner thinks 3,452 and 3,542 are the same size because they use the same digits, rebuild both and compare: the 5 is worth 50 in one but 500 in the other, so the totals differ — the column, not the digit, sets the worth.

If a learner builds 'three thousand and six' as a wrong-length numeral, point to the empty hundreds and tens columns: 'Nothing here and nothing here — but we still write a 0 in each, so it reads 3,006, not 36 or 3,600.'
If the expanded parts get concatenated (3000400502), rebuild from blocks and arrow cards and show 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 lining up under the correct columns, then overlapping into 3,452.
When emptying a column changes the numeral, ask the learner to predict the new numeral and comma position before revealing it.
activities.rationale: Constructing numbers and recomposing them from parts, with blocks, arrow cards, numeral and expanded form kept synchronised, lets learners experience place value as a repeating structure and see placeholders arise from genuinely empty columns rather than as a rule to memorise. Swapping digits between columns surfaces the 'order doesn't matter' misconception directly. A number line adds a magnitude check that guards against comma/grouping misreads. Multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and benefit from explicit placeholder work.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
Generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form (4.NBT.1-2).
The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Extend the familiar H|T|O column bench to Th|H|T|O and assemble a number such as 3,452 using thousand-cubes, hundred-flats, ten-rods and ones.
Drag ten hundred-flats into a tray and watch them fuse into one thousand-cube, saying aloud 'ten hundreds make one thousand' — the same unitising move one column up.
Keep three things in view at once as you build: the blocks, the numeral with its comma (3,452), and the expanded form 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2.
Use arrow (place-value) cards to lay out 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2, then slide them together so they overlap into the single numeral 3,452, linking the expanded form to the compact numeral.
Place the finished number on a 0-10,000 number line to check its rough magnitude, noticing how the comma/grouping helps you read size at a glance.

Swap two digits in your built number — for example exchange the 4 and the 5 in 3,452 to make 3,542 — and compare both on the bench and on the number line to see that moving a digit into a different column changes its value and the whole number's size.
Empty one column at a time (3,452 → 3,402 → 3,002) and describe what happens to the numeral and the expanded form.

In a reverse mode, listen to or read a spoken number such as 'three thousand and six' and build it; leave the hundreds AND tens columns empty so two bold placeholder 0s appear and the numeral resolves to 3,006 (not 36 or 3,600).
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is set by its column, not by the digit itself — so swapping digits between columns changes the number; thousands repeat the ×10 pattern (ten hundreds = one thousand); and empty columns must still be written as 0 so magnitude and the comma are correct.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number decoded
feedback: If a learner reads the 7 in 7,345 as 7 hundreds, point to its column position and count from the ones: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
For 3,006, confirm that the two 0s mark empty hundreds and tens so the 3 stays in the thousands column.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example gives a stable visual anchor and a quick reference for digit values and the hardest multi-zero case. It cannot build arbitrary numbers, so it supports rather than substitutes for hands-on construction.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Study a single four-digit number displayed in a Th|H|T|O chart and tap each digit to reveal its blocks and its value (the 7 in 7,345 → 7 thousands = 7000).
Open a dedicated 3,006 anchor and use a flap or note that explains why the two internal zeros must both be written.
Use this wall as a lookup reference while working on other construction tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's value can be read directly from its column, and internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column's place.

activities.title: Check digit values and expanded form
feedback: For 4,050 = 4000 + ___ + 50 + ___, confirm the hundreds blank is 0 and the ones blank is 0 — the empty columns still count.

If 'three thousand and six' is read as 3,600 (or 36), contrast the candidate forms digit by digit in a column chart to show where each digit sits, making clear that only 3,006 keeps the 3 in the thousands column with 0s holding the empty hundreds and tens.
activities.rationale: Targeted checking items confirm that value-of-digit, expanded-form and multi-zero knowledge is secure. These items use recognition responses: they assess and reinforce but do not themselves elicit independent construction of a number from parts, so they are best used after construction work.
sourceClaims: Generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form (4.NBT.1-2).
learnerActions: Answer 'value of the digit' questions, e.g. state the value of the 7 in 7,345 (7000, not 7 or 700).
Complete fill-in-the-blank expanded forms: 3,452 = 3000 + ___ + 50 + 2 (blank is 400); 4,050 = 4000 + ___ + 50 + ___ (both blanks are 0).
Match numerals to their expanded forms and spoken number names.
For 'three thousand and six', identify the correct written form 3,006 and explain why the incorrect forms 36 and 3,600 must be rejected.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably read off a digit's value by its place and write/complete expanded forms, including where a column is zero.

activities.title: Spot the place-value detective's mistake
feedback: When the learner corrects the character, prompt them to point to the specific empty columns that need a 0.
Ask the learner to generate a second tricky number (e.g. 7,000 or 4,050) and explain its zeros.
activities.rationale: Explaining and correcting a worked error prompts learners to verbalise the placeholder principle. Because it elicits explanation and checking rather than building the column structure with blocks, it works best alongside hands-on construction rather than as the main route.
sourceClaims: The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Work with a character who keeps mis-sizing numbers such as 3,006 (writing 36 or 3,600).
Explain, using a column chart, why the character is wrong and correct the number together.
Say back the rule in your own words: empty hundreds and tens still need a 0 so the thousands digit keeps its place.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a multi-zero number must be written a particular way deepens understanding of placeholders.

constraints: Multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) are the main source of four-digit errors and should be prioritised, with explicit placeholder work.

Keep build, numeral (with comma/space grouping) and expanded form synchronised so learners connect the three representations; arrow cards and a number line are useful extra links to the numeral and to magnitude.
The reference-wall and checking activities assess or anchor understanding but do not let learners construct arbitrary numbers; use them to support, not replace, hands-on building and recomposition.
Checking/matching items use recognition responses and do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a number from parts.
Use place-value counters for larger numbers where physical thousand-cubes become unwieldy, while keeping the column meaning explicit.

Address common slips directly: reading a digit off the wrong column, concatenating expanded parts (3000400502), losing a placeholder, misplacing or ignoring the thousands comma, and assuming digit order doesn't matter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' and argued a 3D thousand-cube 'doesn't make the idea spatial'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been treated as a design preference, not asserted as a universal law. Base-ten blocks (physical cubes or on-screen models) can each support the concept.

The auto-fuse and placeholder-snap interactions are retained as concrete, optional mechanisms that make the unitising and placeholder ideas visible; they are not the only way to teach this and should not be read as mandatory.
The CCSS and NCETM source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; confidence should not be upgraded on migration.

The source assessment's digit-swap / order-matters comparison (value of the 5 in 3,452 vs 3,542; whether swapping the 4 and 5 changes size) and the 'digit order doesn't matter' misconception have now been incorporated into Activity 1's construction and feedback; a further comparison/ordering extension could still be added.
The Gattegno chart extended to the thousands row was not carried into the activities; it remains an available alternative representation for displaying the repeating ×10 row structure.

probeDeeper: What is the value of the 3 in 3,452 — and why is it so much more than the 4?
Build 3,452 for me from thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
If I swap the 4 and the 5, does the number get bigger or smaller? Why?
Which is worth more, the 5 in 3,452 or the 5 in 3,542?
assess.correctAnswer: In 3,452 the 4 is worth 4 hundreds (400). In 3,542 the same digit 4 is worth 4 tens (40). The value changes because the digit's place — not the digit itself — determines its worth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'the 4 is just 4', the same in both numbers, ignoring its column.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition 3,452 with base-ten blocks or a place-value chart; show the 4 as four hundred-flats, then move it to the tens column to see its worth become 40.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child states the value as the bare digit and says it does not change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads value off the wrong column — names the 4 in 3,452 as 4 tens rather than 4 hundreds.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label the four columns (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and point to where the 4 sits; count from the ones rather than guessing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct idea that place matters, but the column is miscounted by one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digit order doesn't matter — thinks 3,452 and 3,542 are the same size because they use the same digits.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compose both from place-value parts (3000+400+50+2 vs 3000+500+40+2) and compare totals to show swapping columns changes the number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the value is unchanged AND the two numbers are equal.

responseLevels.gap: Gives the digit's face value and denies it can change across positions.
responseLevels.full: States each digit's value by its place, explains that position (not the digit) sets the worth, and predicts how swapping digits changes the number.
responseLevels.partial: Knows position matters and can partition, but miscounts a column or is unsure why swapping digits changes the number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the number 3,452, what is the value of the 4? Would that value change if I wrote 3,542 instead? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands place value says the 4 is worth 400 here but 40 there, and grounds it in position. A child on face value says '4' or '400' in both and insists it can't change; asking whether it changes across the two numbers forces the positional idea into the open.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Place Value Problem-Solving
topic.description: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
evidence: Solve a problem requiring rounding, comparing, or ordering numbers beyond 1000
Apply place-value knowledge in a practical context (e.g. population figures, distances)
Explain the strategy used, referencing place-value understanding
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked 'what is the largest 4-digit even number you can make from the digits 3, 7, 1, and 8?', can they work through it systematically and give you an answer?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large numbers — rounding, comparing, ordering, and interpreting real figures (populations, distances, prices) — choosing and justifying a place-value strategy. Applying, not learning, the four-digit toolkit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 10,000] and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding to assess reasonableness, and multi-step contexts.
• Operational details — Pose rich, often multi-step and real-context problems that reward rounding for estimation, comparing/ordering, and flexible partitioning. Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require an explanation of WHY the chosen strategy fits. Emphasise using rounding to check reasonableness and choosing the right degree of accuracy.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): solves a one-step problem (round/compare) with a model. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): solves multi-step place-value problems in context and explains the strategy. Tier C (age 9, extending): selects appropriate accuracy, uses rounding to justify reasonableness, and reasons flexibly with large numbers.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, often multi-step problems (populations, distances, money) that genuinely reward place-value strategies.
Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require justification of the chosen strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and to check the reasonableness of answers.
Teach choosing an appropriate degree of accuracy for the context.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) so strategy selection becomes deliberate.
keyRepresentations: Number line (comparison, rounding, estimation)
Bar model for multi-step problem structure
Place-value chart / counters
Real data sets (populations, distances) as problem material
Estimation/benchmark reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a memorised procedure without checking it fits the problem.
Rounding at the wrong stage or to an unhelpful accuracy.
Comparing/ordering errors carried into problem contexts (multi-zero, mixed length).
Not sense-checking an answer against an estimate.
Losing place-value meaning when numbers get large or contextual.

learn.summary: Ages 8-9 applied place-value problem-solving: children choose and justify a place-value strategy (rounding, comparing, ordering, flexible partitioning) to solve rich, multi-step, real-context problems with increasingly large numbers (populations, distances, prices). This is a META topic — the learning target is deliberate strategy selection and using rounding to check reasonableness, not first-time acquisition of the four-digit toolkit.

activities.title: The large-number problem studio
feedback: Name the strategy the child used ('you ordered first, then rounded to estimate') so the choice becomes explicit and reusable.
After the exact answer, show it next to the child's estimate and ask whether the estimate was close enough for the purpose — reinforcing estimation as a reasonableness check.
If the child reached for a procedure that didn't fit, prompt: 'What is the problem actually asking you to find — a comparison, an order, or an estimate?'
activities.rationale: A META problem-solving objective is served by giving children the full toolkit and making them select among tools, so strategy choice and justification are rehearsed rather than a single procedure drilled. Modelling with number lines, bar models and charts and requiring justification reflects recommended place-value pedagogy.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Read a real-context problem such as: four cities have populations 53,847, 48,206, 51,330 and 49,975 — order them from largest to smallest and estimate the total.

Choose which place-value tool fits the task before computing: a number line (for rounding/estimating), an ordering rail (for comparing/ordering), a bar model (for multi-step structure) or a place-value chart (for partitioning).
Act with the chosen tool — e.g. place each population on the ordering rail, then round each to the nearest thousand on the number line and add the rounded values to estimate the total.
State aloud or in writing WHY that tool fit this problem, referencing place value.
Compute the exact answer and compare it against your rounded estimate to check reasonableness.
activities.intendedInsight: The right place-value move depends on what the problem asks; rounding gives a fast estimate that you can use to sense-check an exact answer.

activities.title: Mixed problem set with strategy matching
feedback: For a wrong 'best estimate' choice, place the candidate estimates and the exact figure on a number line to show which is nearer.
For comparison/ordering slips, draw attention to digit place (especially multi-zero numbers and numbers of mixed length).
Confirm when an estimate correctly predicted the size of the exact answer.
activities.rationale: Assessment-style items give varied practice and surface strategy-selection and comparison errors, though a fixed item set scaffolds strategy choice less richly than an open toolkit bench — so it works best as practice alongside the studio.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Work through varied items: multi-step word problems, 'which is larger / best estimate' choices, estimate-then-check tasks, and fill-in-the-blank computations.
For each item, match the problem to the place-value strategy that fits it (round, compare, order, partition) before solving.
Estimate first using rounding, then compute and confirm the estimate was reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Different problem shapes call for different place-value moves; recognising the shape is the first step to solving it.

activities.title: 'How did you decide?' strategy dialogue
feedback: Probe with: 'How did you decide what amount to round to for this puzzle?'
Probe with: 'When would you actually need the exact figure rather than a rounded estimate?'
Probe with: 'Would "about 30" be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? When might that be fine, and when would you need the exact 27 — for example, when handing out one book each?'
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning externalises reasoning and elicits justification, which suits a META topic focused on metacognitive strategy choice; it supplements rather than replaces varied practice.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a real-figure puzzle posed by a partner or teacher (e.g. 'about how many people live in these two towns together?').
Explain which place-value move you chose and why — did you round, compare, or order, and to what accuracy?
Answer probing follow-ups about your choice of accuracy.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a strategy out loud makes strategy selection deliberate and reveals whether the degree of rounding fits the purpose.

activities.title: Diagnostic: is 'about 54,000' fair?
feedback: If the child rejects 'about 54,000' only because it isn't 53,847: discuss why headlines round — the estimate carries the useful information; contrast a bill (exactness matters) with a crowd (it doesn't).

If the child treats all roundings as equally good: compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line so the child can see that the nearest-thousand estimate (54,000) is much closer than the nearest-ten-thousand estimate (50,000). Then discuss that both are correct roundings, and which is more useful depends on the purpose.
This probe surfaces reasoning — use it to understand the child's stance on approximation rather than to grade a single calculation.
activities.rationale: The key judgement underlying large-number problem-solving is whether only exact figures count or whether a sensibly-rounded number is valid and purpose-fit; this open probe surfaces that stance and the common myth that rounding is 'cheating'.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Consider: a news report says a football crowd was 'about 54,000'; the exact number counted was 53,847.
Decide whether 'about 54,000' is a fair thing to report or wrong because it isn't exact, and explain how you'd decide when a rounded number is good enough.
Compare candidate estimates against 53,847 — is 'about 54,000' closer than 'about 50,000'? Which would be more useful for a news report, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A sensibly rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer; how much to round depends on the purpose of the number, and closeness can be judged on a number line.

constraints: This is applying the four-digit place-value toolkit, not first teaching it; learners should already round, compare, order and partition four-digit numbers before this work.

Choice/estimate items and fill-in-the-blank practice assess and rehearse strategy recognition but do not by themselves require the child to select a strategy from an open field — pair recognition tasks with open problems where the child must choose the tool.
The diagnostic probe is not scored; it is meant to surface the child's reasoning about approximation, not produce a mark.
Degree of rounding must be tied to purpose: an estimate fit for a crowd figure is not fit for a bill or a small exact count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked example: 53,847→54,000, 48,206→48,000, 51,330→51,000, 49,975→50,000 to the nearest thousand; rounded sum ≈ 203,000; exact sum = 203,358 — consistent, so the estimate is a reasonable check. Ordering 53,847 > 51,330 > 49,975 > 48,206 is correct. (Example figures beyond the original crowd number were added to make the studio task concrete; flag if a different data set is preferred.)

The original 'about 54,000' is the nearest-thousand rounding of 53,847, which is correct; the contrast 'about 50,000' is deliberately a less-close candidate used diagnostically, not an error, and is never presented to the child as a valid answer.

Editor fix (second pass): Activity 3's third probe still cited 'about 54,000', a figure belonging to the Activity 4 crowd diagnostic and absent from the figure-free two-towns dialogue; it was rewritten to ask generically about rounding a small exact count (27 children) so the scenario stays coherent. A previous pass had fixed the parallel exact-figure probe but missed this one.

Source claims for CCSS-M and NCETM were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as confirmed. The DfE Year 4 claim was marked verified in the legacy row but has not been re-checked here.

Legacy artefact rankings and the 'no spatial payoff' dismissal of 3D were removed as catalog ranking rather than established pedagogy; the underlying pedagogical ideas (toolkit bench, varied quiz practice, Socratic dialogue, worked-example reference) are preserved as distinct activities, with medium limitations stated as scoped rather than universal.

probeDeeper: Is 'about 54,000' closer to the real crowd than 'about 50,000'? Which is fairer?
When would you actually NEED the exact 53,847?
How did you decide the nearest thousand was the right amount to round to?
Would 'about 54,000' be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response accepts that rounding is legitimate and useful, that 'about 54,000' fairly stands for 53,847 (nearest thousand), and that HOW MUCH to round depends on the purpose of the number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes only the exact number is ever correct — rounding is 'wrong' or 'cheating'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why headlines round: the estimate carries the useful information. Contrast contexts where exactness matters (a bill) with where it doesn't (a crowd).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rejects 'about 54,000' purely because it isn't 53,847.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts any rounding without judging closeness — 'about 50,000' seems just as fine as 'about 54,000'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line; the nearest-thousand estimate is the fair one. Tie the degree of rounding to the purpose.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats all roundings as equally good, ignoring which is nearer.

responseLevels.gap: Treats only the exact figure as correct, or accepts any rounding without judging closeness.
responseLevels.full: Judges a rounded number as fair or not by its closeness and by the purpose, and explains the choice using place value.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts rounding as valid but cannot yet justify how much to round for a given purpose.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A news report says a football crowd was “about 54,000”. The exact number counted was 53,847. Is “about 54,000” a fair thing to report, or is it wrong because it isn't the exact number? How would you decide when a rounded number is good enough?' Surface the reasoning — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe surfaces the child's stance on approximation: whether only exact figures count as 'right', or whether a sensibly-rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer. That judgement — not a single calculation — is what place-value problem-solving with large numbers rests on.
