topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Reading and writing numbers (age 9+)
topic.description: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
evidence: Write 403,072 in words and in expanded form
Compare 548,301 and 543,801 using < and explain the reasoning
Order four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers into the millions — like 1,340,000 — and put a set of large numbers in order correctly?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Read, write, order and compare whole numbers to at least 1,000,000 in numerals, number names, expanded form and via place value — e.g. write 403,072 in words/expanded form; compare 548,301 and 543,801. The system now spans six digits and the thousands-grouping (comma every three places) becomes essential to reading magnitude.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 read/write/compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (Grade 4 to 1,000,000).
• Operational details — Extend the place-value chart to six columns grouped in threes (thousands | ones periods); teach reading by GROUPS ('four hundred and three thousand, and seventy-two') rather than digit by digit. Keep numeral/words/expanded synced. Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) and comparison by highest-place scan. Ground large numbers in real contexts (populations, distances) so the magnitudes mean something.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): reads/writes six-digit numbers with clear groups, no awkward zeros. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): translates among registers incl. multi-zero (403,072) and compares/orders six-digit numbers. Tier C (age 10, extending): reads/writes tricky zero-laden numbers fluently and justifies ordering by place value.
bestPractices: Teach reading by three-digit GROUPS (thousands period, ones period), using the comma as the group marker, not digit-by-digit.
Extend the six-column place-value chart and keep numeral / words / expanded form synchronised.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) — the dominant error source at six digits.
Compare/order using the highest-place-first scan generalised to six digits, aligning by place.
Anchor to real large-number contexts (city populations, distances) for meaning.
keyRepresentations: Six-column place-value chart grouped in threes (periods)
Numeral with comma grouping | number name | expanded form
Place-value counters / Gattegno chart to millions
0-1,000,000 number line for magnitude
Real data (populations) as reading/ordering material
commonMisconceptions: Reading digit-by-digit instead of by groups (misreading 403,072).
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (403,072 → 43,072 or 4,372).
Misplacing the thousands comma so the group boundary and magnitude are wrong.
Ordering by digit count or left-alignment rather than place value.
Saying 'and' in the wrong place / mangling the thousands word.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: read, write, order and compare whole numbers to at least 1,000,000 across numerals, number names and expanded form, determining each digit's value. The central skill is reading by three-digit GROUPS (periods) using the comma as a group marker, with special attention to placeholder zeros (403,072; 500,006) and to comparing by scanning from the highest place first. Large numbers should be grounded in real contexts (populations, distances) so magnitudes carry meaning.

activities.title: Periods-based number translator to a million
feedback: If 403,072 is read as 'forty-three thousand...', the ten-thousands column was skipped: point to that empty column and say its 0 holds the place so the number is four hundred AND three thousand.
If 'four hundred thousand and seven' is written 400,700 or 4,000,007, rebuild it period by period (400 | 007) and count that each period has exactly three digits.
Dictating zero-heavy numbers and asking the learner to place the placeholder 0 themselves surfaces the empty-column error directly.
When forms are linked, changing the numeral should make the words and expanded form update; a mismatch shows a group or zero was read wrongly.
activities.rationale: Acting on a grouped place-value chart where registers stay synchronised lets group-reading and placeholder-zero placement become visible and self-correcting; a live highlight of the active period models reading by chunks. Optional interactions (highlighting the period being read, dictation mode, speaking a chunk aloud, a number-line context) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
Reading large numbers by three-digit periods and explicit multi-zero work reduce reading/writing errors.
learnerActions: Build a six-column place-value chart split by a comma into a thousands period and a ones period (e.g. 403 | 072), and add a millions column when showing 1,000,000, which needs seven digits.

Enter or read a number and keep three linked forms in sync: the grouped numeral (403,072), the number name ('four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two') and expanded form (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2).
Read the number by chunks, one period at a time, rather than reciting single digits.
Work deliberately on zero-heavy numbers: write 500,006; write 'four hundred thousand and seven' as a numeral (400,007); read 403,072 aloud.
Place each number on a 0-1,000,000 number line and tie it to a real quantity such as a city's population.
activities.intendedInsight: A six-digit number is read and built as two three-digit groups; internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column empty, and that empty column still needs its 0 so the magnitude stays correct.

activities.title: Compare and order six-digit numbers from the highest place
feedback: If 543,801 is called larger because 801 > 301, redirect to the first place that differs when scanning from the left: the thousands place decides it (8 > 3).

If ordering is done by the first digit alone, or numbers with different digit counts are compared by lining up their left ends, align the numbers by place value (right-aligned) and compare column by column from the highest place until a difference appears. Comparing digit counts first is valid for whole numbers: more digits means larger.
Reading each number aloud by periods first helps confirm which place is which before comparing.
activities.rationale: Highest-place-first comparison generalises the standard place-value comparison to six digits; using pairs that differ only in a middle place prevents learners from relying on the first or last digit.
sourceClaims: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
Year 5 pupils should 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
learnerActions: Compare pairs such as 548,301 and 543,801, aligning them by place and scanning from the highest place first.
State which single place decides the comparison and stop there (here the thousands digit: 8 > 3, so 548,301 > 543,801).
Order a set of four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest, justifying each step by place value.
Include pairs that differ only in a middle place so the deciding digit is not at either end.
activities.intendedInsight: When numbers are aligned by place value (right-aligned), magnitude is decided by the highest place at which two numbers differ, not by left-alignment, the first digit alone, or the final digits. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, a number with more digits is always larger (100,000 > 99,999), and this is the same rule applied to an extra highest place.

activities.title: Expanded form by place value, not face value
feedback: If a tens digit is expanded as 7 instead of 70, name its place aloud and add the parts: 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2 rebuilds to 403,009, not 403,072.
Always sum the expanded parts to confirm they reconstruct the original numeral.
activities.rationale: Explicitly adding expanded parts back to check reconstruction catches face-value errors that are invisible when expansion is treated as mere copying of digits.
sourceClaims: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
learnerActions: Decompose a six-digit number into place-value parts, naming each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70', not '7').
Rebuild the number by adding the parts back and check it matches the original numeral.
Compare a correct expansion (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2) with a face-value error (400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2) and explain which digit is wrong and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's contribution equals its face value times its place value; dropping the place multiplier changes the number.

activities.title: Read big numbers aloud in a real context
feedback: If the spoken reading is correct but the written numeral drops a zero, compare the two period-by-period to find the missing placeholder.

If your class's naming convention uses 'and' (as in 'four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'), say it only within a period's value, not as a substitute for a missing group. Many US curricula leave 'and' out of whole-number names, so follow the convention your materials use.
activities.rationale: Oral reading has a genuine spoken element; pairing it with written capture elicits production in both registers rather than recognition alone, so the placeholder-zero skill is actually written and practised.
sourceClaims: Reading large numbers by three-digit periods and explicit multi-zero work reduce reading/writing errors.
learnerActions: Hear or read a real large quantity (a city's population, a distance) and read the numeral back aloud by periods.
Then write the numeral you heard, placing any internal zeros as placeholders.
Discuss what the number means at that magnitude using the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent oral reading by groups and accurate written capture of the same number reinforce each other, and real contexts make the magnitude meaningful.

constraints: Reading-aloud alone does not capture written numerals; pair oral work with written production so placeholder zeros are actually practised.
A fixed reference display showing one number across all registers is a useful anchor, but two-way production (building and writing numbers) needs an input surface, not just a picture.

This is a notation and language task with no inherent spatial content, so a 3D/depth representation offers no specific advantage for THIS objective (an objective limit here, not a general claim that 3D cannot teach).
Recognition exercises (e.g. pairing a numeral with its number name) check translation but do not by themselves elicit independent writing of a numeral from dictation; include construction tasks.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) and middle-place comparisons, since these are common error sources at six digits.
Teach reading by three-digit groups with the comma as the group marker, not digit-by-digit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The CCSS-M 4.NBT.2 and NCETM claims are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Evidence strength was not independently confirmed here.

Self-audit: the source's 'correctAnswer' expands 403,072 as 400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2 (correct). The face-value error example in assess, 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2, reconstructs to 403,009; it is retained only as a deliberate non-example, never as correct guidance.

probeDeeper: How do you group 403,072 to read it aloud?
Which single place decides between 548,301 and 543,801?
Write 'four hundred thousand and seven' — where do the zeros go and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 'Four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'; 400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2; 548,301 > 543,801 (decided at the thousands digit, 8 vs 3); 400,007.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads/writes ignoring placeholder zeros or period grouping: 403,072 read as 'forty-three thousand...', or 'four hundred thousand and seven' written 400,700 / 4,000,007
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group digits into three-digit periods (thousands | ones) and read period by period; use a place-value chart so each zero holds its column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The numeral has the wrong number of digits or the zeros land in the wrong places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form uses face value not place value: 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2 (tens digit as 7)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70') and add the parts back to check they rebuild the number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A digit is expanded without its place multiplier.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the wrong end: judges 548,301 vs 543,801 by the later digits (301 vs 801)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare from the highest place; stop at the first differing place (thousands: 8 > 3).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 543,801 is called larger because 801 > 301.

responseLevels.gap: Loses placeholder zeros, expands by face value, or compares from the wrong end.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded), orders and compares numbers to 1,000,000 using period grouping and highest-place-first reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Handles numbers without awkward zeros but slips on placeholders or on comparisons that turn on a middle place.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Read 403,072 aloud, then write it in expanded form. Now compare 548,301 and 543,801 with < or >. Then write “four hundred thousand and seven” as a numeral.' Watch the placeholder zeros and which place the comparison turns on.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 403,072 and 'four hundred thousand and seven' both hinge on placeholder zeros, exposing period-reading and concatenation errors; the comparison 548,301/543,801 differs only at the thousands place, so a child scanning from the wrong end picks wrongly.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Place Value × 10 Pattern
topic.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
evidence: Explain that the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300
Complete: 700 ÷ 70 = __ and explain using place-value reasoning
State how many times greater the value of the 5 in 50,000 is than the 5 in 5,000
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 700, the 7 is worth 10 times more than in 70 — because moving one place to the left multiplies the value by 10?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place is worth TEN TIMES what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the place to its left): the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. This names the multiplicative ×10 structure that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): place value work where pupils recognise the value of each digit and the relationships between places (×10 between adjacent columns).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.1 'a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right'; 5.NBT.1 extends to 1/10 to the left.
• Operational details — Make explicit the multiplicative relationship between adjacent columns using a Gattegno/place-value chart: sliding a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10; one column right divides by 10. Contrast with the ADDITIVE view (partitioning) so children hold both: 3,452 is 3000+400+50+2 AND each place is ×10 the next. Use division sentences (700÷70=10) to expose the relationship.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): states the 3 in 3,000 is worth more than in 300 and by how much with support. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): explains any digit is ×10 the place to its right and computes 700÷70. Tier C (age 10, extending): quantifies 'how many times greater' across non-adjacent places (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000) and links to ×/÷ by powers of 10.
bestPractices: Use a Gattegno / place-value chart: sliding a digit left ×10s its value, right ÷10s it — make the multiplicative move physical.
Hold the additive (partition) and multiplicative (×10 between places) views together so place value is understood both ways.
Expose the relationship with division/multiplication sentences (700 ÷ 70 = 10; 30 = 3 × 10).
Compare the same digit across places ('how many times greater is the 5 in 50,000 than in 5,000?').
Bridge to multiplying/dividing by 10/100/1000 so the pattern has calculation payoff.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno place-value chart (rows scale ×10 down each column)
Place-value chart with a digit sliding between columns
Base-ten pieces showing ten-of-one-unit = one-of-next
Multiplication/division sentences (×10, ÷10) between places
Arrow-card / expanded form as the additive counterpart
commonMisconceptions: Seeing place value only additively and missing the ×10 relationship between places.
Thinking the 3 in 3,000 is '10 more' than in 300 rather than 10 times.
Confusing 'ten times' with 'add a zero' as a meaningless trick (fails for decimals later).
Miscounting the factor across non-adjacent places (×10 vs ×100).
Not connecting 700÷70=10 to the adjacent-place relationship.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: pupils recognise that in a multi-digit whole number a digit in one place is worth ten times what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left). The 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. The aim is to name the multiplicative ×10 structure between adjacent places that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten', and to hold it alongside the additive (partition) view. A central scaffold is a place-value / Gattegno chart where moving a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10 and one column right divides it by 10; a static or paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose.

activities.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
feedback: If a learner says the move 'adds a zero', agree the written numeral gains a zero (for whole numbers) but ask WHY: push for 'because its value became ten times bigger' so the idea still works for decimals later, where 'add a zero' breaks down.
If a learner says 3,000 is '10 more' than 300, build 300 with place-value counters and stack it ten times to reach 3,000, showing it is ten lots of 300, i.e. ten TIMES, not ten more.

Confirm correct answers by having the learner read both numbers aloud with place names (three hundred vs three thousand) so the VALUE, not just the digit, is heard — this also counters 'they're the same, both are 3'.
activities.rationale: Making the ×10/÷10 move physical on a chart turns an abstract multiplicative fact into an observable action and directly contrasts with the 'add a zero' trick. An interactive chart that recomputes the value live as the digit moves (e.g. a '×10' tag flashing on the leftward move) may make the relationship vivid; a static annotated chart or a paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose with the learner stating the change.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
activities.intendedInsight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.

activities.title: How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts
feedback: If a learner answers 'ten times' for a two-shift gap (50,000 vs 500), have them slide the digit place by place and count: one shift ×10, a second shift ×10 again, so ×100 in total.

If a learner gives a subtraction answer ('45,000 more' for 50,000 vs 5,000, or '49,500 more' for 50,000 vs 500), re-voice the question as scaling: 'how many of the smaller value fit into the larger?' and build with counters.
Praise answers that name both the factor and the reason (number of shifts), not just a number.
activities.rationale: Comparing a digit across adjacent and non-adjacent places exposes the common over-application of 'ten times' to any gap, and ties the factor to counting place-shifts rather than to a memorised rule. The adjacent ×10 relationship is the defining structure of base-ten place value; the two-shift ×100 case is its direct consequence.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
A digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (4.NBT.1); extended to 1/10 to the left (5.NBT.1).
learnerActions: Compare the same digit in two different places, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000.
Slide one placement of the 5 towards the other, counting the number of column hops.
State the factor: one hop = ×10, so the 5 in 50,000 is ten times the 5 in 5,000.
Repeat for a non-adjacent pair, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500: count the hops (two), so the factor is ×10×10 = ×100.
Say in words how many times greater, and justify by the number of place-shifts.
activities.intendedInsight: The factor between two placements of a digit equals ten raised to the number of column shifts: one shift is ×10, two shifts is ×100. Non-adjacent places are not automatically 'ten times'.

activities.title: Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step
feedback: If a learner computes 700 ÷ 70 as something other than 10, have them see 700 as ten 70s on the chart (70 shifted one place left) before recomputing.
If a learner gets 10 but cannot explain it, ask them to point to where 70 and 700 sit and say how many columns apart they are.
Give full credit only when the sentence is linked to the place-shift, not just the correct number.
activities.rationale: Using ÷ and × sentences gives the ×10 structure calculation payoff and prevents it from being an isolated verbal fact; linking the quotient to adjacent columns anchors the abstract result in place value.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain the answer using place names, not just the computed digits.
Explain how 700 ÷ 70 = 10 connects to 70 and 700 sitting in adjacent place-value columns (the 7 in 700 is one place to the left of the 7 in 70, so 700 is ten times as much as 70).
Write a few matched pairs showing both directions, e.g. 30 = 3 × 10 and 3 = 30 ÷ 10.
Point to or highlight the two adjacent columns involved for each sentence so the quotient of 10 is seen as a single left/right place step.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication sentences such as 700 ÷ 70 = 10 express the adjacent-place relationship itself: moving one place is ×10 or ÷10.

activities.title: Ten times or ten more? Correcting the claim
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 'ten more' fails, compute 300 + 10 = 310 and compare with 3,000, showing 'ten more' gives the wrong number.
Reinforce that the multiplicative view is what lets the ÷10 direction keep going into tenths and hundredths.
If the learner self-corrects confidently, extend by asking them to state the one-tenth (÷10) relationship: this place is one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left.
activities.rationale: Explicitly confronting the additive-vs-multiplicative confusion, rather than only demonstrating the correct move, gives learners a chance to articulate and repair the misconception. A short Socratic exchange in which a character insists on 'ten more' and the learner corrects to 'ten times' is one way to surface this; it is a proposed scaffold, not the only effective medium.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim that 'the 3 in 3,000 is ten MORE than the 3 in 300' and decide whether it is right.
Explain why it is wrong and restate it correctly as 'ten TIMES'.
Support the correction with evidence: 300 × 10 = 3,000, or ten stacks of 300 reaching 3,000, or the single left-shift on the chart.
Preview the right-hand direction: a dimmed column to the right of the ones is where tenths will later live (the ÷10 direction continues past the ones).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Ten times' (multiplicative) and 'ten more' (additive) are different; place value is multiplicative, which is why the pattern extends consistently into decimals.

constraints: Hold the additive (partition) view and the multiplicative (×10 between places) view together: 3,452 is 3,000+400+50+2 AND each place is ten times the next. Do not drop the partition view.

Avoid teaching 'add a zero' as the rule; name the underlying ×10 relationship so the idea still works when extended to decimals (÷10 into tenths). For whole numbers the written zero is a by-product, not the explanation.
A static or paper place-value chart is a valid reference and teaching tool; an interactive sliding chart may make the live recompute more vivid but is not the only way to teach this relationship.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. '700 ÷ 70 = __', 'which is ten times 400?') are useful for consolidation and assessment but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and explain the place-shift reasoning; pair them with tasks that ask for the factor AND its justification.
When comparing non-adjacent places, require the number of place-shifts to be counted (one shift ×10, two shifts ×100); do not let any gap be treated as a single ×10.
Distinguish the digit's face value (3 in both 300 and 3,000) from its place value (300 vs 3,000) whenever learners say the numbers are 'the same'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source citations for CCSS-M (4.NBT.1 / 5.NBT.1) and the NCETM Primary Mastery claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

Arithmetic check: 300 × 10 = 3,000; 700 ÷ 70 = 10; 300 + 10 = 310 (≠ 3,000, correctly showing 'ten more' ≠ 'ten times'); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000 = one shift = ×10 (ratio 10); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500 = two shifts = ×100 (ratio 100). The additive-difference '2,700 bigger' (3,000 − 300) appears only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The source Tier C example '5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000' is labelled a 'non-adjacent' comparison but is in fact adjacent (one shift, ×10); the activities use the correct factors and reserve the two-shift ×100 case for 50,000 vs 500.

The non-adjacent over-application error (answering 'ten times' for a two-shift gap) is a critical learner error; it is addressed directly by requiring the learner to count place-shifts, not merely flagged.
Source claims support the adjacent per-place ×10 convention; the two-shift ×100 composition in activity 2 is a mathematical derivation of that principle, not an independently cited claim.

Independent re-audit found the content mathematically sound and internally coherent across summary, insights, actions, feedback and constraints; no unsupported categorical modality claims remain and medium-efficacy wording is appropriately qualified.

probeDeeper: Now the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000 — how many times bigger? Why?
And the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500 — is it still ten times? (two shifts)
Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain it using places.
assess.correctAnswer: Ten times bigger. Each place to the left is worth ten times the place to its right, and 3,000 is one place to the left of 300, so its 3 is worth ten times as much.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the two values by subtracting instead of by a scale factor: '3,000 is 2,700 more than 300'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-voice the question as scaling: '300 fits into 3,000 how many times?' Build both with place-value counters and show 300 stacked ten times to reach 3,000.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an additive difference when asked 'how many times'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attends to the face value of the digit, not its place: 'they're the same — both are 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast value vs digit: the digit is 3 in both, but its VALUE is 300 vs 3,000. Read each aloud with place names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says there is no difference because the digit is 3 in both.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-applies 'ten times' to non-adjacent places, treating any gap as a single ×10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the place-shifts explicitly: one shift = ×10, two shifts = ×10×10 = ×100. Have them slide the digit place by place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the follow-up (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500) the child still answers 'ten times' rather than 'a hundred times'.

responseLevels.gap: Gives an additive difference or says the digits are 'the same', with no scaling idea.
responseLevels.full: States each left place is ×10, and composes shifts multiplicatively (two places = ×100), justifying with place-value reasoning and inverse (÷10).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'ten times' for the adjacent pair but treats it as a rote 'one more zero' rule and calls non-adjacent pairs ten times too.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 300 and 3,000 side by side. Point to the 3 in each. Ask: 'The value of this 3 compared with that 3 — how many times bigger is one than the other? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A multiplicative place-value thinker says 'ten times' and justifies by the single left-shift; an additive thinker gives the difference ('2,700 more'); a face-value thinker says 'they're the same, both are 3'. The reason tier, plus the non-adjacent follow-ups, separates a rote 'count the extra zero' rule from genuine ×10-per-place reasoning.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Working with Large Numbers
topic.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
evidence: What is the largest six-digit number with digits summing to 15?
A stadium holds 67,450 people. Round to the nearest thousand for a news report
Order the populations of five cities and find the difference between the largest and smallest
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the population of a city is 2,347,819, can they read that number aloud correctly and say roughly how many millions it is?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers to 1,000,000 — e.g. 'largest six-digit number whose digits sum to 15', round a stadium capacity for a headline, order five city populations and find a range. Applying the whole Year-5 place-value toolkit flexibly and in context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'solve number problems and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 1,000,000]'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA multi-step problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding for reasonableness.
• Operational details — Pose rich, multi-step and real-context problems (populations, distances, money, digit-constraint puzzles) that reward choosing among reading, comparing, ordering, rounding and place-value reasoning. Model with number lines, bar models, place-value charts; require justification and appropriate accuracy. Include 'construct a number' puzzles that exercise place value creatively.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): solves a one-step large-number problem with a model. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): solves multi-step problems in context, choosing and explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 10, extending): tackles digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and selects appropriate accuracy.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, multi-step problems (populations, distances, budgets) plus digit-constraint puzzles.
Provide the full toolkit (number line, bar model, chart) and require the child to choose and justify a strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and check reasonableness; choose appropriate accuracy for the context.
Include 'build the largest/smallest number with these constraints' tasks to exercise place value creatively.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud then child-explains) so strategy choice becomes deliberate.
keyRepresentations: Number line (compare/round/estimate)
Bar model for multi-step structure
Place-value chart / counters
Real data sets (populations, distances)
Digit-tile constraint puzzles
commonMisconceptions: Applying a memorised procedure without checking it fits.
Rounding at the wrong stage / to unhelpful accuracy.
Ordering/comparing errors with multi-zero or mixed-length numbers.
Not sense-checking against an estimate.
In digit-constraint puzzles, ignoring the place-value impact of digit position.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: solve multi-step number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000. Learners apply the full place-value toolkit flexibly in context (populations, stadium capacities, distances, budgets) and tackle digit-constraint puzzles such as building the largest number with a given digit sum. The central insight is that place value drives strategy: to maximise a number you load the biggest digits into the highest-value places first. Rounding, ordering and estimation are chosen deliberately to fit each problem and checked for reasonableness.

activities.title: Build the largest number: a digit-constraint puzzle
feedback: If a learner spreads the sum evenly or fills low places (e.g. 333,330, which sums to 15, or 111,138, which also sums to 15), the number is not maximised: compare it against 960,000 column by column. A 9 in the hundred-thousands place beats any arrangement with a smaller leading digit, so the leading place dominates.
If the digits no longer sum to 15, recount the chosen digits before judging size — any counterexample used here must itself sum to 15.
Prompt: 'Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?' to surface that the leftmost place carries the most value.
activities.rationale: A constructive, manipulable puzzle lets children test arrangements, see the value update, and work toward the place-value principle rather than guess. Arranging movable digit-tiles into a chart and comparing candidates can make the strategy explicit; this is a proposed design, not a claim that only this format can teach it.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Take the task: 'Make the LARGEST six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.'
Arrange digit choices into a six-column place-value chart (hundred-thousands down to ones) and write the value they build.
Compare two of their own candidate numbers place by place, starting from the highest place, and decide which is larger and why.
State the rule they discovered in their own words: to make a number as large as possible, put the biggest digits in the highest-value places first.
Verify the digits still sum to 15 after arranging them (9 + 6 = 15, then zeros gives 960,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Magnitude is controlled by the highest-value places, so maximising a number means front-loading the biggest digits into the leftmost columns while respecting the digit-sum constraint.

activities.title: Round in context for a headline
feedback: If a learner rounds 67,450 up to 68,000, they may be rounding in steps (the 5 tens lift 67,450 to 67,500, then that rounds up to 68,000) or treating the tens digit 5 as the decider: isolate the decider. For nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit — 4 is less than 5, so round down.
Use the number line: 67,450 sits left of the midpoint 67,500, so it is nearer 67,000.
Prompt: 'Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?'
activities.rationale: Rounding errors in context often come from attending to the wrong digit or to the full tail. Naming the deciding digit and anchoring on a number line targets this directly.
sourceClaims: Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a real-context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.'
Identify the deciding digit for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit) before rounding.
Place 67,450 on a number line between 67,000 and 68,000 and judge which it is nearer.
Give the rounded answer (67,000) and justify it from the deciding digit (the hundreds digit, 4), not by rounding in steps from the tens digit (67,450 → 67,500 → 68,000).
Explain in a sentence why 450 keeps the thousands the same (rounds DOWN to 67,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to a named place depends on the single deciding digit immediately to the right of that place; here the hundreds digit is 4, which is below 5, so the thousands stay the same.

activities.title: Order populations and find the range
feedback: If a learner orders by the first visible digit (e.g. treating 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as equal or mis-ordering them because each starts with 9), line the numbers up right-aligned in columns and compare starting from the highest place.
Prompt: 'Order 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 — what do you compare first?' to make column alignment the deciding move.
After finding the range, compare the exact difference to a rounded estimate to catch slips.
activities.rationale: Multi-zero and mixed-length numbers are a classic source of comparison errors; explicit column alignment and highest-place-first comparison address the misconception.
learnerActions: Take five city populations (mixed-length numbers, some with internal zeros) and right-align them by place-value column.
Compare from the highest place downward to order them from smallest to largest.
Order the trio 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as a focused check, saying which place you compare first.
Find the range by subtracting the smallest from the largest and sense-check the answer against a rounded estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct ordering comes from aligning place-value columns and comparing from the highest place down. For whole numbers, more digits means a larger number, but when numbers have the same number of digits you must compare place by place, not just look at the first visible digit.

activities.title: Choose and justify the strategy (think-aloud)
feedback: If a learner applies a memorised procedure without checking it fits the question, ask them to name the tool and why before computing.
If an answer is wildly off a rounded estimate, treat the mismatch as a signal to recheck rather than to accept the computation.
Naming the strategy after solving (e.g. 'I rounded to estimate, then compared from the highest place') can reinforce transfer.
activities.rationale: This is a META problem-solving topic: externalising reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) and estimation-checking support flexible strategy selection. A spoken dialogue and a worked anchor example are useful supplements for eliciting reasoning, not the sole route.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: For each problem, first answer 'which tool fits?' — number line, bar model, place-value chart, or digit arrangement — before solving.
Hear or read a worked example thought aloud, then re-solve a similar problem explaining each decision.
Estimate first by rounding, then compute the exact answer, and check the exact answer against the estimate.
Discuss with a partner or respond to prompts such as 'how did you decide?' to make the strategy deliberate.
activities.intendedInsight: In multi-step problems the hard part is choosing which place-value tool to use and checking reasonableness; making the choice explicit and estimating first turns strategy into a deliberate repertoire.

constraints: Multi-step and context problems can be assessed with fixed-response items (best-estimate choices, largest-number choices, estimate-then-check sliders, fill-in-the-blank), but recognition-only items do not themselves elicit the independent construction that the digit-building puzzle requires; use a construction task for the maximising strategy.
A worked, tapped-through example (e.g. a solved population-range problem) is a reference anchor, not varied practice; pair it with problems the learner solves themselves.

A live-updating value display and movable digit-tiles are optional supports that make the place-value mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory mechanisms, and the same insight can be reached on paper with a drawn chart.
For this abstract/contextual numeric reasoning there is little spatial payoff, so 3D manipulation adds little here; prefer number lines, bar models and place-value charts.
Any 'spread evenly / fills low places' counterexample used with the digit-sum-15 task must itself sum to 15 (e.g. 333,330 or 111,138); do not use 333,300, which sums to 12.

Tier expectations: emerging learners solve a one-step large-number problem with a model; secure learners solve multi-step context problems choosing and explaining a strategy; extending learners tackle digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and select appropriate accuracy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original-row arithmetic error corrected: the error pattern cited '333,300' as a number summing to 15, but 333,300 sums to 12. Replaced with 333,330 (sums to 15) in the learner-facing activity; the original figure is kept only here and in preservationAudit.uncertain.

Self-audit of worked values: the largest six-digit number with digit sum 15 is 960,000 (9+6=15, remaining places 0) — the maximum by front-loading. 67,450 to the nearest thousand is 67,000 because the deciding hundreds digit 4 < 5. The ordering 9,000 < 90,000 < 900,000 is confirmed. These match the source's stated correct answers.

sourceClaims adjusted: the general curriculum requirement (DfE source-1 claim) was removed from activities where it supported only the topic, not the specific teaching principle; activity 3 (ordering) has no directly supporting source claim and is left as [].
Two source claims (CCSS-M 4.NBT/4.OA and NCETM/nrich) are marked unverified in the original row; their citation here is not evidence of empirical efficacy or of testing of these specific activities.

The original framing that the construction puzzle 'cannot be solved by trial alone' is softened: trial-and-error can reach the answer, but the puzzle is designed to make the place-value strategy the efficient, reasoned route.

probeDeeper: Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?
Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?
Order 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 — what do you compare first?
assess.correctAnswer: 960,000 (load the biggest digits into the highest places: 9 + 6 = 15, then zeros); and 67,000 (450 is below 500, so round down).

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't prioritise place value for magnitude — spreads the digit-sum evenly or fills low places, so the number isn't the largest (e.g. 333,300 or 111,138)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare two candidates place by place: a 9 in the hundred-thousands beats any arrangement with a smaller leading digit. Make the leading-place-dominates idea explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The number sums to 15 but isn't maximised; big digits aren't front-loaded.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the wrong way in context: 67,450 → 68,000, treating the 450 (or the 4) as enough to round the thousands up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the decider for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit): 4 < 5 so down. Place 67,450 between 67,000 and 68,000 on a line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The context answer rounds up when the decider digit (hundreds = 4) says round down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares/orders large numbers by first digit or digit-count alone, misaligning place values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line numbers up by place-value columns (right-aligned) and compare from the highest place down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 incorrectly, or calls a number with more digits automatically smaller/larger by looking at the wrong end.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot systematically maximise value or rounds the wrong way in context; orders by the wrong feature.
responseLevels.full: Solves multi-step large-number problems — front-loads places to maximise value, rounds correctly to a named place in context, and orders by comparing from the highest place.
responseLevels.partial: Handles single steps (rounds, or orders) but stumbles when a problem combines maximising, rounding, and comparing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the problem and watch the reasoning: 'Make the largest six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.' Then a context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.' Watch how they place digits to maximise value and which way they round in context.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'largest number' task cannot be solved by trial alone — it reveals whether the child knows value is maximised by loading the most-significant places first. The stadium item checks rounding to a named place IN CONTEXT, where children often round the visible hundreds up regardless of the thousand rule.

topic.name: Numbers to Ten Million
topic.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
evidence: A country's population is 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline
Order the depths of three ocean trenches given in metres including negative values
Estimate the total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that the distance to the Moon is about 384,400 km, can they round it to the nearest 10,000 km and say whether it's closer to 380,000 or 390,000?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000 (a synthesising META-topic).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above' — i.e. the applied capstone over the Y6 place-value objectives (to 10,000,000, rounding, negatives).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): draws on 4.NBT.A (read/write/compare/round multi-digit), 5.NBT.A (place value, rounding) and 6.NS.C (negatives in context) applied to problem contexts.
• Operational details: Pose realistic multi-step problems — populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances — that require choosing WHICH place-value skill to deploy (round for a headline, compare/order to rank, use negatives for depths). Emphasise sense-making: estimate first by rounding, then check the exact answer is reasonable, and interpret the result back in context (a rounded headline vs an exact count).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Population 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline.' Tier B: 'Order three ocean-trench depths given as negatives.' Tier C: 'Estimate total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000 and judge if your estimate is over or under.'
bestPractices: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so pupils choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which
Teach estimate-first: round to get a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate
Require interpretation back in context — when is a rounded headline appropriate, when is the exact figure needed
Blend the sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection
Model judging whether a rounded estimate is an over- or under-estimate, connecting rounding direction to context
keyRepresentations: Number line / magnitude bars for ordering and rounding seven-digit values
Period-grouped place-value chart for reading and writing the numbers in play
Vertical number line for negative contexts (depths, temperatures)
Estimation strips pairing rounded values with the exact figures
commonMisconceptions: Applying a rounding rule mechanically without checking the answer makes sense in context
Ordering by digit count or face value rather than aligned place value for seven-digit numbers
Mishandling negatives in context (ranking −900 m as shallower than −300 m)
Rounding to the wrong place for the purpose (nearest 10 when a million is asked for a headline)
Losing placeholder zeros when reading/writing the large numbers within a problem

learn.summary: Applied capstone for place value to 10,000,000: learners choose and combine place-value tools — rounding to a stated place, ordering/comparing seven-digit and negative numbers, and reading/writing with placeholder zeros — within realistic multi-step problems (populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances). Core habit: estimate first by rounding, compute/compare exactly, then interpret the result back in context and judge whether an estimate is over or under.

activities.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool
feedback: If a learner rounds 8,274,500 to 9,000,000 'because the rest is big', have them underline the millions digit and box only the single digit to its right (2); state 'only that one digit decides' and locate the number on a line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.

If a learner ranks -7,921 m as deepest because '7 thousand is the smallest number', use a vertical number line with 0 at sea level to show that -9,052 m, the most negative reading, sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.

If rounded parts come out the wrong order of magnitude (e.g. reading 214,600 as 21,460), rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) on a place-value grid and read each number aloud by period before rounding.

To decide whether an estimate is over or under, check each addend: did it round up or down, and by how much? Add up the up-adjustments and the down-adjustments and compare them — the estimate is over when the ups outweigh the downs and under when the downs outweigh the ups. Note that rounding can go in mixed directions: for 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 to the nearest 100,000, 214,600 rounds down while 388,050 and 96,700 round up, and here the ups slightly outweigh the down, giving a small over-estimate (700,000 vs exact 699,350).
activities.rationale: The objective is choosing and combining place-value skills in context, so an open workspace where learners select a tool, see the consequence and self-check against an estimate is proposed to target that selection skill directly. An optional interactive version can offer a magnitude number line, a rounding bracket that snaps to a chosen place, comparison/ordering slots, a negative-scale toggle, and an over/under flag on the estimate — these make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same work can be done on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
Applied place-value problem solving draws on read/write/compare/round of multi-digit numbers (4.NBT.A, 5.NBT.A) and negatives in context (6.NS.C).
learnerActions: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.

activities.title: Fluency check on the component skills
feedback: For ordering: the correct deepest-to-shallowest order for -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 is -10,900, -7,200, -4,000, because more negative is lower (further below sea level).
For the estimate: rounding to the nearest 100,000 gives 200,000 + 400,000 + 100,000 = about 700,000; then check the exact total (699,350) is close to it.
For rounding to the nearest million: the deciding digit is the hundred-thousands digit (2), so 8,274,500 rounds down to 8,000,000, not up to 9,000,000.
activities.rationale: The component skills are cleanly assessable, so short targeted items are a useful companion for checking applied fluency. These items check recognition and execution of each skill; on their own they do not elicit the open multi-step tool-selection that the workspace activity targets.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
learnerActions: Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and choose the correct result.
Order three negative trench depths (e.g. -4,000 m, -10,900 m, -7,200 m) from deepest to shallowest.
Estimate a total attendance (e.g. 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700) by rounding each to the nearest 100,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Each component place-value skill — rounding to a stated place, ordering negatives by position, estimating by rounding addends — can be executed accurately on its own.

activities.title: Framing contexts before computing
feedback: If a learner rounds a figure to the wrong place for the purpose (e.g. nearest 10 for a headline about millions), ask what level of precision a reader needs and point them to the relevant period.

If they would round depths used for a ranking, remind them that ranking needs the exact ordering, so the comparison should use exact values: rounding (even consistently to the same place) can make different depths equal, e.g. -8,376 m and -8,420 m both round to -8,000 m to the nearest thousand, so the order is lost.
activities.rationale: Framing and discussion build the sense-making and interpretation the topic emphasises; a dialogue can coach problem framing, while the compute-and-check work is best carried out in the workspace, so this activity should lead into, not replace, the workspace task.
learnerActions: Study a labelled population/depth chart or world map and tap or point to regions to reveal exact figures.
For each figure, state what you would round it to for a fair headline, and which figures you would keep exact for ranking.
Take on a journalist's brief: turn a set of exact figures into fair rounded headlines, then explain why the rounded version is appropriate for a headline but not for a precise ranking.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which place-value tool a situation calls for — and whether a rounded headline or an exact figure is appropriate — is itself part of the problem.

constraints: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so learners choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which.

Teach estimate-first: round for a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate; require interpreting the result back in context (when a rounded headline suffices vs when the exact figure is needed).
Blend sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection.
Recognition/short-answer items check component fluency but do not on their own elicit the open multi-step tool selection; use them as a companion, not a substitute.

A static chart cannot host the compute-and-check work, and a dialogue is better suited to coaching problem framing than to carrying the full multi-step working; treat these as scaffolds leading into the problem-solving rather than substitutes.

Any interactive features (snapping rounding bracket, draggable number line, negative-scale toggle, over/under flag) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the same learning can occur on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked numbers: 8,274,500 rounds to 8,000,000 (deciding hundred-thousands digit 2 -> round down) — correct. Ordering -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 deepest-to-shallowest = -10,900, -7,200, -4,000 — correct. Estimate 214,600+388,050+96,700 rounded to nearest 100,000 = 200,000+400,000+100,000 = 700,000; exact = 699,350, so the estimate is a slight over-estimate (by 650) — consistent; up-adjustments (11,950 + 3,300 = 15,250) exceed the down-adjustment (14,600) by 650.

The over/under feedback in Activity 1 handles the mixed-rounding case correctly: learners weigh total up-adjustments against total down-adjustments rather than assuming all addends round the same way.

The second CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; the standards mapping (4.NBT.A/5.NBT.A/6.NS.C) is retained as sourced but its verification status is unconfirmed, and no claim of medium effectiveness rests on it.
The probe 'Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?' is pedagogically sound and is reflected via the number-line position argument in the ordering feedback.

probeDeeper: For the rounding, which single digit made the decision, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?
Would your estimate be too high or too low compared with the exact total — how can you tell?
What if the reading had been 8,724,500 — would it still round to 8,000,000?

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds using the wrong place — looks at a later digit or rounds 8,274,500 up to 9,000,000 because 'the rest is big', instead of reading the hundred-thousands digit (2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Underline the millions digit and box the single digit to its right; state the rule 'only that one digit decides'. Model on a number line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds to 9,000,000, or hesitates over which digit decides; cannot name the deciding digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders the negative depths by magnitude, treating -4,000 as deepest because '4 thousand is the smallest number'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level; show -10,900 sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks -4,000 as deepest / -10,900 as shallowest, ignoring that more-negative is lower.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the periods in the seven-digit numbers — misplaces commas or reads 214,600 as 21,460 / 2,146,000, so the estimate is off by a factor of ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) with a place-value grid; read each number aloud by period before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded parts are the wrong order of magnitude; total estimate is 70,000 or 7,000,000.

responseLevels.gap: Rounds on the wrong digit, orders negatives by magnitude, or produces an estimate of the wrong order of magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Executes all three fluently — names the deciding digit when rounding, orders negatives by number-line position, rounds each addend before summing, and can say whether the estimate is over or under.
responseLevels.partial: Completes one or two tasks correctly (often the rounding) but cannot reliably order the negatives or justify the estimate's direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks laid out on paper. (1) Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million. (2) Three ocean-trench readings are -4,000 m, -10,900 m and -7,200 m; order them from deepest to shallowest. (3) Estimate 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 by rounding each first.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the working, not the answers. Correct rounding requires looking at the digit to the RIGHT of the millions place (2 → round down) — a child who rounds on the wrong digit or rounds up 'because there's lots after it' is exposed. The negatives task separates children who order by magnitude (calling -4,000 deepest) from those who order by position on the number line. The estimate reveals whether they round before adding or add then round.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Patterns with Powers of Ten
topic.description: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
evidence: Write 10⁴ = 10,000 and explain the exponent means four factors of 10
Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 by describing the decimal shift
Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and explain the pattern
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 10² = 100 and 10³ = 1,000, and why multiplying by 10 just adds a zero — connecting the pattern of zeros to place value?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — explain the pattern in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when ×/÷ by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents for powers of 10 (10³ = 1000).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5/Y6 multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000; exponent notation is a US-forward extension of the same ×10 structure.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.2 — 'Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.'
• Operational details: Build exponent as a COUNT of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), then connect the exponent to both the zero-count in whole-number products AND the number of places the digits shift. Emphasise that DIGITS shift, the point stays; the exponent tells you how many places. Predict-then-check with a place-value chart before generalising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 10⁴ as an ordinary number and say how many zeros.' Tier B: 'Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 using the digit shift.' Tier C: 'Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and justify the pattern.'
bestPractices: Define an exponent as the number of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count is a CONSEQUENCE for whole numbers that breaks for decimals
Tie the exponent simultaneously to zeros in a whole-number product and to the number of places the digits shift, so the child sees them as the same pattern
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed — explicitly reject 'move the decimal point'
Use predict-then-check on a place-value chart before stating the generalisation
Include ÷ by powers of 10 alongside × so the pattern is bidirectional and exponents are seen to shift digits the other way
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with digits sliding N columns for ×10^N (point fixed)
Expanded factor strings: 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with zeros tallied
Exponent stepper linking 10¹, 10², 10³ to 10, 100, 1000 and their zero counts
Arrow cards showing 3.4 → 34 → 340 with '×10' per hop
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplying by a power of 10 just adds zeros' — fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 ≠ 3.400)
Reading 10³ as 10×3 = 30 (confusing exponent with a factor)
Believing the decimal point moves rather than the digits
Miscounting the shift — shifting by the base (10) rather than the exponent (3)
Assuming the exponent equals the number of digits in the result rather than factors of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: explain the patterns in zeros when multiplying whole numbers by powers of ten, and the decimal-point placement when multiplying or dividing decimals by a power of ten, using whole-number exponents (10³ = 1000). The central idea is that an exponent counts factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10) and equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift; the digits move while the decimal point stays fixed. The 'add zeros' shortcut is a consequence for whole numbers only and breaks for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400); any zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original digits.

activities.title: Sweep the exponent on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.400 for 3.4 × 100, show on the chart that each ×10 slides the digits one column left: 3.4 → 34 → 340. The answer is 340, not 3.400 — the digits moved into larger columns and a single zero fills the now-empty ones place, rather than zeros being appended after the decimal point.

If the digits move the wrong way, anchor direction: multiplying a positive number by 10, 100 or 1000 makes it bigger, so digits travel to larger (left-hand) columns; dividing by these makes it smaller, so they move right.
If a learner shifts by 10 instead of by 3 for 10³, re-read the exponent: the little 3 is how many columns, not the base.

Confirm success when the learner predicts the number of columns from the exponent before moving any digit and explains that any zero appearing in the product is a placeholder for an emptied column, not a zero appended to the original digits.
activities.rationale: A live, predict-then-check representation lets the learner see the exponent, the zero-count and the shift-distance change together, which is what can turn a rule into a visible pattern. Including division makes the pattern bidirectional.
sourceClaims: Y5/Y6 pupils multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000.
5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Place a number — e.g. 3.4 — on a place-value chart with the decimal point marked in a fixed position.

Set a power of ten (10¹, then 10², then 10³) and, for each, slide every digit left by the number shown in the exponent; the column count is the total shift from 3.4 and equals the exponent: 3.4 → 34 (10¹, one column) → 340 (10², two columns) → 3400 (10³, three columns), keeping the point pinned.
Alongside, write the power in expanded form (10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000) and tally its zeros.
State in words: 'The exponent tells me how many columns the digits jump.'
Repeat with division by powers of ten (shifting digits the other way, e.g. 3.4 ÷ 10 = 0.34) and with a whole number like 7 (7 × 10 = 70) to compare where zeros appear.
activities.intendedInsight: The exponent equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift, so 'powers of ten' and 'place-value shift' are the same idea. For a decimal like 3.4, multiplying by 10 does not append a zero (3.4 × 10 = 34, not 3.40); any zeros appearing in larger products such as 340 or 3400 are placeholders filling emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original number — so the 'add-a-zero' rule is not the real pattern.

activities.title: Reference ladder of powers of ten
feedback: If a learner reads 10³ as 30, unpack it as repeated multiplication 10×10×10 = 1000 and set it beside 10×3 = 30.

If a learner says the exponent is 'the number of zeros' as a definition, restate it as the number of factors of ten — the zero-count of the power is a result, and using it as an 'add that many zeros' rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400).
This ladder is a static reference; pair it with the moving chart so the digit shift is seen as an action, not only read.
activities.rationale: A revealable ladder is a strong anchor for the factor-string meaning of exponents and directly targets the 10³ = 30 confusion, though on its own it shows values rather than the shifting action.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Reveal each power from 10¹ to 10⁶ one at a time, writing its expanded factor string and ordinary value (e.g. 10⁴ = 10×10×10×10 = 10000).
For each, state the number of factors of ten and the number of zeros, and note that they match for these whole-number powers.
Contrast 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with 10×3 = 30 aloud, so the exponent is not mistaken for a plain multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: An exponent is a count of factors of ten, and for a power of ten written on its own the zero-count equals that factor count — while 10³ is emphatically not 10×3.

activities.title: Defend it against the 'add zeros' rule
feedback: If the learner cannot explain beyond the rule, ask them to say where each digit lands column by column.
Press for 'how many times bigger/smaller' to connect the exponent to the factor (100 for 10², 1000 for 10³).
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken or written justification, not just an answer, discriminates understanding of the pattern from mimicry of a shortcut.
learnerActions: Face a prompt such as: 'A classmate says 3.4 × 10² = 3.400. Explain why that is wrong and give the correct answer.'
Justify using the digit shift: each ×10 moves the digits one column left, so 3.4 → 34 → 340.
Answer and explain 2.56 × 10³ (= 2560) and 2.56 ÷ 10³ (= 0.00256), saying how multiplication and division differ in shift direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the place-value shift exposes why 'add a zero' only looks right when the point sits at the end of a whole number, and why it fails for decimals; the zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied columns.

activities.title: Predict-and-check consolidation
feedback: For 2.56 × 10³ the answer is 2560; 2.56000 just glues zeros on without shifting; 0.00256 divides instead of multiplies; 76.8 treats 10³ as 30.
Use any wrong choice as a cue to return to the place-value chart for that case.
activities.rationale: Short selected- and filled-response items can efficiently consolidate the pattern and surface the three named misconceptions as distractors; this checks that the pattern holds rather than demonstrating why it holds, so keep a task that requires a constructed explanation alongside it.
learnerActions: Complete items such as: fill in 10³ = ____; and choose the correct value of 2.56 × 10³ from options that include the add-zeros error 2.56000, the wrong-direction error 0.00256, and the exponent-as-multiplier error 76.8.
Put 10¹, 10², 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵ in order and match each to its zero count.
For each item, write one sentence saying why the chosen answer is right.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each power of ten corresponds to a fixed number of place-value shifts, with common error patterns ruled out explicitly.

constraints: Define an exponent as the number of factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count of the power of ten is a consequence, and the 'add that many zeros' rule works only for whole-number products and breaks for decimals.

Distinguish appended zeros from placeholder zeros: multiplying a decimal does not append zeros after its decimal point to the original digits, but placeholder zeros may legitimately fill emptied whole-number columns (e.g. 340, 3400, 2560). Do not tell a learner 'no zeros appear' when the displayed product contains them.
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed; avoid teaching 'move the decimal point' as the primary idea, though it can be mentioned as an equivalent description.
Include division by powers of ten alongside multiplication so the shift is seen as bidirectional.
The reference ladder is a static anchor: on its own it does not show the digit shift as an action, so pair it with the moving chart.
Selected-response consolidation checks the pattern but does not elicit the learner's own explanation; keep a task that requires constructing a justification.
Live recolouring/highlighting, digit sliding, a mobile exponent dial, zero tallies and a divide toggle are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one US standard citation as not verified (verified:false for 5.NBT.A.2); treat that citation's status as unconfirmed.

Clarified the lead activity's column-count wording so each total shift is tied to its exponent (10¹→one column, 10²→two columns, 10³→three columns), avoiding a reading where a single ×10 hop is labelled two columns.

Corrected the original 'the columns fill without any zeros being added' framing: 3.4 × 100 = 340 and 3.4 × 1000 = 3400 do contain placeholder zeros, and 34 → 340 appends a placeholder; the guidance distinguishes zeros appended after the decimal point (the 3.400 error) from placeholder zeros filling emptied columns.

The source's correct-answer phrasing 'the decimal point moves three places right' is retained only as an equivalent secondary description, subordinated to the 'digits move, point fixed' framing per the pedagogy's own best practice.

probeDeeper: Why does the answer get bigger, and by how many times exactly?
What does the little 3 in 10³ actually tell you to do?
Would 'add three zeros' work for 2.56 × 10³? Why or why not?
What is 2.56 ÷ 10³, and how is it different from multiplying?
assess.correctAnswer: 2,560. Multiplying by 10³ means ×1000, so every digit becomes worth a thousand times more and shifts three places to the left (equivalently the decimal point moves three places right, and a zero fills the empty ones place).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add three zeros' rule — appends zeros to the written digits, giving 2.56000 for 2.56 × 10³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that ×10 shifts every digit one place left (2.56→25.6→256→2560); the 'add a zero' shortcut only works for whole numbers because the point sits at the end.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Zeros are stuck onto the decimal without the point moving; answer keeps the decimal in place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the point the wrong way — divides instead of multiplies, giving 0.00256.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor direction: multiplying makes it bigger, so digits move to larger places (left); rehearse on a place-value chart with the point fixed and digits sliding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is smaller than the start; point moved left for a multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the exponent as a plain multiplier — reads 10³ as 30, so 2.56 × 10³ becomes 2.56 × 30 = 76.8.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unpack 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000; contrast with 10×3 = 30 so the exponent is seen as repeated multiplication.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child multiplies by 30 (or says 10³ = 30), confusing exponent with base×exponent.

responseLevels.gap: Appends zeros, moves the point the wrong way, or treats 10³ as 30.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the result via place-value shift, explains the exponent as repeated ×10, and handles decimals and both × and ÷ by powers of ten consistently.
responseLevels.partial: Gets whole-number cases right by rule but the pattern breaks with a decimal like 2.56, or cannot explain why the point moves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Without calculating it out, what is 2.56 × 10³? Explain why the digits or the decimal point move the way they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the pattern explains it by place-value shift (×10 three times moves digits left) and correctly gets 2,560. A child running the 'add three zeros' rule writes 2.56000; one who thinks the exponent is a multiplier gets 76.8 (×30). The explanation, not just the answer, reveals whether the zero-pattern is understood or mimicked.
