topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Place Value × 10 and ÷ 10
topic.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
evidence: Explain that the 4 in 0.04 is 1/10 of the 4 in 0.4
State that a digit moving one place left is ×10 and one place right is ÷10
Compare the value of the 6 in 6,000 and in 0.006
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 4.56, the digit 5 is worth 5 tenths — ten times less than the 5 in 54, and ten times more than the 5 in 0.056?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — recognise that a digit represents 10× the place to its right and 1/10 the place to its left (the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship, now extended in BOTH directions across the decimal point).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to 3 decimal places' and multiply/divide by 10/100/1000; the reciprocal ÷10 direction underpins Y6 decimal work.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 — 'Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.'
• Operational details: Treat place value as a single self-similar structure that continues seamlessly through the decimal point — each step left is unitising (×10), each step right is partitioning (÷10). Contrast digits of equal face value in different places (the 4 in 0.4 vs 0.04 vs 4000) so the child articulates the multiplicative, not additive, gap. Use a Gattegno/place-value chart where a digit physically slides between columns and its value recomputes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'The 4 in 0.4 is ten times the 4 in ___.' Tier B: 'Explain why the 6 in 6000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.' Tier C: 'A digit moves two places right — what happens to its value and why?'
bestPractices: Present place value as one continuous ×10/÷10 chain that runs unbroken through the decimal point — do not teach whole-number and decimal place value as separate systems
Use a Gattegno chart or place-value slider so a digit physically moves between columns and its value visibly recomputes (×10 left, ÷10 right)
Contrast the SAME face-value digit sitting in different places (4 in 4000 vs 0.4 vs 0.04) and require a multiplicative statement ('ten times', 'one tenth of'), never 'bigger/smaller'
Anchor the ÷10 direction in concrete partitioning — one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth — before abstracting to the rule
Vary the non-example: ask why moving a place is NOT 'add a zero' when decimals are involved, exposing the multiplicative meaning
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (digit slides between columns, value scales ×10 or ÷10)
Place-value chart spanning millions to thousandths with the decimal point fixed and digits mobile
Arrow/relationship cards labelling adjacent columns '×10 →' and '← ÷10'
Base-ten / Dienes extended to decimal flats-longs-units where the 'one' can be reassigned
commonMisconceptions: Believing 'moving a place left just adds a zero' — a rule that breaks for decimals (0.4 → 4, not 0.40)
Treating the decimal point as moving rather than the DIGITS moving relative to a fixed point
Thinking the gap between places is additive (0.4 is '0.36 more than' 0.04) rather than multiplicative (ten times)
Assuming longer decimals are always larger, ignoring place value (0.004 seen as bigger than 0.4)
Losing the self-similar structure at the decimal point — seeing tenths as unrelated to ones

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: understand that each place in a number is worth ten times the place to its right and one tenth of the place to its left, and that this ×10/÷10 structure continues unbroken through the decimal point. The core goal is for a learner to state multiplicative relationships ('ten times', 'one tenth of') between the same digit sitting in different places, and to justify them by position rather than by face value or decimal length.

activities.title: Slide the same digit across the places
feedback: If a learner says the two 4s are 'the same because both are 4', redirect to position: the digit is identical but the places differ, so the worth differs — ask them to read each value aloud (four tenths vs four hundredths).
If a learner counts a single move as ÷100 or ÷2, have them count the columns crossed: tenths to hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; show 0.004 to illustrate what two steps (÷100) would look like.
Reinforce correct multiplicative language: accept 'ten times' / 'one tenth of', and gently reject 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation of value by place, so performing the move and reading the recomputed value makes the multiplicative gap concrete rather than merely stated. An optional live readout and a proportional magnitude bar that is ten times longer per leftward step can make the multiplicative (not additive) gap visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
The Gattegno chart is a canonical representation for building the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship across whole numbers and decimals.
learnerActions: Work on a place-value chart with columns from millions down to thousandths and a fixed decimal point.
Take a single digit, for example a 4, and place it in the tenths column so it reads 0.4.
Move the same 4 one column to the left to read 4, then 40, then 400, then 4000; each move, say aloud 'ten times as much' and write the ×10 relationship.

Before moving right, split one tenth into ten equal parts and check that each part is one hundredth (and one hundredth into ten parts gives thousandths). Then move the same 4 one column to the right from 0.4 to 0.04 to 0.004; each move, say aloud 'one tenth of' and write the ÷10 relationship.
Park the same 4 three columns apart (for example 4000 and 4, or 4 and 0.004 — each three steps, so ×1000) and state how many times larger one is than the other.
Finish the sentence: '0.4 is ten times 0.04; 0.04 is one tenth of 0.4.'
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth changes multiplicatively (×10 each step left, ÷10 each step right) according to its place; the decimal point stays fixed while the digit moves, and the same self-similar rule runs through the decimal point.

activities.title: Why isn't it just 'add a zero'?
feedback: If a learner insists 'add a zero' works, show 0.4 → 4: adding a zero gives 0.40, which is still four tenths, not four.
Confirm understanding when the learner states the rule as '×10 when moving left, ÷10 when moving right' and can apply it to a decimal example.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a tempting but faulty shortcut with the multiplicative rule surfaces and addresses the common 'add a zero' misconception.
sourceClaims: Y5 requires recognising the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places and multiplying/dividing by 10, 100 and 1000.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'moving a digit one place left just adds a zero.'
Test it on whole numbers: 4 → 40 (works) and then on a decimal: 0.4 → 4 (not 0.40).
Explain in your own words why 'add a zero' fails for decimals but ×10 always works.
Write a corrected rule that holds for both whole numbers and decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The underlying operation is multiply/divide by ten, not a digit-appending trick; 'add a zero' is a surface pattern that breaks for decimals, exposing the multiplicative meaning.

activities.title: Compare across many places and across zero
feedback: If a learner ranks the 4 in 0.04 as larger because it comes 'further along', use the number line to show 0.04 sits close to zero while 0.4 is near halfway.
If a learner cannot bridge 6,000 and 0.006, have them step through the places one at a time, tagging each ×10 (six steps), to reach a million-fold difference.
activities.rationale: Spanning many places and crossing the decimal point counters the 'longer decimal is larger' and 'face value' errors, and a number line makes the shrinking rightward value visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the 6 in 6,000 with the 6 in 0.006: count how many ×10 steps separate the two places (six steps).
State and justify how many times larger the 6 in 6,000 is (6,000 is 0.006 × 1,000,000).
Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 number line (0.4 near the middle, 0.04 close to zero) to see the value shrinking to the right.
Explain which stays the same and which changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value relationship holds across several steps and across the decimal point; value decreases to the right and increases to the left, regardless of decimal length.

activities.title: Explain and defend your reasoning
feedback: A full response states the ten-times / one-tenth relationship, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places.
A partial response can order the values and say one is smaller but cannot justify the exact ÷10 factor or muddles it; prompt the learner to count places and name the single ×10/÷10 step.
If the learner says one tenth of a tenth is a twentieth or a tenth, have them partition one tenth into ten equal parts to see each part is a hundredth.
activities.rationale: Requiring a justified comparison rather than a memorised ranking discriminates true positional understanding from surface rules, and asking the learner to explain the partitioning met earlier (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) checks that the ÷10 direction rests on concrete meaning rather than a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?'
Answer a deeper probe: 'Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?'
Explain, with reasons, why the 6 in 6,000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.
Anchor the ÷10 direction in partitioning: explain why one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the exact ÷10/×10 relationship by position — not just order the values — is what demonstrates genuine place-value understanding.

constraints: Present whole-number and decimal place value as ONE continuous ×10/÷10 chain running through the decimal point, not two separate systems.
Require multiplicative language ('ten times', 'one tenth of'); do not accept 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation of the relationship.

Recognition-only tasks (for example choosing from multiple options or filling a blank) can consolidate and assess the rule but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own justification; include tasks where the learner states and defends the relationship.

A static annotated chart with reveal cards is a useful reference, but it tells rather than lets the learner perform the slide; treat it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the learner moving a digit and reading the recomputed value.
Partitioning (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) should be established concretely before abstracting to the divide-by-ten rule.
Keep worked examples arithmetically exact: columns N apart differ by a factor of 10^N (three columns apart is ×1000, two columns apart is ×100).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit confirmed: 0.4 = 0.04 × 10 and 0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10; 6,000 vs 0.006 differ by six ×10 steps (a factor of 1,000,000); one tenth of one tenth = one hundredth; three columns apart = ×1000 and two columns apart = ×100. The example pairs 4000 and 4, and 4 and 0.004, are genuinely three steps apart and consistent with the ×1000 framing.

The original claim that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' and 'risks implying value scales with physical size' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; a spatial model could still be used — it is simply not required here.

The original framing that manipulation is 'necessary' while dialogue is merely 'possible' reflects catalog fit ranking, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; both a manipulable chart and a Socratic exchange are retained as legitimate approaches serving different purposes.
CCSS-M 5.NBT.A.1 and the NCETM Gattegno-chart claim were marked unverified in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?
How does the 6 in 6,000 compare to the 6 in 0.006 — how many tens apart are they?
If I move the 4 in 0.4 one place LEFT instead, what happens to its value?
What stays the same and what changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 in 0.04 is worth one-tenth of the 4 in 0.4 (0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10). A digit one place to the right is worth ten times less, because each place is a tenth of the place to its left.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'they're the same, both digits are 4', ignoring position.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with place-value counters or a Gattegno chart: slide the 4 from tenths to hundredths and show its worth divides by ten; the digit is the same but its place is not.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both digits are 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says equal value and justifies by the digit alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-decimal-is-larger / places grow to the right — thinks the 4 in 0.04 is worth more because it is 'further along'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 line (0.4 near halfway, 0.04 close to zero) so the shrinking value to the right is visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is bigger because it comes further along.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 0.04's 4 as the bigger value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right direction, wrong factor — says the 0.04 four is a hundredth (or half) of the other, not a tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the places moved: tenths→hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; contrast with 0.004 to show what ÷100 would look like.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is one hundredth of the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child knows it is smaller and moved one place, but names ÷100 or ÷2.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the digit or by decimal length; cannot say one value is a tenth of the other.
responseLevels.full: States the ten-times / one-tenth relationship between adjacent places, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places (e.g. 6,000 vs 0.006).
responseLevels.partial: States the 0.04 four is smaller and can order them, but cannot justify the exact ÷10 relationship or muddles the factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands positional value says one is a tenth of the other and can say why (the place, not the digit, carries the value). A child stuck on face value says 'same, both are 4'; a child with the longer-is-larger error says the 0.04 one is bigger. The REASON separates true place-value understanding from a memorised comparison.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write decimals like 3.047 or 0.625, say what each digit means (3 ones, 0 tenths, 4 hundredths, 7 thousandths), and put a set of decimals in order?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, < on place-value meaning.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 read/write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparison and ordering of decimals to three places.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.3 — 'Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. (a) Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form... (b) Compare two decimals to thousandths based on the meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, < symbols.'
• Operational details: Read decimals as fractions of the whole ('five and sixty-two thousandths', not 'five point zero six two') to keep place meaning audible. Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers (3×(1/10)+9×(1/100)+2×(1/1000)). Compare by aligning place value left-to-right, using equalising trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to defeat the 'longer-is-larger' error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write five and sixty-two thousandths as a numeral.' Tier B: 'Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and justify.' Tier C: 'Write 347.392 in expanded form with unit fractions.'
bestPractices: Read decimals using place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the meaning stays audible
Build expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers (×1/10, ×1/100, ×1/1000) to bind each digit to its place
Compare left-to-right by place value, and equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to expose 'longer-is-larger' as false
Use a thousandths grid / decimal place-value chart so 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 are seen as nested tenths-of-tenths
Move fluently among numeral, words and expanded form in both directions
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths
Thousandths grid (10×10×10 nesting) or 1000-cube partition of the unit
Three-pane numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded-form translator
Number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison; trailing-zero alignment tool
commonMisconceptions: 'Longer decimal is larger' (0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits)
'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit

learn.summary: Learners aged 10–11 read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, and compare with >, =, < based on place-value meaning. The central hurdle is the 'longer-is-larger' error (judging 0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits). Guidance centres on place-value alignment, equalising with trailing zeros, naming decimals by their place ('sixty-two thousandths') to keep place meaning audible, and building expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers.

activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner picks 0.372 as larger because '372 > 38', line the decimals up tenths-under-tenths and compare the tenths first (3 vs 3, equal), then the hundredths (7 vs 8), so 0.372 < 0.38. Padding to 0.380 shows equal-length strings so the digit-count argument disappears.
If the grid shading surprises them — the 'shorter' 0.38 shades MORE squares than the 'longer' 0.372 — ask them to restate why: 0.380 > 0.372 because the deciding place (hundredths) has 8 > 7.
Reinforce by naming the deciding place aloud: 'they are equal in the tenths, so the hundredths decides.'
activities.rationale: Comparison to thousandths depends on place-value alignment. Aligning columns, padding trailing zeros and identifying the first differing place makes the >,=,< decision follow from meaning rather than memorised rules, and directly targets the 'longer-is-larger' misconception. A grid and a number line give two further views of the same magnitude relationship.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).

activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths', ask which place the word 'thousandths' names (the third place). The 2 must sit there, so 62 becomes 062: 5.062.
Check the reverse: ask them to read 5.62 and 5.062 aloud and notice these are different numbers (sixty-two hundredths vs sixty-two thousandths).
activities.rationale: Reading digit-by-digit ('point zero six two') hides place meaning. Naming the place of the final digit forces correct placement and surfaces the need for placeholder zeros, addressing the dropped-zero error.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.

activities.title: Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers
feedback: If a learner writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths digit, extend the ×10-to-the-left / ÷10-to-the-right pattern through the point: the place right of ones is 1/10, so the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10.
If a digit is attached to the wrong unit fraction (e.g. 1/10 given to the hundredths digit), re-read the chart left-to-right naming each place in turn.
activities.rationale: Expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers binds each digit to its place and prevents expanding decimal digits with whole-number multipliers. A static labelled number with revealed place values is a useful anchor but does not itself perform the comparison alignment, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Tap or point to each digit of a number such as 347.392 and name its place and value.
Write the expanded form binding each digit to its place: 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000).
Say what each digit is worth, e.g. 'the 9 is worth 9 hundredths, 9×(1/100)'.
Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the decimal point: each place is one tenth of the place to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
Check a tricky case: the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10, NOT by 10 or 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Expanded form makes each digit's value explicit. Decimal places continue the base-ten pattern to the right with unit-fraction multipliers (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000), one tenth of the place to the left.

activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)
feedback: If the learner argues from digit count, redirect to the tenths-under-tenths alignment and ask which place first differs.
Accept a correct answer only with a place-value justification, not just the right symbol.
activities.rationale: A discussion that baits and corrects the 'longer-is-larger' error can usefully surface a learner's reasoning, though learners should still manipulate aligned place values to resolve the comparison. Treat talk as a complement to the alignment work, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.

activities.title: Check and order several decimals
feedback: For a comparison item, mark a digit-count answer wrong and prompt a place-value re-check with padded zeros.
For the ordering item, have the learner write all values to the same number of places first (0.300, 0.290, 0.305, 0.310), then order the aligned strings.
For the fill-in item, confirm the placeholder zero lands in the tenths place (5.062, not 5.62).
activities.rationale: Comparing, writing from words and ordering mixed-length decimals checks the key skills and misconceptions. This verifies understanding built through manipulation and discussion; it does not by itself build the alignment intuition.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.

constraints: Read decimals with place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the place meaning stays audible.
Equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) when comparing; this exposes 'longer-is-larger' as false without changing value.
Watch for over-correction to 'shorter-is-larger' (fewer digits = closer to the whole); length alone decides nothing — only the first differing place does.
5.062 is not 5.62: keep placeholder zeros when a spoken place name requires the final digit to sit further right.

A static labelled number with revealed place values anchors reading and expanded form but cannot carry out the padding/alignment that resolves comparisons; use it alongside the comparison activity, not instead of it.
Recognition or multiple-choice checks verify the skill but do not require the learner to construct alignment reasoning independently; include tasks where they write and justify.

Grid shading, column-highlight tools and a number line to hundredths/thousandths are illustrative, complementary supports for the comparison mechanism, not required equipment; the reasoning can also be carried out on paper by writing values to equal length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's 'quiz' companion and 'conversation' options were retained as the check/ordering activity and the discussion activity respectively, with product and fit-ranking vocabulary removed.
The source keyRepresentations listed a 'number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison'; it is reinstated as an optional comparison representation in Activity 1 and the constraints.

The source claimed decimal notation is 'planar and symbolic' so '3D adds no explanatory power' for this topic; this is a reasonable scoping judgement for comparison/notation but is not an established universal law, so it is not asserted as one here.

The original framing that an interactive comparator uniquely makes comparison 'felt, not memorised' is softened: alignment, grid and trailing-zero reasoning can also be done on paper; the interactive example is one concrete medium.
The second CCSS-M source is marked unverified in the row (verified:false); its claim is retained as stated but not treated as independently confirmed.
Activity 5's insight was narrowed to the forms it actually tests (numeral/word forms and ordering); expanded-form checking remains in Activity 3.

probeDeeper: Line up 0.372 and 0.38 by place — which is bigger and why?
Write sixty-two thousandths on its own — where does the 0 go?
In 347.392, what is the 9 worth?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Longer decimal is larger': says 0.372 > 0.38 because 372 > 38 / it has more digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align by place (tenths under tenths); compare tenths first (3 vs 8). Pad with a zero (0.380) to see equal-length strings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The decimal with more digits is chosen regardless of place value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero in a spoken decimal: writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third place, so 062 fills tenths–hundredths–thousandths → 5.062.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sixty-two thousandths is placed in the tenths/hundredths instead of hundredths/thousandths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form mishandles the fractional places: writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths instead of 3×(1/10)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the point: each place is 1/10 of the one to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Decimal digits are expanded with whole-number multipliers.

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'longer-is-larger', drops placeholder zeros, or expands decimals with whole-number multipliers.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded) and compares decimals to thousandths by place value, keeping placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads/writes tidy decimals but slips on comparisons of unequal length or on spoken thousandths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38? Line them up to decide. Write “five and sixty-two thousandths” as a decimal. Then write 347.392 in expanded form.' Watch the comparison reasoning and the placeholder zero in the thousandths write.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 0.372 vs 0.38 is the classic 'longer-is-larger' trap — a child comparing digit-strings picks 0.372. 'Sixty-two thousandths' needs a placeholder zero in the tenths (5.062), catching the child who writes 5.62. Expanded form checks each decimal place carries its unit fraction.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 10 million — like 4,302,617 — and say the value of any digit in the number?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10 000 000 and determine the value of each digit.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.A.2 (read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, <) extended by 5.NBT place value; CCSS does not name a 10,000,000 ceiling explicitly.
• Operational details: Group digits into three-digit PERIODS (ones, thousands, millions) separated by commas/spaces; read each period as a three-digit number followed by its period name. Stress that the comma structure, not the raw digit count, drives reading. Handle placeholder zeros within and between periods (7,045,200). Order by scanning from the most significant digit; align by periods.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 4,302,561 in words.' Tier B: 'State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200.' Tier C: 'Order four seven-digit numbers and justify using the leading digits.'
bestPractices: Teach reading by three-digit periods (ones/thousands/millions): read the period as a 3-digit number, then say its name — the comma grouping is the reading tool
Foreground internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (7,045,200) as the main difficulty; require the child to hold empty places
Order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time
Move fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, and value-of-a-digit statements ('the 7 is worth seven million')
Use real 7-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful, not just symbol-copying
keyRepresentations: Period-grouped place-value chart with Millions | Thousands | Ones panels
Three-pane translator: numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form
Comma/space separators as period boundaries
Number line / magnitude bar for ordering seven-digit values

Losing period boundaries and reading digit-by-digit for very large numbers
Confusing face value with place value (the 7 as 'seven' not 'seven million')
Assuming more digits always means larger without aligning periods when digit counts match
Inserting or omitting 'and' / mis-segmenting when writing in words

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and state the value of each digit. The core difficulty is the three-digit PERIOD structure (ones, thousands, millions) and holding placeholder zeros (e.g. 7,045,200). Learners should build numbers, translate fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, state digit values as place value (the 7 in 7,045,200 is 'seven million'), and order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time.

activities.title: Period builder with live three-way echo
feedback: If the words and the numeral stop corresponding (e.g. reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping the internal zero), rebuild in the period-labelled grid and read each three-digit group, then attach its period name.

If a digit's value is misnamed (e.g. the 7 as 'seven' or 'seven hundred thousand'), count columns from the right in threes to find the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
Point out explicitly that the internal zero in 7,045,200 is doing a job: it holds a place even though it is not spoken.
activities.rationale: A live builder that groups digits into periods and simultaneously echoes numeral, words and expanded form is intended to make the period structure and placeholder-zero handling operative as the child constructs numbers, rather than only described. Linked numeral/words/expanded panels and live recomputation are optional interaction examples that make the reading mechanism concrete. The cited standards describe the content and the numeral/number-name/expanded-form representations being practised; they are not evidence that this interaction is more effective than another medium.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
4.NBT.A.2: read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, <.
learnerActions: Set each digit onto a place-value chart labelled Millions | Thousands | Ones, grouped into three-digit periods.

As each digit is placed, watch the number appear three ways at once: the comma-grouped numeral (e.g. 7,045,200), the words read period by period ('seven million, forty-five thousand, two hundred'), and the expanded form.

Deliberately build numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (e.g. set the hundred-thousands place — the leading digit of the thousands period — to 0, as in 7,045,200) and observe how the words panel skips the empty place without dropping the period boundary.
State aloud, for a chosen digit, its full place value (e.g. 'the 7 is worth seven million').
activities.intendedInsight: The comma/period grouping — not the raw digit count — is what lets you read a large number aloud; each nonzero three-digit period is read as a number then given its period name (the ones period has no spoken name, and a period that is all zeros, as in 7,000,200, is skipped entirely), and an internal zero silently holds a column without being spoken.

activities.title: Write, value and order on paper (consolidation)
feedback: If ordering is done by length or first digit only, align the numbers vertically by place and compare digit by digit; with equal leading digits, keep comparing rightward until a difference appears — here 3,204,000 and 3,240,000 agree until the ten-thousands digit (0 vs 4) within the thousands period.
After writing in words, re-check the period breaks: 'How did you know where to put the comma/period breaks?'
Probe the placeholder zero: 'What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?' and extend with 'Write the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.'
activities.rationale: These read/write/value/order tasks are directly assessable and consolidate the notation-heavy procedure. The near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) discriminates place-by-place comparison from shortcuts like length or first digit. These are proposed consolidation tasks, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Write 4,302,561 in words (answer: four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one).
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 (answer: seven million).
For the ordering, align the numbers by place and compare left-to-right, moving right only when digits tie; say which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing, valuing and ordering seven-digit numbers all rely on the same period structure and on place-by-place comparison, including when leading digits agree.

activities.title: Labelled reference number with tap-to-reveal periods
feedback: If a learner relies only on this fixed example, move them to constructing their own numbers so they practise assembling arbitrary values and resolving orderings themselves.
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled example with tap-to-reveal period names and digit values is a useful reference anchor; it supports recognition and recall but does not by itself require the learner to assemble arbitrary numbers or resolve orderings. Pair it with build/write tasks.
learnerActions: Study a labelled seven-digit number (e.g. 4,302,561) and tap each three-digit period to reveal its name and read-out.
Tap an individual digit to reveal its place value.
Use this as a reference anchor while writing or ordering other numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly period-labelled example makes the millions/thousands/ones structure and per-digit place values visible as a stable reference.

activities.title: Dictation and 'why isn't the zero spoken?' discussion
feedback: If the dictated number is written with wrong grouping (especially around an internal zero), rebuild it in the period grid and align each spoken group to a period.
Prompt the learner to justify comma/period placement rather than count digits.
activities.rationale: Spoken dictation plus responsive discussion can probe the reasoning behind placeholder zeros and period breaks; it may complement, rather than replace, interactive construction of the notation. This is a proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Listen to a mentor dictate a large number in words and write it as a comma-grouped numeral.
Explain why a placeholder zero (e.g. in 7,045,200) is not spoken yet must still be written.
Discuss how the comma/period breaks map to the spoken words.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why an internal zero holds a place without being spoken is intended to support and strengthen the learner's grasp of the period structure.

constraints: Target objective: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine each digit's value, including numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros.
State digit values as place value (e.g. 'seven million'), not face value ('seven').
Order by scanning most-significant-digit-first with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time; do not order by digit count or first digit alone when lengths/leading digits match.

The tap-to-reveal labelled number is a reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not elicit independent construction of arbitrary numbers or ordering decisions; pair it with build/write tasks. This is a narrow affordance limit, not a claim that reference examples cannot teach.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice value-of-digit) can assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct words or resolve an ordering; include production tasks (writing in words, assembling numbers, ordering).
Use real seven-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful rather than symbol-copying.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the UK DfE National Curriculum claim as verified=true and the CCSS 4.NBT.A.2 claim as verified=false; retained as provided without re-checking.
The source observes that CCSS does not explicitly name a 10,000,000 ceiling; the upper bound comes from the UK Y6 standard. Treated as a scope note, not a universal claim.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' and framed a quiz as only a 'co-consolidator'; these are catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws, and have been expressed as affordance/limit statements rather than claims that any medium cannot teach.

The original correct answer writes 'three hundred two thousand' without 'and'; UK convention often inserts 'and' (e.g. 'three hundred and two thousand, five hundred and sixty-one'). Retained as given; the pedagogy notes mis-insertion/omission of 'and' as a known writing error.

The curriculum source claims attached to the builder activity support the content and representations (numeral/number name/expanded form), not the effectiveness of the interactive medium; efficacy wording is kept conservative throughout.

probeDeeper: How did you know where to put the commas when writing it in words?
What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?
For the ordering, which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000?
Write me the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one. (2) seven million. (3) 3,024,000; 3,204,000; 3,240,000; 3,420,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Period/grouping error — misreads 4,302,561 (e.g. 'four hundred thirty thousand...') or writes it as digits with wrong grouping, especially around the internal zero.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the number in a period-labelled place-value grid (millions | thousands | ones); read each three-digit group then attach its period name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words and digits do not correspond; the millions or thousands period is mislabelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place when valuing a digit — gives the 7 in 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred thousand' or just 'seven'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns from the right in threes to name the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit value is off by one or more powers of ten; child counts columns unreliably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by length or first digit only — with equal leading digits, compares wrongly or guesses, ignoring later place values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the numbers vertically by place and compare left-to-right digit by digit, moving right only when digits tie.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ordering breaks on the near-identical numbers; child stops comparing once early digits match.

responseLevels.gap: Misgroups periods, misvalues digits by powers of ten, or orders by length/first digit.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes, values and orders seven-digit numbers reliably, using period structure and left-to-right place comparison, including numbers with internal zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most seven-digit numbers but stumbles on internal zeros or on comparing numbers that agree in the leading digits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks on paper. (1) Write 4,302,561 in words. (2) State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200. (3) Order these smallest to largest: 3,240,000; 3,204,000; 3,024,000; 3,420,000.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch how the child handles the periods and the internal zeros. Reading to millions requires grouping digits into millions/thousands/ones periods and holding placeholder zeros; the near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) exposes whether comparison is done place-by-place or by a shortcut like length or first digit.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Powers of Ten Notation
topic.description: Interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; convert between ordinary numbers and standard form
evidence: Convert large and small numbers into standard form A × 10ⁿ
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary notation
Compare and order numbers given in standard form
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write 3,400,000 as 3.4 × 10⁶ and convert back — understanding that standard form is a shorthand for very large or very small numbers?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 12–14 — interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ (1 ≤ A < 10, n an integer); convert between ordinary numbers and standard form.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ A < 10, where n is a positive or negative integer.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 8.EE.A.3 (express and estimate very large/small quantities as a single digit times a power of ten) and 8.EE.A.4 (operate with and compare numbers in scientific notation).
• Operational details: Standard form re-expresses a number as one digit before the point (1 ≤ A < 10) times a power of ten; positive n for large numbers, negative n for small. Converting is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift counted: n is how many places the point moves. Compare by exponent first (bigger power = bigger number, for positive values), then by A. Enforce the 1 ≤ A < 10 normalisation (34 × 10⁶ is not standard form).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 12): 'Write 4,500,000 in standard form.' Tier B: 'Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number.' Tier C: 'Order 6.1×10⁵, 9.8×10⁴ and 2.3×10⁶ and explain your method.'
bestPractices: Connect standard form directly to the ×10/÷10 place-value shift — the exponent counts how many places the digits move
Enforce the normalisation 1 ≤ A < 10 and use non-examples (34×10⁶, 0.5×10³) to police it
Handle positive n (large numbers) and negative n (small numbers) together so the exponent's sign carries meaning
Compare numbers in standard form by exponent first, then mantissa A, rather than converting everything back
Ground very large/small quantities in real contexts (astronomical distances, atomic sizes) so standard form is seen as a tool for scale
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with the point shifting n places for ×10ⁿ
A × 10ⁿ template with a normalisation guard on A (1 ≤ A < 10)
Number line / scale strip spanning many orders of magnitude
Ordering cards comparing by exponent then mantissa
commonMisconceptions: Leaving A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 (writing 34 × 10⁵ or 0.34 × 10⁷)
Miscounting the exponent — using the number of zeros incorrectly, or wrong sign for small numbers
Moving the digits the wrong direction for negative exponents (3.2×10⁻⁴ written as 32000)
Comparing by mantissa first and ignoring the exponent's dominance
Thinking a negative exponent makes the number negative rather than small/positive

learn.summary: For learners aged 12–14: interpret, convert and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is any integer. The central idea is that the exponent counts and directs the ×10/÷10 place-value shift — positive n for large numbers, negative n for small positive numbers — and that A must be kept in the range 1 ≤ A < 10 so each number has a unique form. For positive values, comparison is done by exponent first, then by A to break ties.

activities.title: Dial-the-exponent place-value converter
feedback: If you converted 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to 32000, you moved the wrong way — a negative exponent means ÷10 each time, so the decimal point moves LEFT (the digits shift right into smaller place values), giving 0.00032. Convert back: 0.00032 = 3.2 ÷ 10,000 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴.

If you left A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 (e.g. 34 × 10⁵ or 0.34 × 10⁷), adjust A and n together: making A ten times smaller means n increases by one, so 34 × 10⁵ = 3.4 × 10⁶; making A ten times larger means n decreases by one, so 0.34 × 10⁷ = 3.4 × 10⁶ — the ordinary number must stay the same.
If your exponent is off by one, convert back and count: 4.7 × 10³ = 4,700, which is not 47,000, so recount the place-shifts to get 4.7 × 10⁴.
activities.rationale: Linking a mantissa–exponent control to a live place-value chart makes conversion and the 1 ≤ A < 10 normalisation visible as place-value movement, directly addressing the common errors of wrong-direction shifts for negative exponents and mis-normalised A. A live converter with a normalisation guard and a scale strip are optional mechanisms that make this concrete; the same learning can be done on paper with a place-value chart and counted point-moves. The interactive mechanism is a proposed, untested scaffold.
learnerActions: Set up two linked views: an ordinary number shown on a place-value chart, and an A × 10ⁿ expression you can change.

Starting with A = 4.5 and n = 0, increase n and watch the digits slide LEFT into higher place-value columns (equivalently, the decimal point moves right) one column per unit of n until 4.5 becomes 4,500,000 (4.5 × 10⁶); describe what each change of n does to the place value.

Now set A = 3.2 and n = −4; watch the digits slide RIGHT four columns into smaller place values (equivalently, the decimal point moves left four places) to give 0.00032, and state in words why the result is small but still positive.

Deliberately type an expression like 34 × 10⁵ and notice it is flagged as not in standard form; renormalise it yourself to 3.4 × 10⁶ by adjusting A and n together, then check the ordinary number is unchanged.
Record a short rule: 'n is how many places the point moves — right for positive n, left for negative n — and n never makes the number negative.'
activities.intendedInsight: Standard form is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift turned into notation: the exponent counts and directs how many columns the digits move, and a negative exponent makes a number small, not negative.

activities.title: Order standard-form numbers by scale
feedback: If you said 9.8 × 10⁴ > 3.2 × 10⁵ because 9.8 > 3.2, convert both: 98,000 vs 320,000 — the larger exponent wins, so compare exponents first and use A only to break ties.

If you ranked by coefficient alone — for example calling 9 × 10² the largest because its coefficient 9 is the biggest — remember 9 × 10² = 900 but 1.5 × 10³ = 1,500: a higher power of ten outweighs a larger coefficient.
Good: comparing exponents first and converting back as a check are two reliable ways to confirm your order.
activities.rationale: Ordering tasks that force a conflict between a large mantissa and a larger exponent target the documented 'compare by mantissa first' error and establish the exponent-first comparison rule for positive, normalised values.
learnerActions: Place 6.1 × 10⁵, 9.8 × 10⁴ and 2.3 × 10⁶ in order from smallest to largest; a magnitude scale strip can help you position them.
First decide the order by comparing exponents only (for these positive numbers, a bigger power means a bigger number), then use A only to break ties.
Test the trap directly: decide which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴; justify by exponent (5 beats 4) and confirm by converting to 320,000 vs 98,000.
Order 2 × 10³, 9 × 10² and 1.5 × 10³ and explain why 9 × 10² is smallest even though its coefficient 9 is the largest.
Write one sentence explaining your comparison method.
activities.intendedInsight: For positive numbers in standard form with A normalised to 1 ≤ A < 10, the exponent dominates the comparison; the mantissa A only matters when exponents are equal.

activities.title: Consolidate with two-way conversion checks
feedback: 4,500,000 = 4.5 × 10⁶ (count six place-shifts from 4.5).
3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032, not 32000 — a negative exponent moves the decimal point left (the digits shift right into smaller place values).
47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴ and 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10⁻³; if you got 4.7 × 10³ or 3.2 × 10⁻², recount by converting back.

If an answer fails its reverse-check, the error is often an off-by-one in the exponent, but it may be a wrong-direction shift (such as 32000 for 3.2 × 10⁻⁴) — recount the point moves and check their direction.
activities.rationale: Converting both directions and comparing standard-form numbers are cleanly checkable tasks that consolidate the procedure once the place-value shift is understood; the reverse-check builds self-correction. This reinforces fluency rather than first-time concept building. The reverse-check routine is a proposed practice, not an empirically validated intervention.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: 4,500,000 = ___ × 10ⁿ, keeping 1 ≤ A < 10 and stating n.
Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number, resisting the tempting wrong answer of 32000.
Convert 47,000 and 0.0032 into standard form, then convert each answer back to check you land on the original number.
For every answer, verify by reversing the conversion so an off-by-one exponent is caught immediately.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion, with a reverse-check habit, catches exponent miscounts and wrong-direction shifts.

activities.title: Argue about the negative exponent
feedback: If you said 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ is negative, note that 10⁻⁴ = 1/10,000, a positive fraction, so 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032 > 0.
A convincing argument separates 'sign of the number' from 'sign of the exponent': the exponent only tells you how many times to multiply or divide by 10.
activities.rationale: A structured dialogue can surface and challenge the 'negative exponent = negative number' misconception by demanding justification; it may complement, rather than replace, the procedural digit-shift practice. Note that a dialogue can prompt justification but does not by itself exercise the procedural conversion.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Is 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ a negative number? Convince me.'
Explain, using 10⁻³ = 1/10³, why a negative exponent produces a small positive amount, not a negative value.
Contrast 10³, 10⁰ and 10⁻³ on a place-value scale to show how the exponent's sign controls size but never the sign of the number.
activities.intendedInsight: The sign of the exponent controls how large or small the number is, separately from whether the number itself is positive or negative.

activities.title: Ground standard form in real scales
feedback: Check that, in a base unit such as metres, very small quantities (atomic sizes) use negative exponents and very large ones (astronomical distances) use positive exponents.
A static scale illustrates purpose well but cannot perform or check your conversions — do the conversions yourself and verify them.
activities.rationale: Grounding very large and very small quantities in real contexts motivates standard form as a tool for scale. An annotated scale is illustrative; it supports motivation and reading of values but does not by itself enforce normalisation or exercise conversion.
learnerActions: Examine an orders-of-magnitude scale (for example from a grain of sand to a galaxy, or atomic size to astronomical distance) and express several labelled quantities in standard form.
For each quantity, state whether n is positive or negative and what that tells you about the size.
Explain why standard form is useful for writing very large and very small quantities compactly.
activities.intendedInsight: Standard form is a practical tool for expressing and comparing quantities that span many orders of magnitude.

constraints: Enforce 1 ≤ A < 10; use non-examples such as 34 × 10⁶ and 0.5 × 10³ to make the normalisation rule explicit.
Teach positive n (large numbers) and negative n (small positive numbers) together so the sign of the exponent carries meaning.
A fixed scale poster or illustration motivates and displays values but cannot perform conversions or enforce normalisation; use it alongside, not instead of, active conversion practice.

Recognition-only or single-answer selection consolidates fluency but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify conversions; include tasks where learners produce the conversion and check it.
Keep the sign of the number distinct from the sign of the exponent throughout: a negative exponent never makes a number negative.
Scope the exponent-first comparison rule to positive, normalised values (1 ≤ A < 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources are national/standards documents (listed as verified:false in the source row); they support the curriculum scope (interpret/convert/compare standard form; express and estimate very large/small quantities using powers of ten) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity, mechanism or medium. Accordingly, every activity's sourceClaims is [], because each rationale rests on a specific teaching mechanism or framing (interactive converter, conflict-ordering, reverse-check habit, real-scale motivation) that no source addresses.

The original row's claim that '3D adds nothing' for this symbolic topic was removed as unsupported catalog-ranking boilerplate; standard form is symbolic and essentially one-dimensional, so a spatial 3D model is simply not the natural representation here, but no universal necessity or medium-superiority claim is asserted.

Self-audit of worked values: 4.5 × 10⁶ = 4,500,000; 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032; 47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴; 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10⁻³; 34 × 10⁵ = 3.4 × 10⁶; 6.1 × 10⁻³ = 0.0061; 3.2 × 10⁵ = 320,000 > 9.8 × 10⁴ = 98,000; 2 × 10³ = 2,000, 9 × 10² = 900, 1.5 × 10³ = 1,500 — all consistent and retained. The deliberately wrong distractor 32000 for 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ is only ever presented as an error to be corrected, never as a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Is 10⁻³ a negative number or a small positive one? How do you know?
Convert your 4.7 × 10⁴ back to an ordinary number — do you land on 47,000?
Order these: 2 × 10³, 9 × 10², 1.5 × 10³.
assess.correctAnswer: 4.7 × 10⁴; 3.2 × 10⁻³; 0.0061; and 3.2 × 10⁵ is larger (exponent 5 beats 4).

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes A outside 1 ≤ A < 10: '47 × 10³' or '0.47 × 10⁴'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the rule and its purpose (one non-zero digit before the point, so every number has a unique form). Adjust A and the exponent together on a few examples.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The coefficient is not a single non-zero digit before the point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a negative exponent as making the number negative: reads 6.1 × 10⁻³ as −6100 or −0.0061
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate sign of number from sign of exponent: 10⁻³ = 1/10³, a small POSITIVE amount. Contrast 10³, 10⁰, 10⁻³ on a place-value scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ordinary-form answer is negative.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by the mantissa, ignoring the power: says 9.8 × 10⁴ > 3.2 × 10⁵ because 9.8 > 3.2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert both to ordinary form (320,000 vs 98,000) to expose the size gap; then formalise: compare exponents first, mantissa only to break ties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The larger number is chosen by the coefficient alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place-shifts, giving an off-by-one exponent (47,000 → 4.7 × 10³, or 0.0032 → 3.2 × 10⁻²)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — have them convert back to check (4.7 × 10³ = 4,700 ≠ 47,000) and recount the decimal-point moves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A is correct but n is one out.

responseLevels.gap: Writes A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 or treats a negative index as a negative number.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions for large and small numbers keeping 1 ≤ A < 10, handles negative indices as small positives, and compares/orders by exponent then mantissa.
responseLevels.partial: Converts straightforward large numbers but errs on small numbers, negative indices, or comparison.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Write 47,000 in standard form. Write 0.0032 in standard form. Write 6.1 × 10⁻³ as an ordinary number. Then: which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴?' Watch the value of A they choose, how they treat the negative index, and how they compare.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each item targets one documented slip: the two conversions check whether A is kept in 1 ≤ A < 10 and whether the exponent is counted correctly in each direction; 6.1 × 10⁻³ checks the 'negative index = negative number' error; the comparison checks whether they order by exponent or wrongly by the mantissa.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a number like 4,738 to the nearest 10 (4,740), 100 (4,700), or 1,000 (5,000) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by deciding which multiple it is CLOSER to on the number line (4,367 → 4,370 / 4,400 / 4,000), using the midpoint as the tipping point and the convention 'halfway rounds up'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line FIRST: mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits. Only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint. Emphasise that the target place determines the bounding multiples, and handle the halfway convention and cascade cases (e.g. 4,970 to nearest 100). Link to estimation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): rounds to the nearest 10 using a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): rounds to 10/100/1000 and explains via nearer multiple / midpoint. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles halfway and cascade cases and uses rounding to estimate calculations.
bestPractices: Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line before any digit rule — the line gives the meaning.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the midpoint is the tipping point.
Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint so it is understood, not memorised.
Make explicit that the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).
Teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100) deliberately; link to estimating calculations.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two bounding multiples and midpoint (the canonical model)
Place-value chart to identify the rounding digit and the decider digit
'Rounding hill'/rollercoaster midpoint image
0-10,000 line for rounding to 1000
Estimation contexts (sensible approximations)
commonMisconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line FIRST — mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits — then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule as a shortcut justified by the midpoint. Core worked example: 4,367 rounds to 4,370 (nearest 10), 4,400 (nearest 100), 4,000 (nearest 1000). Deliberately teach the halfway convention (half rounds up) and cascade/carry cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100). Includes a number-line manipulation activity, a consolidation assessment with targeted traps, and a static reference image as a scaffold.

activities.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
feedback: If a learner rounds 4,367 to 4,300, drag the marker and point to the midpoint 4,350: 4,367 is past it, so it is nearer 4,400.

If a learner uses the wrong digit for nearest 100 (inspecting the 7, which is the ones digit, or the 3, the hundreds digit itself, instead of the 6, the tens digit that decides), name the decider digit — one place to the right of the rounding place — mark it, and look only at that.
If a learner keeps trailing digits (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67), show on the line that the rounded value must be a multiple of 100, so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
For the cascade 4,970 → 5,000, walk the single carry rather than reteaching everything: 4,970 is 49 hundreds and 70, so 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; rehearse near the boundary.
activities.rationale: Grounding rounding in number-line nearness and the midpoint before formalising the digit rule builds understanding and helps avoid rote truncation errors; dragging across the midpoint makes the decision rule concrete and visible. The place selector and cascade animation are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism tangible, not mandatory implementation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).

activities.title: Consolidation across places with targeted traps
feedback: For a halfway case like 2,650 to the nearest 100, if the learner always rounds down (2,600), state the agreed convention (half rounds up, so 2,650 → 2,700) and mark the midpoint on the line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
For 1,970 to the nearest 100, the carried answer is 2,000; if they produce 1,900 or a malformed value, walk the single carry: 1,970 is 19 hundreds and 70, so 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
If a rounded answer is not a clean multiple of the target place, return to the number line to show the rounded value must land exactly on a multiple.
activities.rationale: After the line meaning is built, varied practice across places with specific traps consolidates the procedure and surfaces the remaining failure mechanisms (wrong decider digit, halfway habit, carry past 9). A recognition/fill format is useful for consolidation and checking; note it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the number-line justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Round given numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (e.g. round 4,367 to each place) via fill-in or multiple choice.
First select the target place, then round, so the two steps stay distinct.
Tackle deliberately chosen trap cases: the halfway case 2,650 to the nearest 100 (which rounds up to 2,700), and the cascade case 1,970 to the nearest 100 (which carries to 2,000).
Match numbers to their rounded values across places.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding can be applied reliably across different target places, including the halfway (5) and nine-cascade cases, once the nearness meaning is secure.

activities.title: Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why a number rounds a certain way, point to the midpoint on the hill and ask which side the number is on.
Prompt the learner to then carry out the nearness decision themselves on a live number line, not just read it off the poster.
activities.rationale: A static image or 'roll to nearer multiple' tap is a helpful reference and reminder, but the nearness decision is best made by the learner acting on a line; treat this as a scaffold that supports, rather than replaces, active rounding.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Use a static rounding-hill / number-line poster showing the two bounding multiples and the marked midpoint as a reference while rounding.
Optionally tap a number on the hill to watch it roll to the nearer multiple, with the midpoint marked, as a reminder of the nearness decision.
activities.intendedInsight: A visual 'hill' with a marked midpoint reminds learners that rounding goes to the nearer multiple and that the midpoint decides direction.

constraints: Teach rounding as a number-line nearness decision FIRST; only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint, so it is understood rather than memorised.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).

Deliberately teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade/carry cases (e.g. 4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100); state the convention explicitly since 'half rounds up' is a chosen convention, not a mathematical necessity.
The rounded value must be a multiple of the target place: all digits after the rounding place become zero.
Avoid chained/successive rounding (rounding ones, then tens, then hundreds); rounding to a target place is a single decision from the original number.

The static hill/poster is a reference scaffold; its limit is that it shows rather than requires the learner's own nearness decision. A fill/multiple-choice format consolidates and checks but does not by itself require the learner to construct the number-line justification.
When assessing, watch the working (which digit decides and what happens to trailing digits), not only the final number, to reveal which rule the child is running.

The decider digit for a target place is the digit one place to the RIGHT of it (for 4,367 to nearest 100 the decider is the tens digit 6, not the hundreds digit 3, the ones digit 7, or the thousands digit 4).
Carry arithmetic must match the actual number: 4,970 → 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; 1,970 → 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The candidate originally miscomputed the 4,970 cascade carry as '19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000' (reasoning that belongs to 1,970). Corrected to 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000 at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source's wrong-decider-digit misconception listed 'the 7 or the 4' for 4,367 to the nearest hundred; the 4 is the thousands digit and contradicts the pattern's own description (hundreds digit itself or ones digit). Corrected to the 7 (ones) or the 3 (hundreds digit itself), with 6 (tens) as the correct decider.

The source assessment includes a double-rounding probe (4,347): rounding to the nearest ten gives 4,350, then to the nearest hundred (half-up) gives 4,400, whereas rounding straight to the nearest hundred gives 4,300 — these differ. Any demonstration must make clear the straight-to-hundred answer (4,300) is correct and chained rounding is the error being exposed.

The source correctAnswer '4,400; 2,000; 2,700' maps to the diagnosticPrompt cases (4,367 / 1,970 / 2,650 to nearest hundred), not the probeDeeper prompts (e.g. 2,999 to nearest ten is 3,000); these probe numbers were not reconstructable and were not propagated into learner-facing material. Reviewers should confirm intended probe numbers and answers.

The original row's '3D adds nothing' / 'open dialogue adds little' fit judgements were catalog preferences and are not propagated as universal claims. A number line is naturally planar, but this does not establish that other media cannot support rounding.

Two of three sources are marked unverified in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of the number-line-first approach is not independently established here beyond the cited claim about grounding rounding in nearness.

probeDeeper: Round 2,999 to the nearest ten — what happens to the other digits?
Show me on a number line why 4,367 rounds to 4,400 and not 4,300.
Round 4,347 to the nearest ten, then round THAT to the nearest hundred. Now round 4,347 straight to the nearest hundred — do you get the same? (double-rounding)
assess.correctAnswer: 4,400; 2,000; 2,700 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the hundreds, then replacing all digits after the hundreds place with zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides using the wrong digit — the hundreds digit itself, or the final (ones) digit — instead of the digit one place to the right of the rounding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the 'decider' digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you're rounding to. Mark it, then look only at that. Reground with place-value columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 4,367 to the nearest hundred the child inspects the 7 or the 4, not the 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves the trailing digits unchanged (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line, show the rounded value must be a multiple of 100 — so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rounded answer still carries the original tens/ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Always rounds a 5 down (or always up) regardless of convention: 2,650 → 2,600
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the class convention (half rounds up) and mark the midpoint on a number line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Halfway case is resolved by a fixed 'down' habit rather than the agreed rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to carry when rounding up past a 9: 1,970 → 1,900 or 1,1000 instead of 2,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole procedure — walk the single carry: 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000. Rehearse on a number line near the boundary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The nine-cascade case gives a malformed or non-carried answer.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider digit or leaves trailing digits in place; rounded value is not a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to nearest 10/100/1000 accurately including the 5 and 9-cascade cases, zeroes trailing digits, and justifies by nearer multiple on a number line.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases correctly but mishandles the halfway 5, the carry past 9, or which place to look at.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 4,367 to the nearest hundred. Now round 1,970 to the nearest hundred. Now round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.' Ask them to show it on a number line for at least one. Watch which digit they use to decide and what they do to the digits after it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases are chosen to trip specific mechanisms: 4,367 checks whether trailing digits are zeroed; 1,970 forces a carry past 9 into the thousands; 2,650 is the halfway (5) case. Watching the working — not the final number alone — reveals which rule the child is running.
