topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Rounding Large Numbers
topic.description: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
evidence: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 (460,000)
Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 and explain the boundary case
Use rounding to estimate the sum of 387,412 + 214,560
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a large number like 346,712 to the nearest 1,000 (347,000) or 10,000 (350,000) — identifying which digit to look at for each rounding?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000, using the same number-line nearness / midpoint reasoning applied to a chosen larger place — e.g. 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 is 460,000. Extends rounding to higher places and to boundary/cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Keep the number-line/midpoint meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples; identify the rounding place and the single decider digit to its right (ignore the rest). Rehearse the target place selecting the bounding multiples, the halfway convention, and cascade cases where rounding up rolls a 9 over. Link explicitly to estimating large calculations.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): rounds a six-digit number to the nearest 10,000 using a landmarked line. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): rounds to any specified place and explains via the decider digit / nearer multiple. Tier C (age 10, extending): handles cascade/boundary cases (950,500→1,000,000) and uses rounding to estimate sums.
bestPractices: Scale the number-line/midpoint model to large bounding multiples; keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning.
Identify the rounding place and the SINGLE decider digit to its right; the rest are irrelevant.
Make explicit that the requested place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Rehearse the halfway convention and cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
Link to estimating large sums/differences and checking reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Number line with large bounding multiples and midpoint
Place-value chart marking the rounding digit and decider digit
0-1,000,000 line rescaled per target place
Estimation contexts (populations, budgets)
'Rounding hill' midpoint image scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Looking at the wrong decider digit or rounding to the wrong place.
Successive/chained rounding across places instead of one decision.
Truncating (always down) or always up.
Cascade errors (950,500 to nearest 100,000 mishandled).
Losing place value in the unchanged trailing digits (they become zeros).

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000. Keep the number-line 'nearer multiple' meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples: identify the rounding place, read the single decider digit immediately to its right, zero everything after the rounding place, and handle halfway and cascade/boundary cases (e.g. 950,500 → 1,000,000). Link to estimating large sums and checking reasonableness.

activities.title: Scaled rounding bench: drag across the midpoint
feedback: If a learner reads a column other than the one immediately to the right of the rounding place: mark the target place and its single decider digit on a labelled six-digit place-value chart and look only at that digit.

If the rounded answer keeps later digits (e.g. 456,782 → 456,000 or keeps the 782): on the number line point out the answer must be a multiple of the target place, so everything after it becomes zero.
If a learner rounds step-by-step across several places instead of making one decision: return to the single decider digit for the chosen place only.
Reinforce correct work by having them say 'nearer to ___ than to ___, so it rounds to ___.'
activities.rationale: A draggable marker between large bounding multiples with a visible midpoint makes the nearness decision concrete and lets the decider-digit rule be derived rather than memorised; dragging across the midpoint and watching the result flip, plus watching trailing digits collapse to zero, ties the procedure to meaning. A place selector that rescales the line shows how the requested place chooses the bounds.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Year 5 pupils should 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
learnerActions: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000: place it on a number line between the bounding multiples 450,000 and 460,000, with the midpoint 455,000 flagged.
Decide which multiple it is nearer and state the rounded value (460,000); check it against the midpoint.
Change the target place to nearest 100,000 so the line rescales to the bounding multiples 400,000 and 500,000 (midpoint 450,000), and round 456,782 again (it is past the midpoint, so 500,000).
After each decision, write out the rounded number and confirm every digit after the rounding place is now zero.
Explain which single digit you used to decide (the one immediately to the right of the rounding place) and why the rest are irrelevant.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a large number is the same nearness decision scaled up: the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples and the midpoint, the one decider digit settles the decision, and all trailing digits become zeros.

activities.title: Cascade and boundary cases
feedback: If the boundary case is not carried (950,500 → 900,000): walk only the single carry rather than reteaching the whole rule — 9 hundred-thousands rounding up becomes 1,000,000. Rehearse near the boundary on a number line.
If a learner is unsure at the exact midpoint: state and apply the agreed halfway convention (conventionally round up) and name it aloud.
activities.rationale: Cascade cases are the common failure point and need targeted rehearsal at the boundary; animating or tracing the roll from 9 to the next place makes the carry visible.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
learnerActions: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000, placing it between 900,000 and 1,000,000 with the midpoint 950,000 flagged.
Decide whether it rounds up (it is just past the midpoint) and work the carry explicitly: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000.
Try a case that sits exactly on a midpoint (e.g. 950,000 to the nearest 100,000), state the convention you are using (round half up), and give the result (1,000,000).
Explain in your own words what happens when rounding up rolls a 9 over into the next place.
activities.intendedInsight: When rounding up at a 9, the carry rolls into the next higher place; the rounded value can gain a digit (950,500 → 1,000,000), and this is still a single rounding decision, not chained rounding.

activities.title: Round to estimate a large sum
feedback: If a learner computes the exact sum instead of estimating: ask them to round each number first, then add the rounded values.
If estimates are far off: discuss whether the chosen place was appropriate for the numbers involved.
Confirm a correct estimate such as 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 and relate it back to the rounding decisions made.
activities.rationale: Linking rounding to estimation of large, meaningful quantities gives the procedure a purpose and reinforces place-value reasoning; this is an explicit curriculum aim in the original pedagogy, though no source claim speaks directly to estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding each addend to a sensible place before adding — for example, treat the numbers as two town populations you want a quick combined total for.
Round each number (e.g. to the nearest 100,000: 400,000 and 200,000) and add to get about 600,000.
State why the estimate is reasonable and how it could be used to check a full calculation (e.g. a budget total or population count).
Try estimating to a different place and discuss how the choice of place affects how close the estimate is.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding supports quick, sensible estimates of large real quantities (populations, budgets) and a reasonableness check on exact answers; the chosen rounding place trades precision for simplicity.

activities.title: Consolidation: round to any specified place
feedback: If a rounded value is not a multiple of the target place, it is wrong — re-check that trailing digits are zeroed.

If a learner always rounds down (truncates) or always rounds up regardless of the digits: compare the number to the midpoint and read the decider digit — rounding up and rounding down each happen depending on that digit, not by habit.
For cascade traps, confirm the carry rolled into the next place correctly.
Use the decider-digit explanation as the mark of secure understanding rather than a correct answer alone.
activities.rationale: Practice with varied place targets, halfway and cascade cases consolidates the rule and surfaces the common misconceptions for feedback. This activity emphasises applied practice; items that only require selecting an answer check recognition and should be paired with learners stating their reasoning to elicit the procedure.
sourceClaims: Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Given a six-digit number and a target place, state the two bounding multiples, the midpoint, the decider digit, and the rounded value.
Work a mixed set that includes a cascade trap (e.g. 950,500) and a halfway case.
Match several numbers to their rounded values for a stated place, and spot any that are not clean multiples of the target place.
Choose the place, then round — justify the bounding multiples the place implies.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to any place up to 100,000 becomes fluent and self-checked: the answer is always a clean multiple of the target place.

constraints: Keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning; the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Use only the single decider digit immediately to the right of the rounding place; the remaining digits are irrelevant to the decision and become zeros.
Make one rounding decision per task; do not round step-by-step across successive places (chained rounding is an error).
State and apply a halfway convention explicitly (conventionally round up) and name it when at an exact midpoint.
Rounding direction depends on the decider digit relative to the midpoint; do not always round down (truncate) or always round up.

A static scaled 'rounding hill' or poster is a useful reference but does not itself require the learner to act on the decision; pair it with a task where the learner makes and justifies the rounding decision.
Selected-response items (multiple choice, matching) check recognition; to elicit the procedure, also require the learner to construct or explain the rounding decision.

Number-line nearness is a one-dimensional model, so a flat line with bounding multiples and a midpoint is sufficient and no 3D representation is needed for this objective; this is a scoped sufficiency note, not a claim that other media cannot teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked values: 456,782 → 460,000 (nearest 10,000; decider digit 6 → up; bounds 450,000/460,000, mid 455,000) and → 500,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up; bounds 400,000/500,000, mid 450,000); 950,500 → 1,000,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up, carry rolls 9→10 hundred-thousands); estimate 387,412 + 214,560 ≈ 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000. All consistent.

The original recommendation's '400,000–500,000' for nearest 100,000 are the correct bounding multiples for 456,782, and the rounded value is 500,000 (decider digit 5). There is no original error here.

The original fit judgements ('open dialogue adds little'; conversation/3D as poor fit) are catalog verdicts, not established pedagogy; retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes (planar model suffices here; selected-response checks recognition), not as universal superiority claims.
Halfway convention (round-half-up) is a stated convention; alternative conventions exist and the choice should be made explicit to learners.
CCSS 4.NBT.3 and the NCETM source are marked verified:false in the row; claims are retained as cited without fresh verification.

Watching the columns used exposes the mechanism.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Estimating by rounding
topic.description: Use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values
evidence: Estimate the answer to a calculation by rounding all values appropriately
Calculate upper and lower bounds of a rounded measurement
Express error intervals using inequality notation
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a length is measured as 7 cm to the nearest cm, can {{name}} say the actual length could be anywhere from 6.5 cm to 7.5 cm — understanding that rounding creates a range of possible values?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 12–14 — use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors; express error intervals using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): relates to 7.EE.B.3 (estimate to check reasonableness) and high-school N.Q.A (accuracy, error, appropriate quantities); explicit bound-interval notation is more prominent in UK than US.
• Operational details: A rounded value stands for a RANGE: a measurement given to the nearest unit lies within half a unit either side (a length 'to the nearest cm' of 12 cm means 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5). Find lower and upper bounds as rounded-value ± half the rounding unit, and write the interval with the correct inclusive/exclusive symbols (lower bound included, upper bound excluded by convention). Use rounding to estimate calculation results and judge reasonableness.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 12): 'A mass is 5 kg to the nearest kg — give the smallest it could be.' Tier B: 'Write the error interval for a length of 24 cm measured to the nearest cm.' Tier C: 'Estimate 61.2 × 3.9 by rounding, then state whether your estimate is over or under and why.'
bestPractices: Treat a rounded value as representing a half-unit-wide interval, not a single exact number
Compute lower/upper bounds as value ± half the rounding unit, and use the a ≤ x < b convention (lower included, upper excluded)
Distinguish strict from inclusive symbols carefully at each bound
Use estimation (round each value) to check calculations and judge whether the estimate over- or under-shoots
Ground bounds in measurement contexts (the true length lies within the interval implied by the instrument's precision)
keyRepresentations: Number line with the rounded value central and the half-unit interval bracketed (open/closed ends)
Bound-bracket diagram: lower bound ●──rounded value──○ upper bound
Half-unit strip showing ±0.5 of the rounding unit
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with exact values and over/under flags
commonMisconceptions: Treating a rounded measurement as exact (12 cm means exactly 12)
Using ± a whole unit rather than half a unit for the bounds
Getting the inclusive/exclusive symbols the wrong way round at the bounds
Assuming the upper bound is the rounded value itself (12.5 rounded to 12 but writing x ≤ 12)
Forgetting to halve the LAST place unit (nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05)

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: treat a rounded value as an interval on the number line that is one rounding unit wide (half a unit on each side), compute lower and upper bounds as value ± half the rounding unit, and write error intervals with the correct inclusive/exclusive convention for round-half-up (lower bound included, upper bound excluded, e.g. 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5). Also use rounding to estimate calculation results and judge whether an estimate over- or under-shoots, comparing with the exact value when the rounding directions conflict. The central insight is that a single rounded number stands for a RANGE, and the upper end is excluded because at exactly halfway it would round up to the next value.

activities.title: Bounds explorer on a number line
feedback: If the interval is sized ±1 (e.g. 11 to 13): the interval only reaches HALFWAY to each neighbour, so it is ±0.5 — 11.5 up to 12.5. Mark the midpoints between 12 and its neighbours.
If both ends are drawn closed: ask what 12.5 rounds to — it rounds up to 13, so 12.5 is excluded (open). The lower bound 11.5 rounds up to 12, so it IS included (closed).
If the ±5 / ±0.05 cases are missed: halve the LAST place unit — nearest 10 gives ±5, nearest 0.1 gives ±0.05.
activities.rationale: Bound intervals are spatial regions around a value; a manipulable number line with open/closed ends and a draggable true-value marker is intended to make both the half-unit width and the exclusion of the top end concrete, and dragging the marker to the top end to see it round up is intended to help with the misconception that the upper bound is included. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Enter a rounded value and its rounding unit (e.g. 12 to the nearest cm).
Mark on a number line a closed point at the lower bound (11.5) and an open point at the upper bound (12.5), labelling the interval 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5.
Place a 'true measurement' marker anywhere inside the bracket and check it stays within the half-unit each side.
Drag the true marker to the open upper end and reason about what happens: 12.5 would round up to 13, so it is excluded from this interval.
Change the rounding unit to 'nearest 10' and redraw the bracket at ±5; try 'nearest 0.1' and redraw at ±0.05.
activities.intendedInsight: A single rounded number really stands for an interval one rounding unit wide, with half a unit on EACH side; the upper bound is the excluded (open) end of the bracket because exactly halfway rounds up to the next value.

activities.title: Writing and checking error intervals
feedback: Correct interval for 24 cm to nearest cm: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5.
If both ends are inclusive (23.5 ≤ x ≤ 24.5): 24.5 rounds to 25, not 24, so it is excluded — use <. The lower end 23.5 rounds up to 24, so it is included — use ≤.
Smallest mass for 5 kg to nearest kg: 4.5 kg (included). There is no single largest value: the mass can be any value less than 5.5 kg, and 5.5 kg is the upper bound but is excluded.
If the top is written as ≤ the rounded value (x ≤ 24): the upper bound is 24.5, not 24 — the rounded value sits in the MIDDLE of the interval.
activities.rationale: Once the interval idea is built, stating bounds and writing intervals can be practised with short fill-in and multiple-choice style prompts, intended to consolidate the mixed ≤ / < convention. This format may consolidate and check, but does not by itself build the spatial interval idea, and recognising a correct interval is not the same as producing one.
learnerActions: Write the error interval for a length of 24 cm measured to the nearest cm, using inequality notation.
State the lower and upper bounds separately and choose the correct symbol at each end.
Answer: for a mass given as 5 kg to the nearest kg, what is the smallest it could be?
Explain why the top bound uses < and not ≤ by saying what that top value would round to.
activities.intendedInsight: Bounds are value ± half the rounding unit, and the two ends use different symbols: the lower bound is included (it rounds up into the value) and the upper bound is excluded (it would round up to the next value).

activities.title: Estimate by rounding and judge over/under
feedback: Sensible estimate for 61.2 × 3.9: round to 60 × 4 = 240. Here 61.2 was rounded down and 3.9 up, so the over/under direction is not obvious from rounding alone — compare with the exact value (238.68): the estimate 240 is slightly over.
Sensible estimate for 412 × 5.8: round each to one significant figure, 400 × 6 = 2400. Note 5.8 rounds UP to 6, not down to 5. (Exact is 2389.6, so this estimate is slightly over.)
If the 'estimate' is barely simpler than the exact calculation (e.g. keeping 412 as 412): round to one significant figure so the mental arithmetic is easy.
If 5.8 is rounded down to 5: 5.8 is closer to 6, so it rounds up.
activities.rationale: Estimation through rounding is a distinct procedural skill that supports checking reasonableness; pairing rounded factors with the exact result and flagging over/under is intended to make the effect of each rounding visible.
sourceClaims: 7.EE.B.3 and high-school N.Q.A: estimate to assess reasonableness and reason about accuracy and error in measured quantities.
KS3 pupils use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b.
learnerActions: Estimate 61.2 × 3.9 by rounding each factor sensibly, then check against the exact value to say whether your estimate is over or under the true answer, noting which factor was rounded up and which down.
Estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding each factor to one significant figure, and state what you rounded each number to.
Compare your estimate with the exact value to find the direction of the error, and explain why the rounding alone could not tell you the direction when one factor was rounded up and the other down.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding each value to a convenient figure gives a quick reasonableness check; when both positive factors round the same way the over/under direction of the product is clear, but when they round in opposite directions you must compare with the exact value to see the actual direction.

constraints: The half-unit applies to the LAST place of the rounding unit: nearest unit → ±0.5, nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05.
Use the convention lower bound included (≤) and upper bound excluded (<); keep the strict/inclusive symbols distinct at each end.

A static labelled bracket diagram (e.g. 11.5 ●─ 12 ──○ 12.5 with the convention annotated) can illustrate one case, but on its own does not let the learner test the top-end exclusion or vary the rounding unit — use it as an illustration, not the main investigation.

Fill-in / multiple-choice prompts can consolidate and check stating bounds and intervals, but do not by themselves build the spatial interval concept; recognising a correct interval is not the same as producing one.

A mentor question such as 'the sign says 12 cm to the nearest cm — what is the smallest and largest it could truly be?' can productively challenge the belief that 12 is exact, as a complement to manipulating the interval.

Estimation requires actually rounding to a convenient figure (ideally one significant figure) and comparing with the exact value; when the two factors round in opposite directions, do not assert a single over/under direction from the rounding alone — compare with the exact value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and both listed sources carry verified:false. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording in the rationales has been qualified accordingly.

Activities[0] and [1] have sourceClaims set to [] because no source claim directly supports their design/format rationales (interactive-makes-concrete; fill-in consolidation). The KS3 notation claim supports the curriculum topic only, which is already carried by the objective and constraints.

The original assessment text states the correct answer interval as '23.5 ≤ x < 24.5' while the topic/standard wording cites 'a < x ≤ b'. For a value rounded to the nearest unit under round-half-up, the lower bound rounds up into the value (included, ≤) and the upper bound would round up to the next value (excluded, <), giving 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5. The activities use this correct convention; the quoted standard's 'a < x ≤ b' ordering is reproduced only as the cited claim and may reflect a general notational illustration — flagged for reviewer attention.

The original probe 'Why is the upper bound 24.5 and not 24.49?' is sound: 24.5 is the boundary because every value up to but not including 24.5 rounds to 24; it is retained in spirit within the interval feedback.

For 61.2 × 3.9 the original asks whether the estimate is over or under; because one factor rounds down and the other up, the direction is not determinable from rounding alone — the activity directs comparing with the exact value (238.68), which shows the estimate 240 is slightly over.

probeDeeper: Why is the upper bound 24.5 and not 24.49?
Does 24.5 round to 24 or 25? So which inequality sign belongs at the top?
What did you round 412 and 5.8 to, and why those values?
assess.correctAnswer: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5 (lower bound 23.5, upper bound 24.5); and about 400 × 6 = 2400.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the rounded value as exact, or sizes the interval by ±1 (23 to 25) instead of ±0.5
errorPatterns.nextMove: The interval reaches halfway to each neighbour: 23.5 up to 24.5. Mark the midpoints on a number line either side of 24.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No interval is given, or bounds are 23 and 25.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong inequality at the top — 23.5 ≤ x ≤ 24.5 (including 24.5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what 24.5 rounds to (25, not 24), so 24.5 is excluded: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5. The lower bound 23.5 rounds up to 24, so it IS included.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Both ends are inclusive.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds factors to over-precise or unhelpful values when estimating (e.g. keeps 412 as 412, or rounds 5.8 to 5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round each to one significant figure (400 and 6) for a quick check; note 5.8 rounds to 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The 'estimate' is barely simpler than the exact calculation, or 5.8 is rounded down.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the rounded value as exact or sizes the interval as ±1; estimates with no useful rounding.
responseLevels.full: States bounds as 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5 with correct signs and estimates by rounding each value sensibly.
responseLevels.partial: Gives a half-unit interval but muddles the ≤ / < convention, or rounds inconsistently when estimating.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'A length is measured as 24 cm to the nearest centimetre. Write its error interval using inequalities. Then estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding, and say what you rounded each number to.' Watch the bounds and the inequality signs.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rounded measurement forces the half-unit interval and the mixed ≤ / < convention (24.5 would round up, so it's excluded); the estimate checks sensible rounding of each factor. Watching reveals whether the child treats 24 as exact, mis-sizes the interval, or misuses the inequality signs.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Roman numerals to 100
topic.description: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
evidence: Read and write Roman numerals I, V, X, L, C and combinations up to 100
Convert between Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals (e.g. XLIV = 44)
Explain that Roman numerals have no zero and no place-value system
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like XIV (14) or XLII (42) — and do they know why we stopped using Roman numerals for most things once zero and place value were invented?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and combinations, incl. subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL) and convert to/from Hindu-Arabic. The deeper aim: appreciate BY CONTRAST that our system has place value and a zero, which Roman numerals lack — illuminating why place value is powerful.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; taught in some US curricula as enrichment/history of number.
• Operational details — Teach the symbol values and the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5−1, IX, XL, XC) as the tricky exception. Convert both directions. Crucially, run the CONTRAST explicitly: try 'writing' large or zero quantities in Roman and feel the absence of place value and a placeholder — making our base-ten system's efficiency vivid.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): reads/writes additive numerals (XVII, LX). Tier B (age 8-9, secure): handles subtractive pairs (XLIV = 44) both directions. Tier C (age 9, extending): explains why Roman has no zero/place value and why that makes calculation harder.
bestPractices: Teach symbol values, then the additive rule, then subtractive pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) as the key exception.
Practise conversion in both directions with real artefacts (clocks, dates, chapter numbers).
Run the explicit contrast: attempt a large number or 'zero' in Roman to FEEL the missing place value and placeholder.
Use the contrast to deepen appreciation of base-ten (position carries value; zero holds a place).
Watch the subtractive-notation errors (IIII vs IV, or invalid forms like IL).
keyRepresentations: Roman symbol→value reference (I,V,X,L,C)
Additive decomposition (XVII = 10+5+1+1) vs subtractive (IX = 10−1)
Side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic conversion chart
Real artefacts: clock faces, monument dates, book chapters
Place-value chart as the contrast (what Roman lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and their combinations, including subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL, XC) and convert both ways to Hindu-Arabic numbers. The deeper aim is to appreciate BY CONTRAST that our base-ten system carries value by position and uses zero as a placeholder, which Roman numerals lack — making vivid why place value is powerful. Teach symbol values, then the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5-1) as the tricky exception, and run the contrast explicitly by trying to write numbers that need many repeated symbols, a very large number, and zero in Roman.

activities.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
feedback: If IIII or VIIII is built, show the standard subtractive fix (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1) and explain that a smaller symbol placed before a larger one in one of the allowed pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract.
If an invalid form like IL is built for 49, show the valid XLIX and explain which subtractive pairs are allowed (IV, IX, XL, XC).

During the contrast challenge, place the Roman form beside the tidy base-ten numeral and name the real limits: unwieldy strings of repeated symbols (long for 88, far longer for a number like 3,000 within the taught set, with conventional large-number symbols like M lying beyond the taught set), and genuinely no symbol at all to put where our zero sits.
activities.rationale: Building and converting numerals by action with immediate correction surfaces the subtractive exception at the moment of error, and staging the 'write a long numeral / write zero' challenge lets the learner feel the absence of place value and a placeholder rather than just be told about it. A live value display and invalid-form flagging make the additive-versus-subtractive mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.

activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed
feedback: If the learner thinks the Roman system just needs a zero symbol added, point out that position must also carry value for zero to do its placeholder job.
Prompt the learner to connect the accountant's difficulty adding large numbers to the missing place value, not just unfamiliar symbols.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue may suit the history-of-number objective because the 'why did the system change?' story invites questioning and discussion; recognition tasks alone do not require the learner to articulate the reason. This is a proposed affordance rather than established superiority over other media, and it complements the building activity by foregrounding the reason behind the contrast.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.intendedInsight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.

activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
feedback: If XLIV is read additively as 66, show that a smaller symbol before a larger one in an allowed pair (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract: XL = 50-10 = 40, IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44.

If the learner says the first symbol 'is in the tens place', contrast directly: in 44 position sets value, but in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add or subtract — Roman has no place value and no zero.
Reinforce the standard subtractive forms (IV, IX, XL, XC), reject invalid ones like IL, and treat IIII as a non-standard clock-face variant rather than the standard way to write 4.
activities.rationale: Conversion in both directions, validity-of-form checks and real artefacts anchor the skill in genuine contexts. Recognition and matching tasks are useful for consolidation and checking but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a full explanation, so pair them with the spoken 'how do the two 4s differ?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
learnerActions: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.

activities.title: Reference chart and annotated clock face
feedback: When a learner uncovers a numeral's make-up, confirm whether it is additive (VII = 5+1+1) or subtractive (IX = 10-1).
Use the adjacent place-value chart to point out there is no column or symbol in Roman that behaves like our zero placeholder.
activities.rationale: A fixed chart or annotated image is a valuable reference and can teach symbol values, though it cannot itself be manipulated to compute values or stage the contrast — so it supports rather than replaces the building and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Keep a symbol-to-value reference to hand (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100).
Tap or point to each clock numeral to reveal its value and whether it is built additively or subtractively.
Use a side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic chart to check your conversions, and a place-value chart alongside to see what Roman lacks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference supports recall of symbol values and makes the additive/subtractive make-up of familiar numerals (like clock numbers) explicit.

constraints: The deeper objective is conceptual appreciation of place value and zero by contrast, not just symbol decoding; the contrast must be run explicitly (try to write a long numeral, a very large number, and zero in Roman).

Recognition and matching tasks consolidate and check the skill but do not by themselves elicit an independent spoken or written explanation of why our system differs; include a construct-an-explanation prompt.
A static chart or annotated image teaches symbol values and make-up but cannot be manipulated to compute values live or stage the balloon/zero contrast; treat it as a reference scaffold.

Valid subtractive forms are IV, IX, XL, XC; when writing, treat IIII and VIIII as non-standard (use IV and IX), noting that IIII is a traditional variant still seen on many clock faces, and reject invalid forms such as IL (for 49, use XLIX).
Roman numerals genuinely have no zero symbol and no positional place value — present this as the real system contrast, not as a claim about any particular teaching medium being uniquely necessary.

This topic teaches symbols I to C only; large numbers (e.g. 3,000) should be used to show how numerals become unwieldy within the taught set and that conventional large-number symbols such as M lie beyond those taught — not presented as part of the required symbol set, and not framed as literally 'running out' of symbols.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17 (correct); XL = 50-10 = 40 and IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44 (correct); LXXXVIII = 88 (correct); XLIX = 49 is the valid form, IL is invalid. The legacy additive misreading 'XLIV = 66' is retained only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The row's contrast example '3,000' is conventionally MMM (uses M, outside the taught I–C range); within the taught set it would require roughly thirty C's, i.e. an unwieldy ballooning string. It is therefore treated as a ballooning/beyond-taught illustration, NOT as a case of 'running out of symbols'. The only genuine 'no symbol at all' case is zero.

Two cited sources (CCSS-M absence note and NCETM place-value PD) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.
Comparative-efficacy wording about dialogue versus recognition has been softened to proposed/may phrasing; the source row does not establish superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: In 44, how is the first 4 different from the second 4?
Does the Roman system have a symbol for zero? Why does our system need one?
Read XLIV and split it into its chunks.
assess.correctAnswer: XLIV = 44 (XL = 40 by subtraction, IV = 4 by subtraction). It differs because Roman numerals combine symbols by value with no place value and no zero, whereas in 44 the two 4s mean different amounts (40 and 4) because of their POSITION, and we use 0 to hold empty places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads Roman numerals additively, ignoring subtractive order: XLIV = 10 + 50 + 1 + 5 = 66
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show smaller-before-larger means subtract: XL = 50 − 10 = 40, IV = 5 − 1 = 4. Re-read XLIV as 40 + 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sums all symbols regardless of a smaller-before-larger pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports place value into Roman numerals — thinks a symbol's position gives it a tens/ones value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly: in 44 position sets value; in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add/subtract. Roman has no zero and no place value.
errorPatterns.distractor: In XLIV the symbols get tens/ones values from their position, just like 44.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the first symbol 'is in the tens place' or that our 44 and XLIV work the same way.

responseLevels.gap: Reads Roman numerals additively (XLIV = 66) or claims they work like place value.
responseLevels.full: Reads/writes Roman numerals to 100 with subtraction and explains that Roman lacks place value and zero, unlike our positional system.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple Roman numerals but cannot articulate why our place-value system (with zero) differs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Read XLIV for me. Now tell me: how is the Roman way of writing forty-four different from the way we write 44? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Contrasting XLIV with 44 forces the child to articulate what place value actually does. A child who understands names position (the two 4s differ) and the role of zero; a child who doesn't either reads Roman additively (66) or wrongly imports place value into the Roman symbols. The reason tier exposes the systems contrast.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Roman numerals to 1000
topic.description: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
evidence: Read MCMXCIX as 1999
Write 2024 in Roman numerals (MMXXIV)
Explain the subtractive principle: IV = 4 not IIII
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like MMXIX (2019) or CDXLIV (444) — and recognise the year a film or building was made when it's shown in Roman numerals?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Read (and write) Roman numerals to 1000 including M, and read years written in Roman numerals — MCMXCIX = 1999; MMXXIV = 2024 — applying the subtractive principle (IV=4, CM=900) at larger scales. Consolidates Roman-numeral fluency and the place-value contrast in a real, dated context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; enrichment/history of number in some curricula.
• Operational details — Extend the symbol set to D (500) and M (1000) and the subtractive pairs to CD (400), CM (900); read/convert both directions. Years are the motivating context (film credits, monuments, clock towers) and are tricky because they chain multiple subtractive groups (MCMXCIX). Continue to leverage the base-ten contrast: writing a year in Roman shows how much longer and calculation-hostile it is than our place-value system.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): reads numerals with D and M additively (MDC). Tier B (age 9-10, secure): converts years both directions incl. one subtractive group (MMXXIV). Tier C (age 10, extending): reads multi-subtractive years (MCMXCIX) and explains why the notation is cumbersome vs base-ten.
bestPractices: Extend symbols to D and M and subtractive pairs to CD/CM; convert both directions.
Use years as the motivating real context (monuments, film credits, clock faces).
Parse complex years group by group (M | CM | XC | IX) to manage chained subtractive pairs.
Keep the base-ten contrast alive — note how long/awkward big years are in Roman.
Target multi-subtractive errors (IC for 99 instead of XCIX) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Extended symbol→value chart (I,V,X,L,C,D,M)
Group decomposition of a year (M|CM|XC|IX)
Real artefacts: dated monuments, film credits, clock towers
Side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic year
Place-value contrast chart (what Roman still lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Invalid subtractive forms at scale (IC/IM for 99/999 instead of XCIX/CMXCIX).
Reading chained subtractive groups additively (misreading MCMXCIX).
Confusing D and M values or omitting a group.
Pure-additive over-long strings (writing 900 as DCCCC not CM).
Thinking Roman numerals gained a zero/place value.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: read and write Roman numerals to 1000 (adding D=500, M=1000 and the subtractive pairs CD=400, CM=900), and read/write years such as MCMXCIX=1999 and MMXXIV=2024. The core skill is parsing chained additive and subtractive groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and understanding why, in the allowed pairs, a smaller symbol before a larger one means subtract. Keep a running contrast with base-ten place value: a year written in Roman is usually longer (though not always, e.g. MM for 2000) and is always awkward to calculate with compared with the compact four-digit numeral.

activities.title: Build and decode years with a symbol-tile decoder
feedback: If the string is read as a straight running sum (so IV becomes 6, or MCMXCIX is totalled incorrectly), highlight that a smaller symbol BEFORE a larger one is subtracted (IV = 5 − 1) while after it is added (VI = 6); then regroup into pairs.
If a learner writes IC for 99 or IM for 999, state the convention: subtract only I from V/X, X from L/C, C from D/M, so 99 = XCIX and 999 = CMXCIX (not IC or IM).
If D and M values are confused or a group is omitted, re-show the symbol→value chart and recount groups left to right.
When grouping is correct, name each chunk aloud (one thousand, nine hundred, ninety, nine) to confirm the decomposition.
activities.rationale: Live grouping and two-way conversion make the chained subtractive rule concrete and give immediate correction on invalid forms. Optional interaction examples: colour-coding each group, a value readout that updates as tiles are placed, and a flag with the corrected form when an invalid subtractive pair is built — these illustrate the mechanism but are not required or proven more effective than other media.
sourceClaims: Parsing years by subtractive groups and maintaining the base-ten contrast supports Roman-numeral fluency and place-value appreciation.
learnerActions: Assemble a year from symbol tiles including D and M, or read a given year such as MCMXCIX.
Split the year into coloured groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and state each group's value (1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 1999).
Convert both directions: read a Roman year into Hindu-Arabic, and write a modern year (e.g. 2024 → MMXXIV) in Roman.
Try an illegal shortcut such as IC for 99, see it flagged, and correct it to XCIX.
activities.intendedInsight: A long, intimidating Roman year is really a chain of familiar subtractive/additive groups; each group reads independently, and only certain subtractive pairs are valid.

activities.title: Roman vs base-ten contrast panel
feedback: If a learner thinks Roman numerals have a hidden zero or place value, point out that value comes from the symbols and their order, not from column position, and that there is no zero symbol.
Reinforce by counting how many characters the Roman year needs versus four digits (most years need more, e.g. MCMXCIX has seven, though a few such as MM for 2000 need fewer).
activities.rationale: Keeping the base-ten contrast alive deepens place-value appreciation rather than treating Roman numerals as an isolated curiosity.
sourceClaims: Parsing years by subtractive groups and maintaining the base-ten contrast supports Roman-numeral fluency and place-value appreciation.
learnerActions: Type or write a modern year and place its Roman form beside the compact Hindu-Arabic numeral.
Compare the length and readability of the two, and note that Roman lacks a zero and place value.
Try to imagine adding or multiplying two years in Roman form to feel why it is awkward.
activities.intendedInsight: A place-value system with zero is far more compact and calculation-friendly than additive/subtractive Roman notation.

activities.title: Read dates off real artefacts (guided)
feedback: If a date is misread, return to group-by-group decomposition before giving the full value.
Prompt the learner to justify why their grouping is valid (which subtractive pairs are allowed).
activities.rationale: Authentic dated examples supply the motivating context named in the pedagogy (monuments, film credits, foundation stones; clock faces give hour readings rather than years) and support both reading and spoken explanation. A guide/dialogue format may add motivation and spoken reasoning; it complements rather than replaces written conversion practice.
learnerActions: Look at dated monuments, film credits, foundation stones, or date inscriptions on clock towers that use Roman numerals (a clock face itself shows hours 1–12 rather than a year, and often writes 4 as IIII).
Decode each date into a modern year, saying how you split it into groups.
A guide or partner can read a date aloud and ask you to convert it, or ask you to write today's date in Roman.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman year notation appears in the real world; the same grouping skill decodes authentic dates.

constraints: Restrict subtractive pairs to the valid conventions: I before V/X, X before L/C, C before D/M; reject over-applied subtraction such as IC or IM, and use IV (not IIII) for 4 in standard writing, while noting that many clock faces traditionally show IIII as an accepted variant.

A static annotated artefact (monument date, clock face) is a useful reference and reading task but does not by itself exercise writing/producing Roman numerals; pair it with construction or two-way conversion for the full objective.

Matching and multiple-choice checks consolidate and assess reading, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a year; include tasks where the learner writes the Roman form themselves.
Keep genuinely dated examples (real years) rather than only abstract numerals so the 'recognise years' objective is met.
Interaction examples (colour grouping, live value readout, invalid-form flagging) are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms, and their efficacy relative to other media is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The pedagogy lists 'DCCCC not CM' as a pure-additive error for 900; this is consistent with standard convention (CM is preferred). Arithmetic checks pass: M|CM|XC|IX = 1000+900+90+9 = 1999, 999 = CMXCIX, and MMXXIV = 2000+20+4 = 2024.

Two source claims (CCSS absence; NCETM pedagogy) are marked verified:false in the row; do not treat them as confirmed. The DfE Year 5 statement is marked verified:true in the legacy data but has not been re-checked here. The DfE claim supports the curriculum objective (reading Roman numerals and recognising years) but does not establish the grouping/two-way-conversion teaching method, so it was not retained as a sourceClaim on the method-focused activity; the NCETM claim directly supports the grouping/base-ten method, though neither establishes efficacy of any particular interaction or medium.

The legacy 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and the claim that decoding is 'best drilled on a bench' are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; softened and not asserted as necessity.
The 3D-interactive 'no spatial dimension / adds nothing' judgement was dropped as a catalog ranking rather than an objective pedagogical law.

probeDeeper: Read MCMXCIX and show how you split it into chunks.
Why can't 99 be written IC?
Write 2024 in Roman numerals.
assess.correctAnswer: IV = 4 because a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted (5 − 1). MCMXCIX = M(1000) + CM(900) + XC(90) + IX(9) = 1999, read as subtractive pairs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds all symbols regardless of order: reads IV as 6 (I + V) or MCMXCIX as a running sum
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that a smaller symbol BEFORE a larger means subtract (IV = 5 − 1); after means add (VI = 6). Group MCMXCIX into subtractive pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats every symbol as additive and gets 6 for IV or a wrong total for 1999.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-applies subtraction: writes 99 as IC or 4 as IIII inconsistently, ignoring the same-power rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the convention: subtract only I from V/X, X from L/C, C from D/M; so 99 = XCIX, not IC. Practise valid vs invalid pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child offers IC for 99 or is unsure why IIII is disallowed.

responseLevels.gap: Adds symbols regardless of order, so IV = 6 and 1999 is misread.
responseLevels.full: Explains and applies the subtractive principle within the same-power rule, reading and writing years to 1000 (MCMXCIX = 1999, 2024 = MMXXIV).
responseLevels.partial: Handles simple subtractive pairs (IV, IX) but stumbles on multi-pair years like MCMXCIX or over-applies subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Why is four written IV and not IIII? Now read MCMXCIX for me — and tell me how you split it up to work it out.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The subtractive principle is the conceptual hinge: a child who only adds symbols reads IV as 6 and cannot parse the CM/XC/IX pairs in 1999; a child who understands order-and-subtraction explains IV and decodes 1999 by grouping. The reason tier exposes whether they see position as meaning subtract.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimal place value
topic.description: Round decimals with one decimal place to the nearest whole number
evidence: Round 3.7 to 4 and 3.2 to 3
Place 6.5 on a number line between 6 and 7 and decide it rounds to 7
Round a set of one-decimal-place numbers and explain the rounding rule
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures something as 3.7 m, can they tell you whether that rounds to 3 m or 4 m — and explain why?

pedagogy.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it is closest to on the number line — the tenths digit tells you which half you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is derived, not as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits.
bestPractices: Put the decimal on a number line between its two whole neighbours and ask 'which is it nearer?' before any rule
Mark the halfway point (e.g. 3.5) and treat 'round up at the midpoint' as an agreed convention introduced only once 'nearest' is secure
Distinguish rounding from truncating: 3.7 rounds to 4, it is not chopped to 3
Round to the NEAREST — resist teaching 'if there's anything after the point, go up' (that sends 3.2 to 4)
Have children round a set and articulate the rule as a consequence of distance, then check by estimating
keyRepresentations: Number line 3–4 with 3.7 plotted and 3.5 marked as halfway
Bead string / hundred square segment between two wholes
A 'rounding hill' where a ball rolls to the nearer whole
Place-value chart
commonMisconceptions: Truncates — drops the decimal and always rounds down (3.7 → 3)
Always rounds up when any decimal part is present (3.2 → 4)
Thinks the exact midpoint 3.5 rounds down, or is unsure what to do with it
Confuses rounding with changing the digit (3.7 → 3.10 / 4.0 muddle)

learn.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole number means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it lies closest to on a number line — the tenths digit tells you which half of the interval you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant from both wholes. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is then derived, rather than as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits. Target age 8–9 (Year 4).

activities.title: Which whole is it nearest? Placing decimals on a number line
feedback: If a learner gives 3 for 3.7: on the number line show that 3.7 is only 0.3 away from 4 but 0.7 away from 3, so it is nearer 4; contrast this with simply chopping off the part after the point.
If a learner gives 4 for 3.2: mark the halfway point 3.5 and show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3 — having 'something after the point' does not automatically mean round up.
If a learner is unsure what rounding means: contrast rounding 3.7 (to 4, the nearer whole) with chopping/truncating 3.7 (to 3, just dropping the part after the point) so the difference is explicit.
Reinforce correct reasoning by asking the learner to justify each answer by distance rather than by reciting a rule.
activities.rationale: Positioning the decimal between its two whole neighbours and asking 'which is it nearer?' is intended to make 'nearest' the felt basis of the rule and to help address the two dominant errors (truncating always-down and always-up). Statutory curriculum expects Year 4 pupils to round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number, and guidance recommends understanding rounding as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number' (verbatim statutory wording, Year 4 Number - fractions including decimals).

Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: Draw or use a number line from 3 to 4 with each tenth marked, and plot 3.7 on it.
Ask aloud: is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4, and roughly how much nearer? Measure or count the gaps (0.3 to 4, 0.7 to 3).
Plot 3.2 on the same line and decide which whole it is nearer, explaining from the position (0.2 to 3, 0.8 to 4).
Mark the halfway point 3.5 and say what is special about it.
Repeat with a fresh set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 2.8, 5.1, 7.4), stating each result and why.

Finally state the rule in your own words as a consequence of distance: 'look at the tenths — if it is in the lower half it rounds down, in the upper half it rounds up, and the exact midpoint follows the agreed convention.'
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding is a nearness judgement on a line: the whole you round to is the one the number is closer to. The tenths digit is a shortcut that reports which half of the interval you are in, not an arbitrary 'chop or bump' instruction.

activities.title: The midpoint x.5 and the round-up convention
feedback: If a learner gives 6 for 6.5 or hesitates: establish first that 6.5 is equidistant from 6 and 7, then introduce 'round half up' as a shared rule everyone agrees to use.
If a learner thinks the midpoint 'obviously' goes up for a distance reason: clarify that both wholes are exactly as far away, so the up-choice is a convention, not because 7 is nearer.
Praise a learner who can say 6.5 is the special equidistant case and that the convention is a choice.
activities.rationale: Separating the equidistant midpoint from ordinary nearness cases is intended to help address the misconception that the midpoint defaults down or is undefined, and correctly frames 'round half up' as a convention. This builds on, rather than replaces, the number-line understanding of 'nearest'.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: On a number line from 6 to 7, place 6.5 and measure its distance to 6 and to 7.
Confirm that 6.5 is exactly halfway — equally far from both wholes — so distance alone cannot decide.
Discuss who decides what happens here, and learn that the agreed convention is 'round half up', so 6.5 rounds to 7.
Try other midpoints (e.g. 2.5, 4.5) and apply the same agreed convention, stating that this is a shared choice, not a distance fact.
Explain in your own words the difference between 6.5 (needs the convention) and 6.7 (decided by nearness).
activities.intendedInsight: The exact midpoint is the one case nearness does not settle because it is equidistant; 'round half up' is an agreed convention introduced once 'nearest' is secure, not an extension of the distance rule.

activities.title: Sort and check a set of roundings
feedback: If a learner sorts 3.5 into 'rounds to 3': remind them it is the equidistant midpoint and the agreed convention sends it up to 4.
If a learner sorts 3.2 into 'rounds to 4': return to the halfway mark and show 3.2 is in the lower half, nearer 3.
If a learner sorts everything with a decimal into 'rounds to 4': this is the always-up error — check each against the midpoint.
Confirm a correct sort by asking the learner to re-state the rule as a consequence of nearness.
activities.rationale: Practising over a varied set surfaces both truncation and always-up errors across many cases, and requiring a distance justification keeps the rule grounded in 'nearest' rather than a memorised recipe. This is a consolidation/checking activity rather than the initial teaching.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2) and sort each into 'rounds to 3' or 'rounds to 4'.
For each number, say its distance to each whole, or which half it is in, to justify your sort.

Round 3.7 correctly to 4, then show the two common error patterns on the numbers where each actually goes wrong: truncation wrongly gives 3 for 3.7 (dropping the part after the point), while the always-up error wrongly sends numbers like 3.2 to 4.
Check your whole set by estimating and asking whether each answer is sensible.
State the rounding rule aloud as a summary of what the sort shows.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a set is cleanly checkable, and articulating why each number rounds as it does consolidates the distance-based reason behind the digit rule.

constraints: Teach 'nearest' on a number line FIRST; introduce the 'round up at 5' rule only afterwards and only for the exact midpoint, framed as an agreed convention, not a distance fact.
Do not teach 'if there is anything after the point, go up' — that wrongly sends 3.2 to 4. The tenths digit indicates which half of the interval the number is in.
Distinguish rounding from truncating explicitly: 3.7 rounds to 4; it is not chopped to 3.
Avoid muddling rounding with changing digits (e.g. 3.7 becoming 3.10 or a stray 4.0 confusion); the result is a whole number.

When illustrating error patterns, attach each error to a number where it actually produces a wrong answer: truncation errs on 3.7 (gives 3), always-up errs on 3.2 (gives 4). Do not present the always-up answer (4) as a 'wrong move' for 3.7, whose correct answer is 4.

A static labelled number line with tap-to-reveal can display one rounding as a reference aid, but it does not let a learner test many cases or feel why the midpoint is special, so it is a scaffold rather than the main teaching tool.
Selecting a rounded answer from options checks the outcome but does not by itself elicit the distance justification; pair any selection task with a spoken or written 'why'.
A number line captures nearness in one dimension; added depth or 3D representation is not needed here, though it is not claimed to be harmful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no comparative efficacy of any particular activity format is claimed.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 3.7 is 0.3 from 4 and 0.7 from 3, so it is nearer 4 (rounds to 4) — correct. 3.2 is 0.2 from 3 and 0.8 from 4, nearer 3 (rounds to 3) — correct. 6.5 and 3.5 are exactly equidistant, so 'round half up' is correctly presented as a convention, not a distance consequence. The sort set {3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2} resolves to rounds-to-3 {3.1, 3.4, 3.2} and rounds-to-4 {3.7, 3.8, 3.5} — consistent.
Confirmed the third activity does not treat 4 as a wrong answer for 3.7: 3.7 rounds correctly to 4, and the always-up error is attached to numbers like 3.2.
The source's diagnostic distinctions (truncation 3,3,6; always-up 4,4,7; secure 4,3,7) are internally consistent and preserved across the feedback branches.

Softened one rationale from 'directly confronts' to 'is intended to help address' so no untested activity format carries an unqualified efficacy claim; both cited sources support the number-line 'nearest' framing only, not any specific implementation.

probeDeeper: On the number line, is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4 — and roughly how much nearer?
Which whole is 3.2 closer to? How can you tell from the tenths digit?
6.5 is exactly halfway between 6 and 7 — so which one do we round to, and who decides that?
Does 'round' mean chop off the part after the point? What is different about rounding 3.7 and chopping 3.7?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.7 → 4 (nearer 4), 3.2 → 3 (nearer 3), 6.5 → 7 (exact midpoint, rounds up by convention). Justifies each by distance on the number line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates — chops the decimal and rounds everything down: 3.7 → 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, ask which whole 3.7 is nearer and by how much; contrast rounding with chopping explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 3 for 3.7; ignores the tenths digit entirely; treats 'round' as 'drop the bit after the point'

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds up whenever any decimal part is present: 3.2 → 4 ('there's a bit after the point so go up')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the halfway point; show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 4 for 3.2; rounds up regardless of the size of the tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the midpoint the wrong way or is unsure — 6.5 → 6, treating 'nearest' as undefined and defaulting down
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 6.5 is exactly halfway (equal distance to 6 and 7), then introduce the agreed 'round half up' convention as a shared rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 6 for 6.5, or hesitates and guesses; does not recognise it as equidistant

responseLevels.gap: Truncates (always down) or always rounds up regardless of the tenths; shows no sense of 'nearest'.
responseLevels.full: Rounds all three correctly, explains 3.7 is nearer 4 and 3.2 nearer 3, treats 6.5 as the midpoint that rounds up by convention, states the rule as a consequence of nearest, and transfers to a fresh set.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds 3.7 and 3.2 correctly by nearness on the line, but is unsure at the 6.5 midpoint, or applies '5 and up' without seeing it comes from distance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.7 to the nearest whole number, then 3.2, then 6.5. For each one, show me on a number line why you chose that whole.' Watch how they decide — do not give a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases pull apart the common errors: a truncator says 3, 3, 6; an always-up child says 4, 4, 7; a secure child says 4, 3, 7 and can explain WHY 6.5 is the special midpoint case. 6.5 is the hinge — only a child who understands 'nearest' recognises it as equidistant and knows the round-up convention is a choice, not a distance fact.
