topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimal place value (age 9+)
topic.description: Round decimals with two decimal places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place
evidence: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (3) and to 1 d.p. (3.5)
Round 12.95 to 1 d.p. (13.0) and explain the boundary case
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole number
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a length as 4.67 m, can they round it to the nearest whole metre — and also to the nearest tenth of a metre?

pedagogy.summary: Rounding a two-decimal-place number extends 'nearest' to a chosen precision: to the nearest whole, decide between the two neighbouring wholes; to one decimal place, decide between the two neighbouring tenths. The digit ONE place to the right of the target place is the decider. Two traps carry the topic: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the true nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is the everyday tool for ESTIMATION (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7).
bestPractices: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value; to the nearest whole, only the tenths digit decides (3.47 has 4 tenths, so it rounds to 3)
Identify the single deciding digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to
Handle the carry explicitly on a number line: 12.95 lies between 12.9 and 13.0 and is nearer 13.0, so the whole number changes
Keep the target place value: rounding 3.47 to 1dp gives 3.5, and 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13
Use rounding to estimate and sense-check (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7), and judge whether the estimate is above or below
keyRepresentations: Number line zoomed to the target precision (wholes; then tenths)
Place-value chart marking the target place and the deciding digit
Estimation on a number line for sums like 4.83 + 2.17
Boundary number line 12.9–13.0 for the carry case
commonMisconceptions: Double rounding: 3.47 → 3.5 → 4 to the nearest whole
Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (or a chain of digits) when rounding to a whole
Drops the boundary carry: 12.95 → 12.10 or 12.9 instead of 13.0
Omits the trailing zero / place: writes 13 when 1dp is asked, or truncates

learn.summary: Teaches rounding two-decimal-place numbers to the nearest whole and to one decimal place, treating rounding as choosing between two neighbouring values at a chosen precision, decided by the single digit immediately to the right of the target place. Two central traps: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is linked to estimation (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7); for this particular pair the rounding errors cancel, so the estimate equals the true sum. A zoomable number line is the lead activity because the same number can be rounded to different precisions and the carry can be watched; a set of checkable questions, a static annotated line, and diagnostic prompts are preserved as complementary tools.

activities.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
feedback: If a learner reaches 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole via 3.5, show on the line that 3.47 never reaches 3.5; round once, straight from the original, and only the tenths digit (4) counts.

If a learner writes 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp, show on the 12.9–13.0 line that 12.95 sits exactly halfway between 12.9 and 13.0, and that the usual rule (a deciding digit of 5 rounds up) gives 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
Reinforce keeping the target place: 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal': rounding 4.83 up by 0.17 and 2.17 down by 0.17 cancels, so 7 is neither above nor below 7.00 for this pair — a good moment to see that rounding errors can offset.
activities.rationale: A number line that can be re-zoomed lets the same number be rounded to different precisions so the deciding digit changes visibly, and the 12.95 carry can be watched rather than asserted. The optional zoom control, the midpoint marking, the side-by-side wrong-path comparison, and the 'ticking up' animation make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative, not mandatory. Source guidance frames rounding as choosing between a just-greater and just-less number located on a number line, and warns that applying a procedure without this awareness produces cascading/double rounding and boundary-carry (trail-of-9s) errors.
sourceClaims: Rounding to a chosen precision is 'choosing between two numbers, one just greater and one just less', decided by locating the number on a number line; 'memorising and applying a procedure... without this overall awareness often results in errors', including sequential/cascading rounding up (rounding an already-rounded value rather than in one step) and the 'trail of 9s' boundary carry (e.g. 9999 rounds to 10000), where a rounded digit ripples into the next place.
Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Plot 3.47 on a number line showing whole numbers 3 and 4; mark the 3.5 midpoint and judge that 3.47 sits just below it, so it is nearer 3.

Deliberately try the tempting wrong path: round 3.47 to 3.5 first, then watch 3.5 round up to 4 — the WRONG whole. Compare side by side with going straight from 3.47 (tenths digit 4, below half) which gives 3.
Zoom the line to tenths and round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).

Switch to a 12.9–13.0 view and round 12.95 to one decimal place; notice it sits exactly halfway, so by the usual rule (a deciding 5 rounds up) it snaps to 13.0, and watch the whole-number digit tick from 12 to 13 as the carry ripples in.

Use an estimation view to round 4.83 and 2.17 each to the nearest whole and add (5 + 2 = 7); then compare with the true sum (7.00) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal — here rounding 4.83 up and 2.17 down cancel, so the estimate equals the true total.
activities.intendedInsight: Round in ONE step from the original number; to the nearest whole only the tenths digit decides, so 3.47 → 3. The boundary carry (12.95 → 13.0) is a real event where a rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole, not a rule failure.

activities.title: Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner rounds 3.47 to a whole using the 7 (→ 4), re-establish the target place and show the single digit to its right is the only decider; have them point to it first.
If a learner rounds up 'because there are digits after', clarify that only that one deciding digit matters, not the presence of further digits.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating the target place and its single deciding digit targets the wrong-deciding-digit misconception. A static or tap-to-reveal chart serves as a reference aid; it labels the deciding digit for one case but does not itself animate precision-switching or the carry, so it supports rather than replaces the number-line activity.
learnerActions: Place a number such as 3.47 in a place-value chart and name the place you are rounding to.
Point to the ONE digit immediately to the right of that place as the sole decider before rounding — for rounding to a whole, the tenths digit (4); for rounding to 1dp, the hundredths digit.
Explain why the 7 (hundredths) does NOT decide the nearest whole of 3.47.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciding digit is exactly the one place to the right of the target place (the tenths when rounding to a whole, the hundredths when rounding to 1dp) — never a chain of digits.

activities.title: Checkable rounding and estimation questions
feedback: Answer 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole signals double rounding — revisit the one-step number-line comparison.
Answer 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp signals a dropped carry; 12.10 signals a mishandled carry — revisit the 12.9–13.0 line.
Answer 13 (without the .0) signals a lost trailing place — the question asked for 1dp, so write 13.0.
For the estimate, 'exactly equal' is correct here: the +0.17 and −0.17 rounding errors cancel, so accept it rather than requiring above/below.
activities.rationale: Rounding to a stated precision and estimation are cleanly checkable, and targeted distractors (4 from double rounding, 12.9 from a dropped carry, 13 from a lost place) surface specific misconceptions. This checkable format is well suited to practising and checking the procedure and surfacing these specific errors; it does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line makes visible, so it works best following the number-line work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (answer 3).
Fill the blank: 12.95 to 1dp = ___ (answer 13.0).

Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole (5 + 2 = 7) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the true total (7.00) — for this pair the rounding errors cancel, so it is exactly equal.
Round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can round correctly to a stated precision in one step and use rounding to estimate and sense-check a sum.

activities.title: Diagnostic sequence and probing questions
feedback: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure learner reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder gets 3.5 then 4.
12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: secure → 13.0; dropped carry → 12.9; wrong carry → 12.10.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal' as the correct relationship for 4.83 + 2.17: the rounding errors (+0.17 and −0.17) offset exactly, so the estimate 7 equals the true sum 7.00 — do not require above/below.
Finish by asking the learner to transfer the method to a new two-decimal-place number.
activities.rationale: These prompts come directly from the assessment design and separate the three error patterns (double rounding, carry-handling, truncation) while requiring the learner to articulate reasoning, supporting transfer to a new number. The estimate relationship is left open in the prompt so it genuinely diagnoses the learner's reasoning, with the 'errors cancel' explanation reserved for feedback.
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, then round 3.47 to one decimal place; say which single digit tells you each answer and why not the 7.
Round 12.95 to one decimal place and explain what happens to the whole-number part and why.
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole; then say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the real total.
If you said 3.5 and then 4 for the nearest whole, redo it going straight from 3.47 — which whole is it actually nearer?
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the deciding digit and the carry, in one step from the original, distinguishes secure rounding from double rounding, dropped/mishandled carry, and truncation.

constraints: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value.
Keep the target place value: rounding to 1dp requires the trailing place (write 13.0, not 13).
The static annotated number line and place-value chart are reference/scaffold aids: they can label the deciding digit for one case but do not demonstrate precision-switching or the carry dynamically.

The set of checkable questions checks answers and surfaces misconceptions via distractors; this format does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line shows, so pair it with the number-line work rather than treating it as the sole route to the nearness concept.
For the estimation example 4.83 + 2.17, the estimate (7) equals the true sum (7.00); do not require learners to pick 'above' or 'below' — accept 'exactly equal'.
Prerequisite reteach for double rounding and wrong-deciding-digit errors is flagged to an earlier place-value micro-topic in the source assessment.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original-row error corrected: the assessment's probe 'estimate 4.83 + 2.17 — is your estimate above or below the real total?' has no above/below answer, because rounding 4.83 up (+0.17) and 2.17 down (−0.17) cancel, giving estimate 7 = true 7.00. All learner-facing actions now allow 'exactly equal'; the diagnostic prompt is left open with the explanation in feedback. The original binary phrasing is noted here and in preservationAudit.uncertain, not reproduced as a required answer.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 3.47 to nearest whole = 3 (tenths 4 < 5), to 1dp = 3.5 (hundredths 7 ≥ 5); 12.95 to 1dp = 13.0 (carry correct); 4.83 → 5, 2.17 → 2, estimate 7 vs true 7.00 (equal). Distractors '4' (3.47) and '12.9'/'12.10'/'13' (12.95) are intentional wrong options and must never be presented as correct.

The source's 'poor fit' claims that depth 'adds nothing' and that a mechanical procedure offers no worthwhile dialogue are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws; omitted from learner-facing guidance rather than asserted as universal.

The source 'possible' claim that a static line 'cannot show precision-switching or the carry dynamically' is retained narrowly as a scaffold limitation, not as a claim that static images cannot teach.
Catalog artefact vocabulary ('quiz') was replaced with neutral descriptions ('set of checkable questions') in the summary and constraints.

probeDeeper: To round 3.47 to the nearest whole, which single digit tells you the answer — and why not the 7?
You said 3.5 and then 4 — what do you get going straight from 3.47? Which whole is it actually nearer?
Round 12.95 to one decimal place — what happens to the whole-number part, and why?
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each — is your estimate above or below the real total?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.47 → 3 (nearest whole; tenths digit is 4) and 3.5 (to 1dp); 12.95 → 13.0 (to 1dp, the carry ripples into the whole); 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Double rounding: rounds 3.47 to 3.5 first, then rounds 3.5 up to 4 for the nearest whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round once, straight from the original: to the nearest whole only the tenths digit (4) counts, so 3.47 → 3. Show on the line it never reaches 3.5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole, and explains it by first getting 3.5

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or mishandles the boundary carry: 12.95 → 1dp gives 12.9 or 12.10 instead of 13.0
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a 12.9–13.0 line, show 12.95 is nearer 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds the tenths up but leaves the whole unchanged (12.9), or writes an impossible 12.10

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (7) when rounding 3.47 to a whole, or rounds up because 'there are digits after'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the place being rounded to and the ONE digit immediately to its right as the sole decider; practise pointing to it before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds 3.47 to a whole by the 7 (→ 4), or cannot say which single digit decides

responseLevels.gap: Truncates or rounds by the wrong digit; cannot round to a stated precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to the nearest whole and to 1dp in ONE step from the original, handles the 12.95 → 13.0 carry, uses rounding to estimate 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7, explains which digit decides at each precision, and transfers to a new number.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds correctly to one precision but double-rounds when finding the nearest whole, or mishandles the 12.95 carry, or drops the trailing .0.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, and then round 3.47 to one decimal place. Next, round 12.95 to one decimal place. Finally, estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding.' Watch each step — especially whether they go via 3.5 for the whole, and what happens to 12.95.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure child reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder rounds to 3.5 first, then up to 4 — a different, wrong answer. 12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: a secure child gets 13.0, while others write 12.9 (ignored the carry) or 12.10 (carried wrongly). Together they separate double rounding, carry-handling, and truncation.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimal place value
topic.description: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
evidence: Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places (3.46)
Use rounding to estimate 4.83 × 2.17 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a decimal like 3.748 to one decimal place (3.7) or two decimal places (3.75) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy'; Y5 round decimals with two places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.4 'Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place' and 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
• Operational details: Round via NEARNESS on a number line — locate the number between the two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer. Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint (5-and-above is at/past halfway) rather than teaching it as an unexplained rule. Cover rounding both decimals (to dp) and large whole numbers (to nearest 10^k), and rounding for estimation (4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Round 3.46 to 1 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 and justify with the midpoint.' Tier C: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp and explain which digit decides it.'
bestPractices: Round as a nearness decision on a number line: mark the two candidate values, mark the midpoint, place the number, decide which it is closer to
Derive the next-digit rule from the midpoint (≥5 means at or past halfway → round up), rather than asserting it
Practise rounding decimals to a stated dp AND whole numbers to a stated place with the same nearness logic
Address the boundary/round-up cascade explicitly (rounding 3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, and 9.96 → 10.0)
Connect rounding to estimation — round each factor to check a calculation — so rounding has a purpose beyond the drill
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two rounding candidates and a marked midpoint
Place-value chart to isolate the rounding place and the deciding next digit
'Rounding hill/valley' visual (nearer candidate is downhill) for the midpoint decision
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with the exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: round decimals to any place and whole numbers to a required degree of accuracy by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line. Learners locate the number between its two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer — deriving the 'look at the next digit' rule from the midpoint rather than memorising it. Work covers decimals to a stated number of places, large whole numbers to a stated place, carry/round-up cascades over a 9, placeholder zeros, the risk of double rounding, and rounding for estimation.

activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
feedback: If the learner chops instead of rounding (e.g. 3.4567 to 2 dp written as 3.45), have them look at the digit just past the cut: 6 ≥ 5 means 3.4567 is past the midpoint 3.455 and so is nearer 3.46. Place it between 3.45 and 3.46 to see which is closer. (To 1 dp, chopping would give 3.4, but the correct answer is 3.5.)

If they round digit-by-digit (double rounding), use 3.4547 to 2 dp to show why it fails: rounding to 3 dp first gives 3.455, which then rounds up to 3.46, but a single decision at the hundredths place (decider thousandths 4 < 5) gives 3.45. Double rounding changed the answer — compare the full number to the single midpoint for the target place.
When a carry crosses a 9 (3.798 → 3.80), confirm the trailing zero stays because '2 decimal places' means two digits after the point.
If they are unsure about the exact-midpoint case, reinforce that at the midpoint and beyond the number rounds up to the higher candidate.
activities.rationale: Deriving the next-digit rule from the midpoint gives the procedure a reason, directly targeting double-rounding and 'always round 5 down' errors; the 3.4547 contrast makes the double-rounding hazard observable because the two routes disagree. An interactive number line that auto-brackets candidates, marks the midpoint, lets the learner place the number, lights the nearer segment, and highlights the deciding digit can make the nearness judgement concrete; these interaction examples are optional ways to realise the mechanism, not requirements.
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.

activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
feedback: If the learner gives 3.5 when 2 dp is asked, have them count decimal digits: 2 dp needs two, so the answer is 3.46.
If the wrong place is read for a large number, re-anchor on the chart: find the hundred-thousands column, then look one column to its right (the ten-thousands digit decides).
Keep the focus on the single decider digit, not on re-rounding digits further along.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart separates the target place from its decider, addressing wrong-precision errors and misreading places in large numbers. A static chart illustrates a case clearly; it is a scaffold that does not by itself let learners test arbitrary numbers or feel the boundary cascade.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.4: use place value understanding to round decimals to any place; 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
learnerActions: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.intendedInsight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.

activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
feedback: If the learner writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, point out it now shows only one decimal place; the correct answer is 2.40.
Distinguish this from a rounding mistake — the rounding was right, only the recorded precision is missing the zero.
For 9.96 → 10.0, confirm the whole-number carry still leaves a tenths place that must read 0.
activities.rationale: Carries that produce placeholder zeros are a distinct performance slip from the rounding decision itself, so they need their own targeted practice.
learnerActions: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.

activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
feedback: If the estimate is far from the exact answer, check whether each factor was rounded to a sensible place.
Encourage stating the chosen rounding place so the estimate's accuracy can be judged.
activities.rationale: Connecting rounding to estimation gives the skill a real use and reinforces the nearness idea across operations.
learnerActions: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.

constraints: Multiple-choice, slider, and fill-in response formats can consolidate and check rounding outcomes (e.g. a truncation distractor of 3.4 for 3.48), but recognising a correct rounded value does not by itself show the learner is reasoning from the midpoint; pair outcome checks with working that reveals the method.
A static annotated number line illustrates a single rounding case but does not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or experience a boundary cascade; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Dialogue prompts (e.g. 'you rounded 3.4567 to 3.46 — walk me through why, not digit by digit') can surface double-rounding and truncation errors; the nearness decision can also be made where the number is placed and compared spatially.
Round in one decision at the target place; do not round digit-by-digit (double rounding) and do not truncate.
Treat the exact midpoint and above as rounding up to the higher candidate; avoid 'always round 5 down'.
Preserve trailing/placeholder zeros that record the required place (2.40, not 2.4; 10.0, not 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Common Core claim as verified:false and the DfE claim as verified:true; confidence of the original row was 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

Self-audit: 3.4567 to 2 dp = 3.46 (decider 6 ≥ 5); to 1 dp = 3.5 (candidates 3.4/3.5, midpoint 3.45). 3.4547 to 2 dp = 3.45 directly, but 3.455 then 3.46 by double rounding (illustrates the hazard). 2.397 to 2 dp = 2.40 (carry keeps placeholder zero). 7,654,321 to nearest 100,000: midpoint 7,650,000, value above it, rounds to 7,700,000 (decider ten-thousands digit 5). 3.798 to 2 dp = 3.80. 9.96 to 1 dp = 10.0. 4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2 = 10 (exact ≈ 10.48). All consistent and checked.

The original row and recommendation wrote the 1-dp candidates as '3.40 and 3.50', displaying two decimal places for a one-decimal-place rounding; corrected in the learner action to '3.4 and 3.5' (midpoint 3.45) to avoid reinforcing a precision confusion.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale is a number-line/midpoint-derivation teaching principle that neither curriculum claim directly supports (the claims establish the topic/standard, not that pedagogy). The place-value-chart activity retains the CCSS 'use place value understanding' claim, which does support its principle.
The original diagnostic listed '2.40 (keeping the final zero)' for rounding 2.397 to 2 dp, which is correct; retained as the placeholder-zero teaching point.
The non-preferred 3D option was dropped because the source itself only noted it adds nothing for a one-dimensional number-line task; no universal claim about 3D is asserted.

probeDeeper: Round 2.397 to 2 dp — why must you keep the 0 on the end?
Round 3.4547 to 3 dp first, then to 2 dp. Now round 3.4547 straight to 2 dp — same answer? (double-rounding)
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 — which digit decides?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.46; 2.40 (keeping the final zero); 7,700,000 — deciding by the digit one place beyond the required accuracy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates instead of rounding: chops 3.4567 to 3.45 rather than 3.46
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the digit just past the cut (6 ≥ 5 → round up). Place 3.4567 between 3.45 and 3.46 on a number line to see which is nearer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The kept digits are correct but never rounded up when the next digit is 5 or more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero after a carry: writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, so it no longer shows 2 decimal places
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach rounding — note that '2 dp' means two digits after the point, so the carried result is 2.40; the 0 must stay.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer to 2 dp has only one decimal digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to the wrong precision — gives 1 dp when 2 dp is asked, or reads the wrong place for large numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the required place, then its decider digit; count decimal places explicitly. Reground with a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3.4567 comes back as 3.5, or the whole number is rounded to the wrong place.

responseLevels.gap: Truncates instead of rounding, or rounds to the wrong precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds decimals to any number of places and whole numbers to any place, handling carries and placeholder zeros, and avoids double-rounding.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds simple cases but drops carried placeholder zeros or slips on the required number of places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places. Round 2.397 to 2 decimal places. Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000.' Watch whether they round or chop, and what they do at the carry.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4567 distinguishes rounding from truncating (3.46 vs 3.45); 2.397 forces a carry that produces a placeholder zero the child must keep to show 2 dp (2.40, not 2.4); the whole-number item checks the same rule transfers to large places. Watching reveals which mechanism is running.

topic.description: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
evidence: State the value of each digit in 2.635 (2 ones, 6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths)
Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places (each place is ten times smaller)
Write a number given digit values (e.g. 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073)
topic.assessmentPrompt: In the number 4.378, can {{name}} tell you that the 7 represents 7 hundredths — not 7 tenths or 7 thousandths?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 recognise place value of digits in numbers with up to 3 decimal places; Y6 applies this to determine each digit's value.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 and 5.NBT.A.3a — understanding the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, with each place one tenth the place to its left.
• Operational details: For each digit, state its value as digit × place-unit (7 in 4.378 = 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths). Reinforce the ten-times-smaller relationship between adjacent decimal places. Reverse the task — given digit values, reconstruct the number — to prove flexible understanding and to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?' Tier B: 'Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places.' Tier C: 'Write the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths.'
bestPractices: Require each digit's value as digit × place-unit ('7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100'), not just its place name
Explicitly state and re-derive that each place is one tenth of the place to its left (the ÷10 chain through decimals)
Run the task in reverse — give digit values, reconstruct the numeral — to force placeholder-zero handling (0 tenths → 4.073)
Contrast identical digits in different places within one number (the two 3s' values differ) to separate face value from place value
Use a decimal place-value chart so each column's unit is explicit as the child reads a digit
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths with unit labels 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000
Digit-value cards: '7 → 7 hundredths → 0.07'
Thousandths grid showing each place as ten of the next-smaller
Reverse-build slots (digit-into-place) with a live numeral readout
commonMisconceptions: Naming the place but giving the wrong value (the 7 is 'in the hundredths' but stated as '7' or '0.7')
Reading the decimal part as one whole number (378) rather than digit-by-place values
Confusing tenths and hundredths (off-by-one place), especially with a leading zero
Dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing (writing 4.73 for 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths)
Believing adjacent places differ additively rather than by a factor of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths, 7 × 1/100 = 0.07). Learners state each digit's value as digit × place-unit, re-derive that each decimal place is one tenth of the place to its left, and reconstruct a numeral from given digit-values to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073). A key discrimination is that 3 tenths is worth more than 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.

activities.title: Reveal each digit's value (digit × place-unit)
feedback: If a learner gives just the digit or just the place name ('7' or 'hundredths'), ask them to finish the sentence '7 × 1/100 = ___' so the value is named, not only the place.
If they say the 7 is worth 7, rebuild the chart and read 4.378 aloud as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each digit to its fraction.
If they miscount by one column (calling the 7 tenths or thousandths), count columns aloud left-to-right from the point — tenths, hundredths, thousandths — landing deliberately on the 7.
Confirm the two 3s in 2.335 differ because one sits in the tenths column, worth ten times the adjacent hundredths column — separating face value from place value.
activities.rationale: Requiring value as digit × place-unit (not just the place name) and contrasting identical digits in adjacent columns directly targets the common error of naming the place but stating the wrong value, and separates face value from place value. An optional interactive form — tapping a digit to bloom its value with the column highlighted and ÷10/×10 arrows to neighbours — can make the ten-times relationship concrete, but a labelled chart with spoken/written values teaches the same idea.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Write or display a number to three decimal places, e.g. 4.378, above a place-value chart with columns labelled Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths and units 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000.
For each digit, say and write its value as digit × place-unit: the 7 is 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths = 0.07; the 8 is 8 × 1/1000 = 8 thousandths = 0.008.
State explicitly how adjacent places relate: the hundredths place is one tenth of the tenths place (÷10 moving right, ×10 moving left).

Within a single number containing two identical digits in adjacent decimal columns, e.g. 2.335 (2 ones, 3 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths), compare the two 3s and explain why their values differ (3 tenths = 0.3 versus 3 hundredths = 0.03) even though the digit is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is its face value times the unit of the column it sits in; adjacent decimal places differ by a factor of ten, not by addition, so the same digit can mean very different amounts.

activities.title: Reverse build: reconstruct the numeral from given values (placeholder zeros)
feedback: If a learner writes 4.73, point out that the 7 has slid from the hundredths column into the tenths column (and the 3 from thousandths into hundredths) — ask which column each digit now occupies and whether that matches the given values.

If they omit the zero, have them read both numbers aloud — 4.73 as '4 and 73 hundredths' and the correct 4.073 as '4 and 7 hundredths 3 thousandths' (73 thousandths) — to hear that these are different numbers.
Confirm success when they keep the 0 to hold the tenths column and can say why the zero is not optional.
activities.rationale: Running the task in reverse forces explicit placeholder-zero handling, which the forward 'name the value' task can hide. This addresses the documented error of dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing. A drag-and-assemble interface with a live numeral readout is one effective way to make the empty column visible, but the same learning occurs by writing digits into chart cells on paper.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Given a set of digit-values — 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths — place each into its column on a place-value chart and read off the numeral.
Write the resulting number: 4.073.
Deliberately try leaving the empty tenths column blank and read what you get: 4.73. Compare 4.073 with 4.73 and explain why they are different numbers.
Repeat with another set that includes a zero in a middle place (e.g. 3 ones, 0 tenths, 0 hundredths, 5 thousandths = 3.005) and justify each zero's job.
activities.intendedInsight: A placeholder zero is worth 0 itself, but it does real work by holding a column open; omitting a zero that comes before other digits shifts every later digit into the wrong place and produces a different number. Reconstruction proves flexible, two-way understanding of place value.

activities.title: Which is worth more — the smaller digit or the larger?
feedback: If a learner ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths, place 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line so the sizes of the chunks are visible.
If they say the 7 is worth more because it comes later (further right), re-anchor each digit to its fractional unit and compare the units, not the positions.
Confirm when they justify 3 tenths > 7 hundredths by comparing place-units rather than digits.
activities.rationale: This comparison is the discriminating task: it exposes 'bigger-digit-is-bigger-value' and 'later-is-larger' misconceptions and demands reasoning from place-units. A spoken, responsive discussion lets a mentor probe why the values differ; a 0–1 number line gives a concrete size check.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the value of the 3 and the 7 in 4.378: state the 3 is 3 tenths (0.3) and the 7 is 7 hundredths (0.07).
Decide which is worth more and justify it — the 3, because tenths are ten times bigger chunks than hundredths, so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.
Mark 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 number line to see that 3 tenths is a bigger portion than 7 hundredths.
Discuss: when 4.378 becomes 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's? Explain using the columns: both changed, since the 7 and 8 swapped between the hundredths and thousandths places.
activities.intendedInsight: Place, not face value, determines worth in a decimal: reasoning about the column must override the surface impression that the bigger digit is worth more or that a digit further right is larger.

constraints: Learners must state each digit's value as digit × place-unit (e.g. '7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100 = 0.07'), not only name the place.
Include the reverse reconstruction task; naming values forward alone can hide the placeholder-zero error, so reconstruction from values is needed to prove two-way understanding.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. 'value of the 3 in 2.635', 'reconstruct 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths = ___') can consolidate and check understanding but do not themselves build the place-unit link; pair them with construction and explanation.

A fixed labelled diagram with revealed per-digit values is a strong reference for the reveal step but cannot host the reverse-build that tests placeholder zeros, so it is a partial scaffold for this objective.

Optional interactive affordances (tap-to-reveal, drag value tiles into columns, live numeral readout, ÷10/×10 arrows) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; equivalent learning is possible with a paper chart and spoken reasoning.

When contrasting identical digits, use a number where the repeated digit appears in genuinely different places and state the correct factor between those places (adjacent columns = ten times; non-adjacent columns differ by a larger power of ten).
Checkpoint tiers: age-10 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?'; explain 'the relationship between adjacent decimal places'; write 'the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified in the original row and one (CCSS-M) was marked unverified; verification status was not re-checked here.

The original candidate's identical-digits example 3.303 contained three 3s (not two) and had a 'ten times' feedback that was false for its non-adjacent columns; it was replaced with 2.335, which has exactly two 3s in adjacent columns (tenths and hundredths) so the ten-times relationship holds.

In this independent review, activity 2's zero-dropping feedback was corrected: both read-aloud phrases previously named 4.073, so the intended contrast failed; the feedback now reads 4.73 as '73 hundredths' versus 4.073 as '7 hundredths 3 thousandths'.

Original diagnostic/answer text uses 4.378 with digits 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths; one checkpoint/compare example uses 2.635 (6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths). These are internally consistent and preserved as distinct examples.

The original 'possible'/'poor' fit framing (conversation and 3D) was converted to pedagogical notes: dialogue is retained as a genuine teaching option for the comparison task rather than dismissed; no universal 'static image cannot teach' or '3D adds nothing' claim is asserted.

probeDeeper: Which is worth more, the 3 or the 7 — and why isn't it just 'the bigger digit'?
What is the value of the 8 in 4.378, and how does it relate to the 7?
Write me a number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths and 3 thousandths.
If I change 4.378 to 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's?
assess.correctAnswer: The 7 represents 7 hundredths (0.07); the 3 represents 3 tenths (0.3). The 7's place is worth ten times less than the 3's place, so the 3 is worth more even though 7 is the larger digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number — 'the 7 is worth 7', treating .378 like three hundred seventy-eight.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the places with a decimal place-value chart; read 4.378 as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each column to a fraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Values are stated as bare digits with no fractional place named.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place by one — calls the 7 'tenths' or 'thousandths' instead of hundredths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns aloud left-to-right from the point (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), landing deliberately on the 7; do not just supply the name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct idea of fractional places but the label is off by one column.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer/later-is-larger — thinks the 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes further right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line; show tenths are bigger chunks than hundredths so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths.

responseLevels.gap: Reads decimal digits as whole numbers or cannot name fractional places.
responseLevels.full: Names each digit's fractional value, states the ten-times relationship between adjacent places, and correctly judges 3 tenths > 7 hundredths with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Names 7 hundredths correctly but defaults to 'bigger digit = bigger value' when comparing with the 3, or is off by one place under pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the number 4.378, what is the value of the 7? And how does that compare with the value of the 3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads decimal place value names 7 hundredths and sees the 3 is worth more despite being the smaller digit — the reasoning must override the surface 'bigger digit'. A child reading the decimal as a whole number, or miscounting places, or applying longer-is-larger gives a different answer and a revealing reason.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decimal place value (age 11+)
topic.description: Round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
evidence: Round numbers to a given number of decimal places
Round numbers to a given number of significant figures
Choose an appropriate degree of accuracy for a given context
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a measurement like 12.3746 km to 2 decimal places (12.37 km) or 3 significant figures (12.4 km) — and explain when each level of precision is appropriate?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–13 — round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy (e.g. to a number of decimal places or significant figures).'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); significant figures are not a named CCSS strand but appear in science/measurement and high-school modelling (N.Q). Emphasis in US is on appropriate precision.
• Operational details: Extend nearness-based rounding to (a) a stated number of decimal places and (b) significant figures. The key new idea is IDENTIFYING significant figures — the first significant figure is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros are not significant; trailing/placeholder zeros hold magnitude. Round using the digit AFTER the last significant/required place (midpoint rule), then restore place value with zeros (2 sig figs of 34,700 → 35,000). Choose accuracy to suit context.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures.' Tier C: 'Round 34,750 to 2 sig figs and explain why the answer needs its zeros.'
bestPractices: Teach significant-figure identification first: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder zeros preserve magnitude
Keep rounding as a nearness/midpoint decision, then RESTORE place value with the right zeros (35,000, not 35)
Contrast dp and sig figs on the same number so pupils see they can differ (0.004982 to 2 dp = 0.00 vs to 2 sf = 0.0050)
Attend to the round-up cascade and trailing zeros that record precision (2.988 to 2 dp → 2.99; 1.998 to 2 dp → 2.00)
Link accuracy to context — choose dp/sf appropriate to the measurement's precision
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart marking the rounding place and the deciding next digit
Number line with the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint
Significant-figure highlighter (first non-zero digit onward)
Side-by-side dp-vs-sf comparison of the same number
commonMisconceptions: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0049 seen as 4 sig figs)
Dropping the placeholder zeros after rounding to sig figs (35,000 written as 35)
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Truncating instead of rounding, or double-rounding through intermediate digits
Losing the trailing zero that records the rounded precision (2.90 written as 2.9 when 2 dp is required)

learn.summary: For ages 11–13: round numbers and measures to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures, and choose an accuracy appropriate to context. The central new skill is identifying significant figures (first sig fig = first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder/trailing zeros do real work holding magnitude and recording precision), then making a single nearness/midpoint rounding decision and restoring place value with zeros (34,750 to 2 sf → 35,000, not 35).

activities.title: Highlight the significant figures, round once, rebuild the size
feedback: If a learner writes 34,750 to 2 sf as 35, ask them to say the value aloud — 35 is thirty-five, not thirty-five thousand; the thousands zeros are load-bearing placeholders.
If leading zeros are counted (treating 0.004982 as having significant leading zeros), re-establish that counting begins at the first non-zero digit (the 4); leading zeros only hold place.

If a learner rounds digit-by-digit (e.g. 3.1449 to 2 dp: 3.1449 → 3.145 → 3.15), show that only the digit immediately after the required place matters (here the 4), so the decision is made once and gives 3.14; chain rounding made the answer drift to 3.15.
If the trailing zero is lost (0.0050 written as 0.005, or 2.90 to 2 dp written as 2.9), point out the final zero records the rounded precision and is required.
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal here is identifying significant figures and restoring place value, which is the step learners find new and error-prone. Making the highlighting, the single deciding digit, and the zero-restoration visible is intended to target the conflation between dp and sf and the 'drop the zeros' error. A live sig-fig highlighter, a number-line midpoint marker, and a dp/sf toggle on the same number are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
learnerActions: Take a number such as 34,750 and decide to round it to 2 significant figures.
Mark the counted significant digits (the 3 and the 4), confirming you start at the first non-zero digit.

Identify the single deciding digit immediately after the last required place (the 7) and place the number on a number line between its two candidate rounded values (34,000 and 35,000) and their midpoint (34,500); decide the round-up in one step.
Reassemble the answer as 35,000, writing in the placeholder zeros that keep the number in the thousands — do NOT stop at 35.

Now take 0.004982 and round to 2 significant figures: cross out the leading zeros as 'not significant', count the 4 and 9, apply the deciding digit (8) so 49 rounds up to 50, and write 0.0050 — keeping the front zeros for magnitude and the trailing zero for precision.
Repeat 0.004982 rounded to 2 decimal places (= 0.00) and place both answers side by side to see that dp and sf give genuinely different results.
activities.intendedInsight: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit; zeros can be placeholders that hold a number's size or trailing zeros that record precision, so they cannot simply be dropped. Rounding is one nearness decision based on the next digit, after which place value must be restored.

activities.title: Contrast decimal places with significant figures on one number
feedback: If both methods give the same answer, check where the first significant figure is. With the same count (e.g. 2 dp and 2 sf), the answers agree when the first non-zero digit is in the tenths place (e.g. 0.364 → 0.36 both ways). They differ for numbers with leading zeros after the decimal point (0.004982) or with digits before the decimal point (3.14159, 47,320).
If a learner says the rules are 'the same', show 0.004982: 2 dp = 0.00 but 2 sf = 0.0050.
activities.rationale: Contrasting dp and sf on the same number is intended to address the named dp-vs-sf confusion. Presenting the comparison explicitly may help learners see that the two instructions are not interchangeable.
learnerActions: Pick a single number (e.g. 0.004982) and round it both to 2 decimal places and to 2 significant figures.
Record the two answers side by side (0.00 vs 0.0050) and write a sentence explaining why they differ.
Do the same for a large number such as 47,320: to 2 sf it is 47,000 (zeros needed), and note how that differs from a decimal-place instruction.
State in your own words when leading zeros are ignored and when zeros must be kept.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal places and significant figures are different rules: dp counts from the decimal point, while sf counts from the first non-zero digit. The difference is most striking with leading zeros and with large numbers that need placeholder zeros, but they also differ for ordinary numbers (3.14159 is 3.14 to 2 dp and 3.1 to 2 sf). The same number can give very different rounded values under each.

activities.title: Choose and justify an appropriate degree of accuracy
feedback: If the justification ignores magnitude, prompt: does your rounded answer still describe roughly the same quantity as the original?
If a learner cannot name the deciding digit, revisit that only the digit immediately after the required place determines the round.
activities.rationale: The standards emphasise choosing accuracy appropriate to context (US N.Q; UK 'appropriate degree of accuracy'). Requiring spoken or written justification is intended to build reasoning beyond procedural execution. A short mentor-style challenge can surface the 'drop the zeros' and 'leading zeros count' errors during teaching; this is one useful format, not the only way to teach the procedure.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
Rounding to accuracy builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); appropriate precision is emphasised in high-school modelling (N.Q).
learnerActions: Given a context such as measuring a room's length, decide whether rounding to 2 decimal places or 2 significant figures is more appropriate, and explain why.
Explain to a partner (or in writing) why 47,320 to 2 sf needs its zeros on the end but 47 to 2 sf would not.
Respond to a challenge like: 'You rounded 34,750 to 2 significant figures and wrote 35 — convince me that is the right size.'
Justify which single digit decided each of your roundings and why the remaining digits did not matter.
activities.intendedInsight: Accuracy should suit the precision of the measurement or context, and learners should be able to justify both the rounded value's size and the choice of dp vs sf.

activities.title: Consolidation: quick-check rounding problems
feedback: For 0.004621 to 2 sf, confirm the answer is 0.0046 (the 4 and 6 are the sig figs); 0.00 would come from confusing sf with 2 dp.
For 47,320 to 2 sf, confirm 47,000; an answer of 47 has lost its magnitude.
For 1.998 to 2 dp, note the cascade carries to 2.00 and the trailing zeros must be written.
For 0.004982 to 2 sf, confirm 0.0050; the 0.00 option reflects the dp-vs-sf confusion.
activities.rationale: Short closed-response items can consolidate and check outcomes efficiently, including with a deliberate distractor exposing the dp/sf confusion. Such items check outcomes rather than build the identification skill, so they suit practice after the construction activities rather than instead of them.
learnerActions: Round 3.14159 to 2 decimal places (answer 3.14).
Round 0.004621 to 2 significant figures (answer 0.0046).
Round 47,320 to 2 significant figures (answer 47,000).
Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures, choosing from answers that include the dp-confusion value 0.00 so you can check you avoid it (the correct value is 0.0050).
Round 2.988 to 2 dp (→ 2.99, a simple round-up) and 1.998 to 2 dp (→ 2.00, where the round-up carries through several places and the trailing zeros must be written).
activities.intendedInsight: After building the identification skill, learners can reliably apply dp and sf rounding, including the round-up cascade and placeholder/trailing zeros, in short targeted items.

constraints: Teach significant-figure identification before rounding to sf: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit, leading zeros never count, and placeholder/trailing zeros hold magnitude and record precision.
Treat rounding as a single nearness/midpoint decision using only the digit immediately after the required place; avoid digit-by-digit chain rounding, which can make the answer drift.
Always restore place value with zeros after rounding large numbers to sf (35,000 not 35; 47,000 not 47) and keep trailing zeros that record precision (2.90, 0.0050).
Contrast dp and sf on the same number so learners see the rules diverge, especially on leading zeros and large magnitudes.
Closed-response/quick-check items check outcomes and do not, on their own, build significant-figure identification; use them to consolidate after construction work, not instead of it.
A single static worked example illustrates one case but cannot cover arbitrary numbers or let a learner test the dp-vs-sf divergence interactively; use it as a reference, not the whole task.

The legacy row's claim that '3D adds nothing' to this one-dimensional symbolic task was removed as an unsupported universal; 3D was simply not adopted as a format here, without asserting it can never help.

probeDeeper: Which single digit decided each rounding, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is 0.0046 to 2sf, not 0.00 — which zeros count and which don't?
Why does 47,320 to 2sf need the zeros on the end but 47 to 2sf wouldn't?
For measuring a room, would you round the length to 2 decimal places or 2 sig figs — why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts leading zeros as significant figures — rounds 0.004621 to 2sf as 0.00 or 0.0046 treated as 4 sf.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that significant figures start at the first non-zero digit (the 4), so the 4 and 6 are the two sig figs; leading zeros only hold place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Significant-figure count starts at the decimal point or at the first zero, not the first non-zero digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chain / digit-by-digit rounding — rounds 3.14159 stepwise (→3.1416→3.142→3.14) or rounds each digit in turn.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round in one step: look only at the digit immediately after the required place (the 1 in the thousandths) and decide once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Multiple intermediate roundings appear; the final answer sometimes drifts (e.g. 3.15).

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops digits without placeholder zeros for large numbers — rounds 47,320 to 2sf as 47 instead of 47,000.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the two significant digits (4 and 7) but preserve place with zeros so the value stays in the ten-thousands; check the size is still reasonable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded large number loses its magnitude (answer is 47, not 47,000).

responseLevels.gap: Confuses sig figs with decimal places, counts leading zeros, or drops magnitude on large numbers.
responseLevels.full: Rounds accurately to a specified number of decimal places and significant figures, handles leading/trailing zeros, and chooses an appropriate degree of accuracy for a context with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds to decimal places correctly but is unreliable on significant figures with leading or trailing zeros.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Round these, showing your steps. (1) 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. (2) 0.004621 to 2 significant figures. (3) 47,320 to 2 significant figures.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch which digit the child treats as significant and how they handle the deciding digit. Decimal-place rounding and significant-figure rounding pull apart on leading zeros (task 2) and on large numbers needing placeholder zeros (task 3); a child conflating the two rules, counting leading zeros as significant, or chain-rounding will produce revealing errors.
